document_name: Семінар «Штучний інтелект у дії: практичні рекомендації для публічного сектору та закладів освіти»
body:
The goal of the event is to promote a responsible approach to the implementation and use of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies in public administration and higher education institutions by presenting practical recommendations for public servants, educators, students, and academic staff.

On 19 June, a seminar titled “Artificial Intelligence in Action: Practical Recommendations for the Public Sector and Educational Institutions” was held. The event was organised by the Higher School in cooperation with the National Agency of Civil Service of Ukraine (NACS), the Ministry of Digital Transformation, and the Igor Sikorsky Kyiv Polytechnic Institute (NTUU “KPI”).
The seminar brought together nearly 5,000 public servants, educators, students, and academic staff to discuss the challenges and opportunities related to the implementation of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies. The focus was on practical recommendations for their responsible use.
Key highlights of the event included presentations of the Guide on the Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence for Public Servants and the Recommendations for Implementing Artificial Intelligence Technologies in Higher Education Institutions. Both documents are intended to serve as guidelines for the effective, safe, and ethical implementation of AI in the public sector and the education system.
Additionally, the seminar featured a masterclass on the principles of how artificial intelligence technologies function.

category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
title: Towards the Food Factory of the Future
body:
Towards the Food Factory of the Future is an initiative led by Flanders’ FOOD that aims to drive the digital and sustainable transformation of the agri-food industry in Flanders. By bringing together research institutions, technology providers, and food manufacturers, the initiative fosters collaboration to enhance automation, AI-driven quality control, and energy-efficient production processes. It supports food companies in adopting cutting-edge digital technologies, such as machine learning

Towards the Food Factory of the Future is a roadmap by Flanders’ FOOD to modernize the agri-food sector in Flanders. It connects producers, researchers, and technology providers to make food production smarter, more sustainable, and more people-focused. The initiative targets four areas: better quality control through sensors and data, digital automation, circular use of resources, and workforce skills. Through projects and partnerships, it aims to especially help SMEs test and adopt tools like AI, machine learning, and energy-efficient systems.

category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
title: TiNAI (Tamil Nadu Land Use Information System) (Subnational: Tamil Nadu State)
body:
TiNAI (Tamil Nadu Land Use Information System) is an AI-enabled geospatial and Digital Twin platform designed to support evidence-based land-use planning. It uses artificial intelligence to analyse multi-sector data and generate clear insights that help policymakers understand climate, urban, and environmental challenges. The platform was created to address fragmented data and improve coordinated, transparent decision-making across sectors.

TiNAI (Tamil Nadu Land Use Information System) was developed to address a persistent research–policy disconnect in land-use governance. Although large volumes of spatial, environmental, and sectoral data existed across departments, they remained fragmented, limiting cross-sector interpretation and evidence-based planning. TiNAI responds to this challenge by integrating multi-sector datasets into a unified geospatial Digital Twin platform supported by artificial intelligence, enabling holistic analysis of land, climate, water, energy, agriculture, forests, disaster risks, and urban systems.

The initiative aims to strengthen scientific decision-making by transforming complex spatial datasets into interpretable insights for policymakers. Through AI-assisted pattern analysis, KPI synthesis, and scenario exploration, the platform supports fiscal planning, resource optimisation, environmental sustainability, and climate resilience. TiNAI includes thematic modules such as Land Use and Land Cover (LULC), climate indicators (temperature trends, rainfall, heat stress), forest monitoring, renewable energy suitability (solar and wind potential), disaster risk (landslides, forest fires), coastal vulnerability, agriculture trends, water resource analytics, and urban growth dynamics. These modules are accessible through interactive maps, dashboards, and analytical tools that enable multi-dimensional assessment.

Since its initial development as a land-use information system, TiNAI has evolved into an integrated AI-enabled spatial intelligence and Digital Twin architecture. The platform has progressively expanded its modules, analytical tools, and key performance indicators, while strengthening interdepartmental data integration. Its adoption in planning workflows demonstrates its role in supporting fiscal allocation and identifying strategic development opportunities. Looking ahead, TiNAI is expected to institutionalise cross-sector data integration further by incorporating health, housing, municipal, and additional statistical datasets. This expansion will enhance monitoring of Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), disaster risk reduction frameworks, and climate resilience metrics. With an open, scalable architecture, the platform has potential for replication across other states or regions seeking integrated, AI-driven land and resource governance systems.

category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
title: The swedish Digitalisation Strategy 2025–2030
document_name: Sveriges digitaliseringsstrategi 2025-2030
body:
AI is part of the cross-cutting themes throughout the entire strategy and are integrated across all five strategic areas - digital skills, private sector, public administration, public welfare, and connectivity.

1. Digitalisation of the private sector - AI is highlighted as a key technology for strengthening companies’ capacity for innovation, competitiveness, security, and sustainability. The strategy emphasizes the importance of collaboration between the government, businesses, and organizations to promote the use of AI in the business sector.
2. Public administration - AI will be used to streamline digital services within the public sector. The aim is to create user-friendly, secure, and reliable services through AI- and data-driven development.
3. Public welfare - AI is expected to contribute to more preventive, person-centered, and location-independent services. The goal is to improve quality of life for citizens and the working environment for staff.

category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
title: The Stargate Project
body:
The Stargate Project is a US-based AI infrastructure initiative established by OpenAI, SoftBank, and Oracle, with an investment commitment of $500 billion over four years. Launched in January 2025, it aims to build large-scale AI data centres across the United States, beginning in Texas. The initiative targets nearly 7 gigawatts of planned capacity and over 25,000 on-site jobs.

The Stargate Project was announced in January 2025 at the White House alongside President Trump, as part of a broader effort to spur investment in American AI infrastructure. The initial equity funders are SoftBank, OpenAI, Oracle, and MGX, with SoftBank holding financial responsibility and OpenAI holding operational responsibility. Masayoshi Son serves as chairman. Key technology partners include Arm, Microsoft, NVIDIA, Oracle, and OpenAI. The project intends to deploy $100 billion immediately, with the remaining investment phased over four years.
Five new US data centre sites have been announced under Stargate: three developed by Oracle in Shackelford County (Texas), Doña Ana County (New Mexico), and Wisconsin; one by SoftBank in Lordstown (Ohio); and one in Milam County (Texas) developed with SB Energy. These join the flagship campus in Abilene, Texas, already operational on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. The five sites were selected following a review of over 300 proposals from more than 30 states. Combined with ongoing projects with CoreWeave, total planned capacity reaches nearly 7 gigawatts, with over $400 billion in investment over the next three years.
The project is expected to create over 25,000 on-site jobs and an important number of additional jobs across the United States. On the infrastructure side, Oracle began delivering the first NVIDIA GB200 racks in June 2025, with early training and inference workloads already underway. The initiative is framed as serving both economic and national security purposes, aiming to secure American leadership in AI and provide strategic capability to protect the national security of America and its allies. Additional US sites are expected to be announced as the initial $500 billion commitment is met and surpassed.

category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
title: The Interministerial AI Assistant
document_name: L'Assistant IA interministériel
body:
The AI Assistant is a secure chat tool for public servants, designed to help them write, summarize and find information faster. It was developed to give government teams an easy and trusted way to use generative AI in their daily work. The goal is to improve efficiency while reducing duplicated efforts across ministries.

The AI Assistant is a secure, government-wide chat tool designed for public servants. It helps users draft and improve text, summarize long documents, and answer day-to-day questions more quickly, while keeping a clear focus on safe and responsible use in a public administration context. The initiative was developed to address a growing need across ministries: many teams were exploring generative AI, but often with separate tools and duplicated technical efforts. By providing a shared assistant, the government aims to make AI easier to access for public servants, reduce fragmentation, and support productivity gains in routine tasks.

In 2025, the AI Assistant was piloted across 8 ministries with up to 10,000 volunteer users. It helped public servants draft, summarize and search information faster, supporting everyday work and reducing the need for separate ministry-by-ministry tools. Impact has been tracked through user adoption (registrations and active use), usage statistics (queries, features used), and qualitative feedback from pilot administrations. Future results are expected to include wider adoption, more time saved on routine tasks, and improved consistency and security in how generative AI is used across government.

Key challenges included ensuring strong security and compliance for government use, scaling computing capacity cost-effectively, and building trust among users. Another risk was fragmentation, with ministries developing separate assistants and duplicating effort. These challenges were addressed by hosting the service on secure infrastructure, monitoring usage to manage costs, and designing the Assistant as a shared tool that can evolve with ministry needs. Lessons learned include the importance of starting with clear, high-value everyday tasks (writing, summarising), providing user guidance and support, and collecting feedback early to improve the service. Success depends on reliable performance, strong governance, and gradual scaling based on real adoption.

Over time, the AI Assistant is expected to expand its user base and offer more advanced features, including stronger connections to trusted public information sources and the ability to work with internal document collections. It is designed to scale progressively, in line with security requirements and real usage needs, while remaining interoperable with other government digital tools.

category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
title: The Government strengthens AI skills among professionals and students
document_name: Regeringen stärker AI-kunskaper hos yrkesverksamma och studenter
body:
AI is increasingly affecting everyday life. Professionals need up and reskilling in AI. Therefore, seven higher education institutions have been assigned to develop short courses with a focus on AI.

The Government strengthens AI skills among professionals and students.AI is increasingly affecting everyday life. Professionals need up and reskilling in AI. Therefore, seven higher education institutions have been assigned to develop short courses with a focus on AI.According to the AI Commission, Sweden is lagging behind internationally in the field of AI, despite the fact that there is good basic education on innovation. AI will affect everyday life more in the future, and professional roles may change, among other things, because of increased automation. This means that those who work as, for example, nurses, teachers, or engineers may need to supplement their previous education to better meet the requirements for competence that are set because of the development of AI.Knowledge about AI among professionals can be increased through short, skill-developing courses, among other things. The Government is therefore investing so that seven higher education institutions can develop courses with a focus on AI for professionals in various sectors.Higher education institutions must report on the development of AI in education. Sweden's students need to be well prepared for future professional life and understand the opportunities and challenges of AI tools. Therefore, the higher education institutions are tasked with reporting on how they work with the development of the educational offerings regarding AI, and efforts to integrate AI elements in the courses where it is relevant. The assignment is in accordance with the recommendations of the AI Commission.

title: The First Regional Forum on the Implementation of Artificial Intelligence
document_name: Перший регіональний форум про впровадження штучного інтелекту
body:
The First Regional AI Forum in Odesa gathered educators, civil servants, and digital experts to explore the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in education and public administration. The initiative aims to promote responsible and ethical AI implementation at the local level. More than 150 participants from the region discussed practical tools, human rights safeguards, and developed skills for effective AI use.

The First Regional AI Forum, held in Odesa, was launched to address the growing need for responsible and effective adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) at the local level in Ukraine. The initiative responds to the increasing relevance of AI in public administration and education, and the necessity to ensure that AI technologies are introduced in a way that respects human rights, promotes trust, and supports inclusive digital transformation.
Organised by the Ministry of Digital Transformation of Ukraine and the Ministry of Education and Science of Ukraine, the forum brought together over 150 educators, public servants, digital transformation officers, and community leaders.
Objectives:
It served as a regional platform to present national and international frameworks on ethical AI use and offered practical tools for implementing AI in schools and public institutions. A key feature was the presentation of recommendations on AI use in education and civil service, including the Council of Europe’s HUDERIA methodology for assessing AI’s impact on human rights and democracy.
Impact:
This forum marked the beginning of a broader effort to institutionalise AI education and awareness at the regional level in Ukraine. Future plans include expanding the CDTO Campus AI programmes, scaling the HUDERIA methodology to more regions, and replicating the forum format in other parts of the country. The initiative helps build a foundation for informed and ethical AI transformation, with direct benefits for public administration, education, and local communities."

title: TWIST
body:
This initiative, running between 2025 and 2031, is aimed at strengthening innovation within existing companies and adapting to industrial and technological shifts. It emphasises supporting AI research and industrial applications through strategic investments, with a specific focus on AI, quantum technologies, and semiconductors. The first call for projects targets AI R&D.

The TWIST programme (2025–2031) is aimed at helping Czech companies adapt to rapid technological shifts. It focuses on strengthening innovation in key fields such as AI, quantum technologies, and semiconductors. The first call supports AI research and development, giving firms the chance to secure subsidies of up to CZK 30 million for projects that often involve cooperation with SMEs or research organisations.
Its main goal is to raise the innovation capacity of established companies and ensure they can compete in strategic technologies critical for long-term growth. The programme will gradually expand, with future calls expected to cover semiconductors and quantum projects, backed by significant state funding and linked to national infrastructure such as Digital Innovation Hubs.

title: Swedish participation in LUMI hosted by CSC in Finland
body:
LUMI is the fastest supercomputer in Europe and part of the EuroHPC Joint Undertaking.

Sweden participates in the LUMI supercomputing infrastructure, hosted by CSC in Finland, to provide researchers with access to one of Europe’s most powerful high-performance computing (HPC) systems. LUMI, the fastest supercomputer in Europe, is part of the EuroHPC Joint Undertaking, which aims to strengthen European HPC capabilities and advance research and innovation across the continent. 
The initiative addresses the growing demand for computational resources for data-intensive scientific research, including artificial intelligence, climate modeling, genomics, and materials science. By leveraging LUMI, Swedish researchers gain access to cutting-edge computational power, enabling complex simulations, AI model training, and advanced analytics that would not be feasible on national infrastructure alone.
Sweden’s participation is coordinated through the National Academic Infrastructure for Supercomputing Sweden (NAISS), which facilitates access for universities, research institutes, and other partners. Researchers can submit proposals to use LUMI for collaborative projects, ensuring that the system supports a wide range of scientific and technological applications.

title: Strategy for the Use of AI in the Judiciary
body:
It sets out a comprehensive vision for the use of AI systems in the judiciary, along with the necessary action plans and measures to achieve this vision. The strategy aims to harness the opportunities offered by AI for the judiciary at federal and state levels, while taking due account of the associated risks and limitations. Notably, the strategy anticipates providing forward-looking support for judicial and administrative processes, enhancing access to justice, and promoting innovation in AI.

The federal government and the states have jointly developed a strategy for the use of artificial intelligence in the judiciary. This strategy was adopted in June 2025. It sets out a comprehensive vision for the use of AI systems in the judiciary, along with the necessary action plans and measures to achieve this vision. The strategy aims to harness the opportunities offered by AI for the judiciary at federal and state levels, while taking due account of the associated risks and limitations. Notably, the strategy anticipates providing forward-looking support for judicial and administrative processes, enhancing access to justice, and promoting innovation in AI.
 Furthermore, the strategy aims to develop a uniform interpretation of the AI Act throughout the federal states and states in order to ensure its coherent and effective implementation within the judiciary. At the same time, it seeks to ensure the AI Act's requirements are fully implemented throughout the judicial system.
 Through the joint strategy and an AI platform, AI solutions initially developed by individual states within the framework of specific projects will be made available for reuse by all states and the federal government in accordance with the EfA principle ('Develop once, use everywhere'). This approach is intended to improve cost-efficiency and increase the pace of innovation within the judiciary.
 According to the current timetable, the conceptual implementation of the AI Strategy is expected to be completed by the end of 2026.

category: Regulations, guidelines and standards
title: Spanish AI regulatory sandbox pilot guidelines for the European Artificial Intelligence Act
body:
The set of 16 guidelines is an initiative developed within the Spanish AI regulatory sandbox pilot to support implementation of the European Artificial Intelligence Act. It includes introductory, technical and checklist materials providing practical recommendations to help organisations comply with regulatory obligations. The guides are non-binding, aligned with EU requirements, structured across thematic areas, and subject to ongoing review and updates as standards and EU guidance evolve.

The initiative consists of a structured set of 16 guidelines developed within the Spanish AI regulatory sandbox pilot, involving participants, technical assistance providers, competent national authorities and an expert advisory group. It is intended to support organisations in applying the European Artificial Intelligence Act by providing practical guidance aligned with regulatory requirements, while remaining non-binding. The materials are designed to contribute to a broader process in which European Commission guidelines will ensure consistent application of the regulation across Member States.
The guidelines are organised into three main components: two introductory guides that explain key concepts, definitions, risk levels and examples; a series of technical guides covering specific requirements for AI systems; and a checklist manual that supports self-assessment. The technical guides address areas explicitly set out in the AI Act, including conformity assessment, quality management, risk management, human oversight, data and data governance, transparency, accuracy, robustness, cybersecurity, records, post-market monitoring, serious incident handling and technical documentation. A complementary set of checklists and examples is also provided.
The initiative outlines measures and procedures that providers and deployers can use to meet obligations, including monitoring systems, documentation practices, reporting processes and operational controls across the lifecycle of AI systems. The inclusion of a checklist manual and self-assessment elements indicates a focus on operationalising compliance in a structured and repeatable way.
The materials are subject to continuous evaluation and periodic updates in line with evolving standards and guidance from the European Commission.

title: South Korea National AI GPU Infrastructure Initiative
body:
South Korea's Ministry of Science and ICT (MSIT) is investing approximately KRW 1.46 trillion (around USD 1.1 billion) to procure 13,000 high-performance GPUs, distributed across three cloud service providers — Naver Cloud, NHN Cloud, and Kakao. Announced in July 2025, the initiative aims to expand domestic AI computing infrastructure, reduce reliance on overseas resources, and support AI research, large-scale model training, and national AI initiatives.

South Korea's Ministry of Science and ICT (MSIT) is investing approximately KRW 1.46 trillion (around USD 1.1 billion) to procure 13,000 high-performance GPUs as part of a national effort to expand domestic AI computing infrastructure and reduce reliance on overseas resources. The initiative is part of South Korea's broader strategy to accelerate AI innovation and strengthen the competitiveness of local technology companies. Following the allocation of a supplementary budget in May 2025, the ministry conducted a month-long selection process involving public bidding, proposal assessments, and on-site inspections, before selecting Naver Cloud, NHN Cloud, and Kakao as project operators.
NHN Cloud manages the largest allocation of 7,656 B200 units with water-cooling systems, of which 6,120 are government-owned and organised into 510-node and 255-node clusters. Naver Cloud oversees 3,056 H200 units, with 2,296 allocated to the government in clusters aimed at universities and research institutions, with full-scale services expected by end of 2025. Kakao deploys 2,424 B200 GPUs, with 2,040 government-operated in a single 255-node cluster, with partial beta services planned before year-end. Over 10,000 GPUs in total are allocated for government-led projects, with remaining units supporting the operational needs of the three providers.
To ensure equitable access, the ministry and operators will establish a unified online GPU support platform through which universities, research institutions, and industry players can apply, with allocations determined by proposal evaluations and project priorities. Idle resources will be dynamically reassigned to maximise utilisation. Once fully operational, the infrastructure will underpin the government's AI Foundation Model Project and other national initiatives. Minister Bae Kyung-hoon described the project as a first step toward building "an AI superhighway" and establishing South Korea as a global AI leader.

title: Social Media Analytics for Water Sector Issues
body:
Social Media Analysis is an AI system that automatically classifies content from X (formerly Twitter) to support the Water Authority’s leadership. It replaces a 4-hour daily manual process with automated sentiment, location, and problem classification. By feeding daily insights into the Observatory Dashboard, it enables higher management to understand citizen feedback and service reports instantly, significantly improving digital transparency and public engagement.

The Social Media Analysis initiative was developed to bridge the gap between massive public discourse on social media and actionable institutional intelligence. Previously, monitoring citizen feedback on X was a labor-intensive manual process requiring roughly four hours daily. This initiative leverages AI and machine learning to automate this workflow, processing data through Google Cloud BigQuery and visualising results via Looker Enterprise. By doing so, it resolves the issue of "information overload" and ensures that critical beneficiary reports are never missed. 
The primary objective is to transform raw social data into structured business insights through several specialised layers: Spam Guard: Uses NLP to filter out advertisements, water filter promotions, and redundant bot replies. Multi-Layer Classification: The system assigns sentiment (Positive, Neutral, Negative), extracts geographic data (City and Neighbourhood), and maps posts to approximately seven business-defined problem categories. Summary Reporting: The data points are synthesised and integrated into the "Observatory Dashboard," providing a single source of truth for leadership and higher management, highlighting emerging trends and public perception. 
The initiative is currently fully operational and success is maintained through a combination of automated infrastructure monitoring on Google Cloud Run and continuous human-in-the-loop validation to ensure the model remains aligned with local context and evolving dialect. Future evolution of the tool is focused on horizontal and functional scaling. The roadmap includes expanding analysis to platforms like Facebook, LinkedIn and Instagram, as well as incorporating video and Reels content analysis. Additionally, we aim to integrate the system directly with CRM platforms to automatically trigger service tickets from social media complaints, further closing the loop between citizen feedback and operational response.

category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
title: ServetIA: AI Research Platform for the Spanish Prime Minister’s Office
document_name: ServetIA: Plataforma de Investigación con IA para el Gabinete de Presidencia del Gobierno de España
body:
ServetIA is an AI-powered research platform developed for the Spanish Prime Minister’s Office to help government staff conduct faster, more thorough policy research. The tool uses large language models with source verification to provide reliable, evidence-based outputs. It was developed to reduce the time public servants spend on information gathering and improve the quality of briefing materials supporting government decision-making. ServetIA is in Beta.

ServetIA is a custom-built AI research platform developed within the PresidencIA programme to support analysis and information retrieval in the Spanish Prime Minister’s Office. Named after Miguel Servet, the Spanish polymath and pioneer of scientific inquiry, ServetIA embodies the same spirit of rigorous, evidence-based investigation applied to modern governance. Government advisors in the Prime Minister’s Office routinely research complex policy topics, prepare briefing documents, and synthesise information from multiple sources under tight deadlines. Traditional methods are slow and resource intensive. Off-the-shelf AI tools raise concerns about data privacy, accuracy, and suitability for sensitive government contexts. ServetIA bridges this gap. Built on large language model technology, it provides a complete suite of tools for research powered with AI, where staff can pose policy questions and receive structured, source-referenced responses, conduct literature review, reach consensus and generate drafts with verified citation. The platform prioritises “grounding”, ensuring outputs are anchored in verifiable sources rather than generating unsupported claims. This responds directly to the government’s need for reliable, citable information. A deep research module handles comprehensive, multi-source investigations that go beyond simple question-answering. The platform is in Beta, deployed and accessible at servetia.eu, with iterative refinements based on government user feedback. Development follows human-centred design: features are prioritised through user interviews and observation during structured Discovery phases within the Prime Minister’s Office. Technical implementation leverages both cloud-based and on-premises models. For sensitive use cases, the platform enables the use of local LLMs instead of Cloud, using open-weight models that can run on local infrastructure, supporting AI sovereignty objectives. This hybrid approach balances performance with data security requirements of a head-of-government institution. ServetIA complements a broader ecosystem within the PresidencIA programme, demonstrating how purpose-built AI tools, developed with government-specific requirements for security, accuracy, and usability, can enhance core government functions. Its architecture is modular and transferable, can be adapted to other departments and ministries, and its methodology, combining user research, iterative prototyping, and security-first design, provides a replicable model for AI tool development in government settings across countries. The tool augments rather than replaces human judgment, positioning AI as a support layer for public servants.

title: Sectoral Workforce Solutions Program (AI-focused projects)
body:
A dedicated CAD 50M federal contribution programme funding sectoral organisations to develop and deliver skills training for workers in industries potentially disrupted by AI, helping them reskill and adapt to an AI-transformed labour market.

The AI stream of the Sectoral Workforce Solutions Program (SWSP) was announced in Canada's Budget 2024, allocating CAD 50M over four years (2025–26 to 2028–29) to support workers who may be impacted by AI through new skills training in potentially disrupted sectors and communities. The SWSP itself was originally established in Budget 2021 with CAD 960M over three years and has since invested over CAD 560M across 55 projects, supporting training for over 115,000 participants. The programme is administered by Employment and Social Development Canada (ESDC) and funds not-for-profit organisations, for-profit organisations, municipal governments, Indigenous organisations, and provincial/territorial bodies that have demonstrated knowledge of sectoral skills issues and established partnerships with national, regional, or local sectoral stakeholders. Projects must address workforce development needs in key sectors (agriculture/agri-food, construction, health, ICT, manufacturing, natural resources and environment, tourism, and transportation) and at minimum 10% co-funding from non-ESDC sources is required. The AI stream specifically targets workers facing job displacement or skills gaps due to AI adoption. Eligible activities include training and reskilling, attracting and retaining workforce, developing sector-wide standards and tools, and implementing creative workforce solutions. Funding per project ranges from CAD 5M to CAD 50M. Projects are national (spanning three+ provinces) or regional in scope.

The Sectoral Analysis developed by the Ministry of Digital Transformation of Ukraine aims to highlight the current state of artificial intelligence (AI) in the country across different sectors. It identifies existing strengths and weaknesses and outlines priority areas for AI development. The analysis reviews the leading AI projects currently being implemented in Ukraine and presents a roadmap for the adoption of a national AI strategy.

The initiative seeks to overcome barriers such as limited funding, outdated education programmes, and weak infrastructure, while capitalising on Ukraine’s IT talent and international integration to position the country as a regional AI hub for testing solutions, GovTech integration, and innovation in priority industries.
Objectives:
Fostering AI growth through sectoral analysis, identifying strengths (e.g. educational programmes) and weaknesses (e.g. low venture funding), and outlining eight priority directions: AI in defence, cybersecurity, healthcare, agriculture, environmental protection, education, Ukrainian-language large language models, and generative AI. It also proposes three flagship projects — the WINWIN AI Center of Excellence for public–private collaboration, Government BI for data-driven governance, and a sandbox for AI and blockchain startups — to drive implementation. These projects aim to enhance economic competitiveness, retain talent, align with EU standards, and achieve strategic goals such as regulatory harmonisation and R&D partnerships.The initiative is designed to address weaknesses in Ukraine’s AI sector and support its long-term development. In addition, the Sectoral Analysis highlights achievements and top priorities in the field and identifies the next steps for AI development in Ukraine through to the end of 2025.

title: SPRIND Next Frontier AI
body:
A EUR 125M pan-European challenge competition run by Germany's Federal Agency for Breakthrough Innovation (SPRIND), funding up to 10 teams for 24 months to build European Frontier AI labs, with up to 3 winners positioned to raise EUR 1B scale-up rounds.

Announced by SPRIND at EurIPS in Copenhagen on 3 December 2025, the Next Frontier AI Initiative is a DARPA-style challenge programme designed to build at least three European Frontier AI Labs capable of developing their own foundation models and competing with US and Chinese AI leaders. Applications are open until 31 May 2026; successful teams begin in July 2026 and are funded for 24 months. Up to 10 teams receive non-dilutive funding in staged tranches totalling up to EUR 27M per team (from the EUR 125M total pool), plus compute access, infrastructure, MLOps support, legal and strategic company-building support, and structured investor/partner matching. In autumn 2028, up to 3 winning labs are selected and positioned to raise EUR 1B scale-up rounds from a pre-aligned investor and corporate partner ecosystem. The programme explicitly targets new model classes, modalities, agentic systems, and efficient training regimes — not AI application layers. An early-bird 'Funke' track was available from February 2026 for concept development ahead of the main challenge. The initiative is pan-European: non-German European teams are eligible and European partners of winning labs may access EU Current AI Foundation funding.

title: Remote Pilot Program
body:
The Department uses drones to provide innovative and expert advice grounded in evidence and science, provide regulatory compliance and surveillance activities, provide land management, visitor safety and infrastructure inspection in Commonwealth Parks, engage and partner with First Nations ranger groups and provide staff safety and wellbeing in operational settings.

Use-Case Examples
The Ghost Nets Initiative is an Indigenous-led design of the use of drones and AI by Indigenous ranger groups in northern Australia to monitor ghost nets and marine debris.Population surveys of threatened animal species using drone-based thermal sensors.Detection of saltwater crocodiles through the development of an integrated sensor network and real-time alerts. The use of drones and AI in detecting, monitoring and controling buffel grass.Results, outcomes and impacts
The remote pilot program demonstrated that drones and AI can safely and efficiently monitor remote environments, delivering better detection of ghost nets, threatened species, crocodiles and invasive buffel grass than traditional methods. Indigenous-led and ranger-delivered approaches improved coverage, accuracy and decision making while building lasting technical capability in communities and agencies. Across use cases, pilots reduced safety risks, costs and time in the field and enabled more targeted, evidence-based management actions. Overall, the program showed clear environmental, cultural and public safety benefits and provided a strong foundation for scaling these technologies into business-as-usual operations.
Challenges and lessons learned
The initiative faced challenges operating in remote and harsh environments, meeting aviation and safety requirements, and producing sufficiently high quality, consistent data to train AI models reliably. Building capability took time, as rangers and staff needed training, accreditation and confidence in both drone operations and AI-enabled workflows, often in areas with limited digital infrastructure. A key lesson was that early, genuine co-design with First Nations rangers was essential to ensure culturally appropriate use, trust, and Indigenous data sovereignty. The pilots also showed that success depends less on technical sophistication than on good data, simple repeatable processes, strong governance, and embedding the technology into business-as-usual decision making.

category: Regulations, guidelines and standards
title: Regulatory Sandbox
document_name: Sandbox Regulatório
body:
The Regulatory Sandbox is an initiative by Brazil's National Data Protection Agency (ANPD), authorised under Complementary Law No. 182 of 2021. It creates a controlled environment for collaborative experimentation between the ANPD, regulated entities, and stakeholders to test AI and machine learning technologies within a regulatory framework, with a current focus on algorithmic transparency and compliance with Brazil's General Data Protection Law (LGPD).

The initiative is aligned with the Regulatory Sandbox Reference Guide of the Attorney General's Office (AGU) and is authorised under Complementary Law No. 182 of 2021. The current pilot operates under Edital de Convocação nº 02/2025, with selected participants now moving to a training phase covering regulation, AI, and experimental regulatory environments.
The sandbox targets a broad range of stakeholders. Innovative companies and public sector entities can test new technologies whilst mitigating regulatory risks. Researchers can assess AI in real-world scenarios, generating empirical knowledge for scientific and regulatory advancement. Civil society organisations can contribute critical perspectives to ensure collective rights are prioritised. The ANPD itself uses the sandbox to identify regulatory gaps and test approaches to balance innovation with the protection of personal data.
The chosen focus for the current pilot is algorithmic transparency, specifically, identifying technical and administrative measures to comply with Article 20, paragraph 1, and the transparency principle under Article 6 of the LGPD. This addresses key challenges associated with machine learning-based AI, including lack of transparency in automated decisions, discriminatory biases, and misuse of personal data. At the conclusion of the process, the sandbox is expected to inform a regulatory framework better adapted to the opportunities and challenges posed by emerging technologies, ensuring innovation is conducted ethically and in line with the rights of data subjects.

title: Recommendations for the Responsible Implementation and Use of Artificial Intelligence Technologies in Higher Education Institutions
document_name: Рекомендації щодо відповідального впровадження та використання технологій штучного інтелекту в закладах вищої освіти
body:
These recommendations provide clear guidance for higher education institutions on how to responsibly use artificial intelligence (AI). They help educators and students safely integrate AI tools to improve learning, research, and administration. The initiative was developed to address the challenges of ethics, data privacy, and transparency in AI, ensuring trustworthy and effective use in higher education institutions.

The recommendations on the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education institutions in Ukraine address the growing need to integrate AI technologies responsibly within the academic environment. As AI tools become increasingly accessible and powerful, universities face challenges related to ethics, data privacy, transparency, and potential biases in AI applications. 
Objectives:
This initiative seeks to provide practical guidance to educators, administrators, and students on how to leverage AI benefits while minimising risks, ensuring that AI enhances rather than undermines educational quality and fairness.
to create a methodological basis for the implementation and rational use of artificial intelligence technologies in higher education institutions; to promote the ethical and transparent use of AI technologies in teaching, learning, research, and administration; to protect personal data and privacy rights of all users; to support human oversight of AI systems; and to build digital literacy and trust within the higher education community. Looking ahead, the initiative is expected to evolve by being integrated into formal university policies and curricula, supporting the development of specialised AI-related courses and training programmes. Institutionalisation will involve cooperation among government bodies, educational institutions, and the private sector to continuously update guidelines in line with technological progress and emerging legal frameworks, such as the EU AI Act. Scaling the initiative nationally and potentially regionally can contribute to modernising higher education and improving its global competitiveness through trustworthy AI adoption.

New Zealand’s Public Sector AI Community of Practice is an active professional network of digital government practitioners meeting monthly online for wide knowledge sharing, learning and connection. Online meetings regularly bring together up to 200 practitioners from a wide range of government organisations to share knowledge on a range of AI-related topics and relevant information.

The Public Sector AI Community of Practice is a centrally led professional network that connects digital practitioners across New Zealand’s wider public sector. In its first full year, membership expanded from 60 to 95 agencies nationwide, with more than 600 practitioners engaged overall. Around 200 practitioners typically join each monthly online session, and the community delivered more than a dozen sessions over the year. Its purpose is to provide a shared space where agencies can learn from one another, explore emerging technologies and strengthen capability across government.
As part of the Government Chief Digital Officer’s AI Work Programme, the community’s agenda is shaped by members’ interests and feedback, ensuring sessions remain timely and relevant. Each monthly gathering is built around the themes of share, learn and connect, combining formal presentations, knowledge‑sharing updates and structured discussions. Agencies routinely present updates on their AI programmes and initiatives, offering insights into practical implementation, lessons learned and developing responsible AI practices. Deep‑dive sessions explore technical topics or emerging developments, often led by subject‑matter experts such as data platform managers and scientists who share specialist knowledge or support training.
Sessions examine active AI use cases and pilots, provide visibility into early exploratory projects and highlight shifts in technology or the operating environment that affect government AI adoption. Sub‑communities have begun to form around shared areas of practice, including a growing Policy Professionals group led by practitioners in the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet.

title: PresidencIA: Generative AI Adoption Programme for the Spanish Prime Minister’s Office
document_name: PresidencIA: Programa de Adopción de IA Generativa para el Gabinete de Presidencia del Gobierno de España
body:
Leveraging on 3 pillars (Community, Applications and Infrastructure), PresidencIA builds AI literacy among staff through workshops, community and best practices, develops custom AI tools for processes in the PM’s Office, and pursues on-premises AI infrastructure for tech sovereignty. It also works to position Spain as a partner for leading AI labs on safety and alignment. The programme addresses the gap between AI’s potential and practical government capacity.

PresidencIA is a comprehensive programme designed to accelerate the responsible adoption of generative AI within the Spanish Prime Minister’s Office (Gabinete de Presidencia). While AI offers significant potential to improve public‑sector decision‑making and service delivery, many administrations lack the internal capacity, tools and infrastructure needed to adopt it safely. PresidencIA responds by combining skills development, purpose‑built applications, sovereign infrastructure and international engagement into a single, integrated approach.

The programme’s first pillar focuses on community and capacity building. Through hands‑on workshops such as Whispering to AIs, Prototyping with AI and Researching with AI, several hundred public servants have developed practical skills in prompt engineering and responsible AI use. These activities prioritise experimentation and peer learning over theoretical instruction, supported by an active community of practice where staff share experiences and best practices. 
The second pillar delivers AI applications tailored to the Prime Minister’s Office. These include ServetIA, a research platform that produces source‑verified analytical outputs to support policy work; CiudadanIA, which automates the summarisation of citizen correspondence addressed to the President, reducing processing time and improving response quality; and GlobalAlert, which provides real‑time geopolitical monitoring and threat analysis. The programme also developed PromptAventura, a gamified AI literacy tool now validated and transferred to the government intranet. In addition, PresidencIA produced open‑source components, including an LLM evaluation workbench used to test prompts and models at scale through LLM‑as‑a‑judge methodologies.

The infrastructure pillar addresses AI sovereignty and secure deployment. PresidencIA has tested open‑weight language models for on‑premises use, enabling sensitive data processing without reliance on external cloud providers. In collaboration with the government IT unit (U.TIC), the programme is assessing the feasibility of a dedicated internal AI compute cluster and fine‑tuning models for specific government use cases. Alongside domestic infrastructure, PresidencIA also pursues international engagement, positioning Spain as a strategic partner for leading AI labs and fostering collaboration on alignment, safety research and responsible deployment of frontier AI systems in government contexts.

title: PALOMA: Artificial Intelligence for Early Detection of Unwanted Loneliness in Older Adults (Subnational: Madrid)
document_name: PALOMA: Inteligencia Artificial para la Detección Temprana de la Soledad No Deseada en Personas Mayores
body:
PALOMA is an artificial intelligence system that makes phone calls to people over 75 who live alone to detect situations of unwanted loneliness. It conducts short conversations with a natural sounding voice, identifies risk signals, and offers information or municipal follow up. The project helps reach more people, detect needs earlier, and connect them quickly with social support.

Unwanted loneliness affects older adults over 75 who live alone in Madrid and can lead to isolation, declining health, and loss of autonomy. Early detection is difficult, as many do not seek help and traditional channels—postal mail or in person visits—are not sufficient to identify those who may be at risk. To address this challenge, the Madrid City Council launched a pilot initiative using artificial intelligence to proactively contact this population group and better understand their situation through brief telephone conversations. 
PALOMA uses natural language processing technology capable of maintaining conversations with a natural sounding synthetic voice and administering a short questionnaire designed by social services professionals. The AI analyzes responses to detect signs of loneliness, classify risk levels, and offer follow up calls or information about municipal services. Cases flagged as relevant are always reviewed by professional staff, ensuring safe, ethical, and tailored intervention. This combination of AI and human oversight expands municipal capacity without replacing the professional role, aligning with principles of trustworthy and human centred AI.

The project has three main goals: improving early detection of unwanted loneliness, enabling more personalized interventions, and increasing access to activities and support services. It also modernizes the relationship between citizens and the administration, showing how AI can support social services in an efficient, accessible, and respectful way. Automated calls make it possible to reach thousands of people quickly and at a cost far lower than traditional alternatives such as call centers, significantly increasing the reach and effectiveness of social policies.

PALOMA carried out 5,163 calls, completed 2,071 conversations, and enabled 646 people to request municipal follow up. Of these, 602 were referred to social programs and 236 accepted a home visit; 84% showed signs of loneliness. The system identified 44 clear high risk cases and reached individuals who would not have contacted the city through other means. AI expanded reach, accelerated detection, and optimized resources. Results were measured through call analysis, conversion rates, referrals, and professional follow up.

A key strength of PALOMA is its capacity to scale. Traditional outreach programmes are limited by staff time, whereas AI enabled calling can reach thousands of people quickly and at low cost. The pilot contacted 5,000 people in only two weeks, leading to 646 individuals requesting follow up and enabling targeted support for those experiencing loneliness. These results demonstrate the potential for broader deployment and for replication in other municipalities facing similar demographic challenges.

body:
The Open Data Policy of Egypt establishes a national framework for releasing non‑sensitive government data to promote transparency, innovation, and public trust. It defines principles, governance structures, licensing rules, and a central data portal to ensure accessible, high‑quality, machine‑readable datasets across public institutions.

This policy aims to expand public access to non‑sensitive government data to strengthen transparency, accountability, and innovation. It addresses the challenge of fragmented data practices across ministries by introducing a unified national framework for data release, licensing, and governance.
The policy seeks to leverage the economic and social value of open data by enabling entrepreneurs, researchers, and citizens to reuse high‑quality, machine‑readable datasets. It establishes guiding principles to ensure data is both trustworthy and usable.
To achieve this, the initiative creates institutional mechanisms such as the National Council for Artificial Intelligence, an interim Interagency Data Release Board, and designated Open Data Officers across government entities. These bodies coordinate dataset review, anonymization, and publication.
Overall, the policy aims to improve service delivery, foster digital innovation, support evidence‑based policymaking, and align Egypt with global open government and open data standards through a national open data portal and harmonized procedures.

title: One Million Coders Programme (OMCP)
body:
The One Million Coders Programme (OMCP) is a Ghanaian government initiative launched on 16 April 2025 by President John Dramani Mahama, aimed at equipping one million Ghanaians with digital skills including coding, artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, and software development. Led by the Ministry of Communication, Digital Technology and Innovations, it operates across 130 learning centres in all 16 regions, with a national rollout beginning April 2026.

Following a 2025 pilot across four cities, Accra, Kumasi, Sunyani, and Tamale, which attracted approximately 94,000 applications within 48 hours and ultimately trained 859 participants (52% female), lessons from the pilot informed the design of the national rollout to ensure the programme delivers practical digital skills and meaningful employment pathways. The national rollout began on 10 April 2026 with the distribution of laptops to institutions and training centres, with each of the 130 learning centres across all 16 regions equipped with 50 customised laptops configured specifically for coding and digital training. A total of 130 constituency-level coordinators have been recruited to oversee training centres and provide technical support, with plans to expand coverage to all constituencies nationwide. Registration is linked to the Ghana Card through a simplified verification system, and the application portal was announced to reopen to allow both previous and new applicants to complete registration.
Key implementing partners include the Ghana Investment Fund for Electronic Communications (GIFEC), Ghana Digital Centres Limited, and the Ghana-India Kofi Annan Centre of Excellence in ICT, where the programme was originally launched. Twelve universities are participating in the initial phase, including the University of Ghana, Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology, and the University of Cape Coast. Private sector support includes MTN Ghana, which contributed approximately US$2 million towards laptop procurement, alongside partners such as Google, Telecel, and the Data Protection Commission.
Courses span a wide range of disciplines, including AI essentials, coding, cloud computing, cybersecurity, data analytics, software development, digital marketing, and UI/UX design,  offered at beginner, intermediate, and advanced levels, both online and in person. The programme is inclusive by design, targeting a 50/50 gender split, and is positioned as a central pillar of Ghana's digital transformation agenda, building a skilled workforce for emerging opportunities in software development, artificial intelligence, and remote digital employment. President Mahama stated that the government aims to train 300,000 Ghanaians under the programme in 2026 alone, describing it as "a national commitment and a social contract."

category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
title: OTT2 : Dynamic Data-Driven Personalisation of Employment Services and Counsellor Decision Support
body:
OTT2 is an AI-powered decision support system that helps Estonia’s Unemployment Insurance Fund prevent long-term unemployment. It combines data from public registries to assess each jobseeker’s employment prospects in real time, enabling counsellors to identify those at highest risk and focus support where it is most needed. With above 98% forecast accuracy, it eliminates laborious and error-prone manual work and it enables a policy pilot to dedicate counselling resource to high-risk customers.

Estonia’s public employment service faces the same challenge seen worldwide: allocating limited support to jobseekers with very different needs. Before 2020, counsellors relied on rules of thumb, personal experience and the manual profiling of roughly 45 indicators ranging from demographic characteristics and work history to health status and local labour‑market conditions. In practice, this volume of information was difficult to process consistently, making it hard to reliably identify people at risk of long‑term unemployment and in need of more intensive support.

This changed with the introduction of OTT1 in 2020, Estonia’s first data‑driven decision‑support tool for counsellors. Using a machine‑learning model, it assessed each jobseeker’s employment prospects at the point of registration. Over several years of operational use, the Estonian Unemployment Insurance Fund (EUIF) strengthened the model, built organisational confidence and gathered the evidence needed to expand its approach. OTT2 represents this next step. Whereas OTT1 produced a single assessment at registration, OTT2 generates dynamic, regularly updated assessments that reflect changes in a jobseeker’s situation—such as completing training or missing an assigned activity—so counsellors can make decisions using the most current information. The model is retrained periodically on new data but does not change autonomously, ensuring stability, transparency and auditability in a high‑stakes service. OTT2 also explains the main factors shaping each prediction and how these evolve over time, helping counsellors interpret results and offer more personalised support.

OTT2 builds on the strong performance of its predecessor, which achieved over 95% prediction accuracy. By updating assessments as circumstances change, accuracy is expected to rise above 98%; this is being tested in a 2026 pilot. The pilot also introduces a targeted service change: the approximately 20% of newly registered jobseekers identified as lowest‑risk will no longer receive mandatory counselling, allowing counsellors to focus more time on individuals at higher risk of long‑term unemployment. Even small reductions in unemployment duration have significant fiscal impact—one day less is estimated to save around 3.8% of annual expenditure.

category: Regulations, guidelines and standards
title: OMB AI Acquisition Guidance (M-25-22)
body:
An OMB memorandum establishing federal procurement requirements for the efficient and responsible acquisition of AI systems, including a 'Buy American' AI provision, risk management obligations, and interoperability protections.

Issued on 3 April 2025 by the White House Office of Management and Budget (OMB), M-25-22 ('Driving Efficient Acquisition of Artificial Intelligence in Government') replaces the Biden-era M-24-18 and implements Executive Order 14179 ('Removing Barriers to American Leadership in Artificial Intelligence', January 2025). It applies to AI systems and services acquired by covered federal agencies under contracts awarded pursuant to solicitations issued from 30 September 2025 onwards (excluding National Security Systems and AI used incidentally). Three core policy themes: (1) fostering a competitive American AI marketplace — agencies must prioritise US-developed AI solutions; (2) safeguarding taxpayer dollars by tracking AI performance and managing risk — contracts must include performance monitoring, regular risk assessments, and minimum risk management practices for high-impact AI; (3) promoting effective AI acquisition through cross-functional engagement — agencies must involve legal, privacy, IT, and programme officials in acquisition. Key contract requirements include: data-use restrictions preventing vendors from training public AI models on non-public government data; IP and data ownership protections; vendor lock-in protections; privacy safeguards; and mandatory AI disclosure provisions. GSA was directed to release AI procurement guides by August 2025 and establish a best-practices repository by January 2026. Complements OMB M-25-21 on federal AI use governance.

title: OECD AI Capabilities Indicators
document_name: OECD AI Capabilities Indicators
body:
This report introduces the OECD's beta AI Capability Indicators. The indicators are designed to assess and compare AI advancements against human abilities.

Developed over five years by a collaboration of over 50 experts, the AI Capability Indicators cover nine human abilities: Language; Social interaction; Problem solving; Creativity; Metacognition and critical thinking; Knowledge, learning and memory; Vision; Manipulation; and Robotic intelligence. Unique in the current policy space, these indicators leverage cutting-edge research to provide a clear framework for policymakers to understand AI's potential impacts on education, work, public affairs and private life. The indicators are presented in scales of five levels, where the most challenging capabilities for AI systems are found towards the top. Grounded in human psychology, this approach offers a structured and high-level perspective on AI development.

category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
title: NugepIA: AI-Powered Judicial Precedent Management System (Subnational: Porto Velho)
document_name: NugepIA: Sistema de Gestão de Precedentes Judiciais Potencializado por IA
body:
NugepIA is an AI tool that organizes repetitive lawsuits to ensure faster and more consistent decisions for citizens. It was developed to replace slow manual processes and spreadsheets that were prone to human error in identifying similar cases. The system now automatically identifies identical cases and extracts dates from documents, making the court’s work more efficient.

NugepIA was developed by the Court of Justice of Rondônia (TJRO) to resolve critical bottlenecks in the management of binding precedents, such as IRDR and IAC, within the court’s NUGEPNAC unit. Prior to its introduction, monitoring of precedents relied on manual spreadsheets and institutional memory, creating fragmented communication, high risk of error and delays in reporting information to the National Council of Justice (CNJ). Judges’ chambers also lacked automatic visibility into suspended cases, negatively affecting productivity and legal certainty.

The initiative’s core objective is to automate the NUGEPNAC workflow using the Collectivus AI tool. The system automatically extracts key procedural dates—such as suspension, judgment and finality—directly from case documents, ensuring accurate and up‑to‑date records. It applies textual‑similarity analysis to group identical or highly similar cases, alerting judges in their workspaces to repetitive litigation and suggesting links to existing or potential binding precedents. In addition, the system performs daily monitoring of the Supreme Federal Court (STF) website to track updates in constitutional‑control actions relevant to ongoing cases.

Development progressed from initial mapping in February 2025 to full implementation by December 2025. Integration was completed across the PJe system, the Nugep System and the Chamber Module, eliminating manual reconciliation between platforms. This milestone institutionalised AI as a support tool for judicial decision‑making and laid the technological foundation for the broader AssessorIA platform, which now scales similarity‑analysis capabilities across the entire court.

Operationally, NugepIA eliminated manual data verification and enabled automated, accurate reporting to the CNJ’s National Precedent Bank (BNP). The AI achieves over 95% precision in grouping similar lawsuits and provides direct, actionable suggestions to judges’ chambers. Impact is measured through reduced screening and verification time, continuous validation cycles parallel to development and improved visibility of first‑ and second‑instance caseloads that were previously unmonitored by the central system.

Implementation addressed several challenges. Manual grouping of cases and spreadsheet‑based communication were error‑prone, and inconsistencies in procedural dates previously prevented automatic validation. These issues were resolved through full system integration and AI‑based date extraction, replacing manual review. Experience showed that successful AI use in the judiciary depends on coordinated planning between technical and legal teams, realistic timelines and continuous testing to mature similarity‑analysis functions.

New Zealand’s AI Strategy, "Investing with Confidence," outlines a national approach focused on adopting existing AI technologies to boost productivity and economic growth.

title: National Roadmap for Data Centres - Rapporteur's Report
body:
Finland’s National Roadmap for Data Centres is a government‑commissioned report prepared in 2025 that proposes national objectives and measures for the development of high‑value data centres, explicitly linking data‑centre location to electricity grid capacity, fossil‑free energy availability and the management of growing AI‑related computing demand.

Finland has prepared a national roadmap for data centres through a government‑appointed rapporteur to inform policy‑making related to the data economy, digitalisation and advanced computing. The report recognises that the rapid expansion of cloud services and artificial intelligence is driving sustained growth in demand for data‑centre capacity, as AI models are increasingly trained and operated in data‑centre environments. As a result, the roadmap treats data centres—and the AI workloads they host—as infrastructure that must be planned in close coordination with the electricity system.
The roadmap explicitly links data‑centre siting to the capacity and resilience of the electricity grid, emphasising that large computing facilities place continuous and significant demands on power generation and transmission. It proposes that data‑centre investments should be attracted to locations where grid capacity can support additional load and where renewable, fossil‑free electricity can be secured through long‑term contracts. Wind power and the expansion of clean generation are identified as important elements in supporting future data‑centre growth.
In addition, the report highlights energy efficiency and system integration as key considerations. It emphasises the reuse of waste heat from data centres—such as integration with district heating networks—as a way to increase the overall efficiency and local value added of data‑centre operations. These factors are presented as criteria for encouraging data centres with higher value added rather than purely capacity‑driven investment.
The roadmap also addresses the implications of AI‑driven growth for grid stability. It notes that rapid expansion of data‑centre capacity could increase price volatility or strain the power system if large users do not contribute to system balancing. As a result, the report proposes that data centres should play a role in demand‑side flexibility, helping to stabilise the electricity system alongside other large industrial users. While current flexibility options are limited, the roadmap identifies stronger flexibility mechanisms and energy‑system integration as necessary to support continued growth in AI‑ and data‑intensive computing in Finland.

title: National Policy on Artificial Intelligence (CONPES 4144)
document_name: Polí­tica Nacional de Inteligencia Artificial (IA)
body:
This initiative aims to maximize the capabilities for research, development, adoption and ethical and sustainable use of AI systems in strategic social, economic and environmental issues in Colombia.

Since the formulation of the National Policy on Digital Transformation and Artificial Intelligence (CONPES Document 3975 of 2019), progress has been made in the construction of enabling conditions for the adoption of digital technologies. However, the country still shows low capacities for research, development, adoption and ethical and sustainable use of AI systems in strategic social, economic and environmental issues.This CONPES document formulates a national Artificial Intelligence policy whose objective is to generate capacities for research, development, adoption and ethical and sustainable use of AI systems in order to promote social and economic transformation in Colombia. To achieve this objective, the policy is structured around six strategic axes: (i) Ethics and Governance: strengthen governance mechanisms and apply ethical principles related to AI systems, to ensure responsible development and use; (ii) Data and Infrastructure: strengthen the infrastructure technology, as well as the availability, exchange and representativeness of data, fundamental for AI; (iii) Research, Development and Innovation (R&D&I): boost research, development and innovation in AI systems in a way that is reflected in knowledge productivity, and benefits for the country; (iv) Capacity Development and Digital Talent: develop the capabilities and digital talent necessary for the design, use and adoption of AI, in addition to promoting the social appropriation of knowledge of this technology; (v) Risk Mitigation: define measures that promote the identification, prevention and mitigation of risks and undesired effects related to AI systems; and (vi) Use and Adoption of AI: Promote the use and adoption of AI systems in public entities, the business fabric and the territories; (vii) Use and Adoption of AI: promote the use and adoption of AI systems in public entities, the business fabric and the territories.

body:
The National Large Language Model is a project to develop a language model that reflects the specifics of the Ukrainian language and culture. It addresses the underrepresentation of Ukrainian in modern AI tools, which limits their effectiveness for Ukrainian users. The model will enable the state to launch AI services for citizens and optimize internal processes, while providing businesses, educational institutions, and citizens with access to modern, locally adapted technologies.

The main goal of the project is to develop and implement a secure, reliable, and culturally relevant model that can serve as the basis for an entire ecosystem of AI solutions. This includes creating tools for automating government services, analysing legislative documents, developing personalised educational platforms, and supporting military technologies. The project also aims to stimulate the development of the local AI market by attracting Ukrainian startups and talent, which will create new jobs and promote economic growth. Another important goal is to ensure digital sovereignty by guaranteeing that the confidential data of citizens and the state is processed and stored within the country. In the future, the model will be continuously improved and scaled, incorporating more and more data and functionalities. This will allow it to become a universal platform that supports innovation in all areas of life. Thus, Ukrainian LLM is not just a technological project, but a strategic initiative aimed at strengthening Ukraine's technological independence, ensuring data security, and creating new opportunities for innovation and development that will serve the national interest. This is an important step towards transforming Ukraine into one of the leaders in the field of AI.

By promoting data altruism, it encourages the sharing of data for public good, ensuring that data is used responsibly and ethically.

title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy of Zambia 2024–2026
body:
The National Artificial Intelligence Strategy of Zambia 2024–2026, led by the Ministry of Technology and Science, sets a national framework to use AI for economic growth, improved public services and inclusive development. It prioritises human capital development, digital infrastructure, data ecosystems, research and innovation, sectoral AI adoption and international collaboration, and establishes governance and ethical oversight through a National AI Council and Technical Working Groups.

The National Artificial Intelligence Strategy of Zambia 2025–2027 sets out a national framework to harness artificial intelligence for economic growth, improved public services and inclusive and sustainable national development. It recognises the promise of AI for Zambia while noting that the national AI ecosystem is still at an early stage, with challenges including limited digital infrastructure, shortages in skilled AI talent, fragmented data ecosystems and the absence of a dedicated AI governance framework.
The strategy is organised around key strategic priorities and pillars. These include establishing a policy and regulatory framework for ethical and responsible AI, developing human capital through AI literacy, education reform and professional training, expanding digital infrastructure and data ecosystems, and promoting research, innovation and entrepreneurship. Sector‑specific AI adoption is prioritised in agriculture, healthcare, education, mining, finance and public services, where AI is intended to improve productivity, efficiency and service delivery. International collaboration and benchmarking are also emphasised to align Zambia’s AI efforts with global best practices.
The strategy builds on identified strengths and enabling factors, including emerging private sector initiatives, early AI applications in healthcare and mining, ongoing digital inclusion programmes, and alignment with international frameworks such as the African Union’s Continental Strategy for Artificial Intelligence, UNESCO’s Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence and the OECD Principles on Artificial Intelligence. It adopts a multi‑stakeholder approach involving government ministries and agencies, academic and research institutions, private sector actors, civil society organisations and international partners.
Governance, ethics and oversight are integral to implementation. Strategic guidance is provided by a National AI Council, with sector‑specific delivery and monitoring supported by Technical Working Groups. Overall coordination is led by the Ministry of Technology and Science, with defined roles for institutions such as the Smart Zambia Institute. A Monitoring and Evaluation framework establishes indicators, reporting mechanisms, mid‑term and end‑term evaluations and public dissemination to ensure accountability, transparency and continuous learning, while ethical principles including fairness, transparency, accountability, data privacy, inclusivity and sustainable development guide responsible AI adoption.

title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy of Libya 2025–2030
document_name: 2023 - 2025 الاستراتيجية الوطنية للذكاء الاصطناعي في دولة ليبيا
body:
The National Artificial Intelligence Strategy of Libya 2025–2030 sets a national framework to use artificial intelligence as a driver of inclusive and sustainable development. It aims to improve public services, enhance security and innovation, and place people at the centre of AI use. The strategy is structured around six pillars covering governance, legislation and ethics, infrastructure and data, human capacity development, priority sectors, and monitoring and evaluation.

Libya’s National Artificial Intelligence Strategy (2025–2030) aims to "enhance the use of artificial intelligence as a driver of comprehensive development, improve services, strengthen security, and foster innovation, with a focus on human‑centred and ethical principles.”
 
The strategy is structured around six main pillars: governance and leadership; legislation and ethics; digital infrastructure and data; human capacities and education; innovation and priority sectors; and monitoring, evaluation, and participation. These pillars reflect the strategy’s key priorities, including the establishment of a national AI governance structure, the development of a legal and ethical framework to ensure safe and responsible use of AI, the strengthening of digital infrastructure and data management, and the building of national capacities through education, training, and research. The strategy explicitly seeks to address weaknesses such as the absence of a unified national AI body, legislative fragmentation, limited availability of high‑quality data, and shortages in specialised skills. 
 
It identifies priority sectors where AI applications are expected to have an immediate and direct impact on citizens’ quality of life. These sectors are health, financial services, education, and public services, with pilot projects proposed in these areas before expansion to other sectors such as national security and energy. It builds on existing national assets, including telecommunications infrastructure and institutional willingness to adopt digital solutions, while promoting innovation, entrepreneurship, and the creation of a supportive ecosystem for startups. Stakeholders involved include government institutions, regulatory bodies, academic institutions, the private sector, and civil society.
