category: U.S. state and local documents
title: Washington House Bill 1999
document_name: Washington HB 1999 (Fabricated Sexually Explicit Images)
body:
Defines digitization to include AI use in creating or altering images. Criminalizes disclosing fabricated intimate images, with AI-defined digitization as a key factor. Establishes defenses and penalties. Provides victims legal recourse for unauthorized AI-altered image disclosures.

Amends Washington state law to address the creation, possession, and dissemination of fabricated intimate or sexually explicit images using digitization, including artificial intelligence.

Defines "fabricated depiction" as images altered to show minors or adults engaging in sexual conduct that did not occur.

Criminalizes disclosing fabricated intimate images without consent, establishing it as a gross misdemeanor or a class C felony for repeat offenders.

Specifies exemptions for disclosures made in the public interest, such as legal, law enforcement, or medical contexts.

Clarifies that interactive computer services and telecommunications providers are not liable for third-party content.

Establishes civil remedies for victims of unauthorized disclosures, including economic, noneconomic, and punitive damages.

Mandates that fabricated depictions remain in law enforcement custody and are not duplicated during legal proceedings.

Specifies timelines for filing civil actions related to unauthorized disclosures, especially for minors.

category: U.S. state and local documents
title: Utah Senate Bill 84, Part 13
document_name: Utah S 84 (Governor’s Office of Economic Opportunity), Part 13. Innovation in Artificial Intelligence Grant Pilot Program
body:
Creates the Innovation in Artificial Intelligence Grant Pilot Program to fund business entities developing AI courses for K-12 students. Requires partnerships with schools, application evaluations, and written agreements. Permits rulemaking and mandates annual reporting on the program's progress.

Creates the Innovation in Artificial Intelligence Grant Pilot Program.

Defines “business entity” as a for-profit or nonprofit organization, “pilot program” as the Innovation in Artificial Intelligence Grant Pilot Program, and “student” as a child enrolled in a public or private K–12 school.

Requires the pilot program to be administered subject to the availability of funds and to award grants to business entities to develop programs, materials, and curriculum that teach artificial intelligence with an emphasis on prepare students for careers in technology.

Requires business entities to submit a grant application detailing how they will fulfill the program’s purpose, work with public or private schools, and establish partnerships to implement the proposal.

Evaluates applications based on their likelihood of achieving program goals and overall viability.

Requires approved business entities to enter into a written agreement with the office specifying the grant amount and the time period and structure for distribution before receiving funds.

Authorizes the office to establish rules for grant application procedures, award criteria, and post-award reporting requirements.

Requires an annual written update on the pilot program to be included in the report outlined in Section 63N-1a-306.

category: U.S. state and local documents
title: Utah Senate Bill 149, Section 13-2-12
document_name: Utah SB 149, Section 13-2-12 (Impact of generative AI on liability for violation of consumer protection law)
body:
Prohibits using generative AI as a defense for consumer protection violations. Requires disclosure of AI interactions in regulated occupations. Imposes fines up to $2,500 per violation. Authorizes courts to issue injunctions, order disgorgements, and impose additional penalties.

Establishes that using generative artificial intelligence (AI) is not a defense against violations of consumer protection laws.

Mandates disclosure when generative AI interacts with a person, requiring clear communication that the interaction is with AI, not a human.

Requires providers of regulated occupations to disclose when generative AI is used in service provision.

Prohibits service provision of regulated occupations via generative AI without meeting legal requirements.

Stipulates that disclosures be made verbally at the start of oral interactions and electronically before written exchanges.

Empowers the Division of Consumer Protection to enforce these provisions, including imposing fines up to $2,500 per violation.

Allows the division to seek court actions, which may result in injunctions, disgorgement of funds, or additional fines.

Permits civil penalties up to $5,000 for violating administrative or court orders, enforceable by the attorney general.

category: U.S. state and local documents
title: Utah Senate Bill 149, Chapter 70
document_name: Utah SB 149, Chapter 70 (Artificial Intelligence Policy Act)
body:
Establishes the Office of Artificial Intelligence Policy to oversee AI development. Creates an AI Learning Laboratory for research and regulatory evaluation. Permits regulatory mitigation agreements for AI testing. Criminalizes offenses committed with AI aid. Repeals the Act on May 1, 2025.

Establishes the Office of Artificial Intelligence Policy to oversee the AI Learning Laboratory Program, which analyzes AI technologies' risks, benefits, and regulatory implications.

Mandates the creation of regulatory mitigation agreements, allowing participants to operate under modified regulations while testing AI technologies.

Sets eligibility requirements for regulatory mitigation, including technical expertise, financial resources, and risk management plans.

Requires participants to report consumer harm, privacy breaches, or unauthorized data usage, with potential removal from the program for violations.

Allows an initial 12-month regulatory mitigation period, with a possible 12-month extension.

Defines using generative AI to commit offenses as a punishable act.

Specifies the program's repeal on May 1, 2025.

Takes effect on May 1, 2024.

category: U.S. state and local documents
title: Utah House Bill 148
document_name: Utah HB 148 (Artificial Pornographic Images Amendments)
body:
Amends Utah law to define and penalize the distribution of intimate and counterfeit intimate images, including AI-generated content. Establishes offenses for sexual extortion and unlawful distribution of such images, with exemptions for certain service providers. Effective May 1, 2024.

Amends definitions related to child and vulnerable adult sexual abuse material, including depictions created or modified using computer-generated images.

Defines "distribute" and "produce" in the context of such materials, emphasizing the inclusion of electronic and computer-generated methods.

Criminalizes the distribution of intimate images without consent, outlining penalties, including misdemeanors and felonies for repeat offenses.

Exempts certain entities like law enforcement, legal proceedings, and internet service providers from liability if they incidentally transmit or store such images without intentional engagement.

Addresses sexual extortion, detailing offenses involving coercion through threats to distribute intimate images, with enhanced penalties for aggravated offenses involving children or vulnerable adults.

Prohibits unlawful distribution of counterfeit intimate images, specifying penalties and exemptions for certain entities and situations.

Specifies that the act takes effect on May 1, 2024, providing ample time for stakeholders to comply with the new regulations.

category: U.S. state and local documents
title: Utah HB 464 (Social Media Amendments)
document_name: Utah HB 464 (Social Media Amendments)
body:
Establishes legal recourse for Utah minors against social media companies for mental health harm from excessive use of algorithmically curated services. Requires parental consent and sets usage limits for minors. Prohibits waiving protections and specifies severability of provisions.

Enacts new provisions governing minors' use of algorithmically curated social media services.

Allows Utah minors or their parents to sue social media companies if minors suffer adverse mental health outcomes from excessive use of such services.

Defines "adverse mental health outcome" and "excessive use," setting presumption rules that favor establishing causation by social media design elements unless companies prove compliance with specific usage restrictions.

Requires social media companies to limit minor usage to under three hours daily, block access during night hours, require parental consent, and disable certain engagement-driven features to avoid liability.

Prohibits waivers of rights provided by these regulations, ensuring public policy enforcement and protecting private rights of action.

Conveys state's responsibility to protect minors from mental health risks associated with social media usage and mandates corrective legislative actions for safeguarding against such harms. 

Repeals existing sections related to social media platform age requirements and protections, effective May 1, 2024, with some provisions effective October 1, 2024.

category: Editors' Picks;Multinational
title: REGULATION (EU) 2024/1689 OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND OF THE COUNCIL of 13 June 2024 laying down harmonised rules on artificial intelligence and amending Regulations (EC) No 300/2008, (EU) No 167/2013, (EU) No 168/2013, (EU) 2018/858, (EU) 2018/1139 and (EU) 2019/2144 and Directives 2014/90/EU, (EU) 2016/797 and (EU) 2020/1828 (Artificial Intelligence Act)
document_name: EU AI Act
body:
Implements a risk-based regulatory framework for AI, with specific attention to single-purpose AI systems used in risky contexts and general-purpose AI systems with significant capability. Imposes risk-dependent requirements related to accuracy, cybersecurity, evaluation, monitoring, transparency, and registration. Defines exceptions, penalties, and governance structures.

Classifies AI systems into unacceptable, high, limited, and minimal risk categories, defining specific regulatory requirements for each category. Requires strict monitoring and quality management for high-risk systems. 

Establishes transparency and cooperation requirements for general-purpose AI models. Imposes additional risk management and evaluation obligations for general-purpose models with systemic risks.

Applies to AI developers and deployers whose systems are used in the EU market, regardless of their physical location, with certain exceptions.

Defines regulatory exemptions for free and open-source AI systems, subject to transparency and licensing requirements.

Establishes the European Commission’s AI Office to lead implementation efforts and enforce compliance. Allows significant penalties for violations. Defines additional AI regulatory roles for advisory boards and national-level authorities.

category: U.S. state and local documents
title: Indiana Senate Bill 2024-150
document_name: Indiana Senate Bill 2024-150 (AI and Cybersecurity)
body:
Establishes an Artificial Intelligence Task Force to study AI use and impact, requiring state agencies to inventory all artificial intelligence technologies in use, being developed or considered by the agency.

Establishes an Artificial Intelligence Task Force to study AI technologies used by Indiana state agencies, assessing their benefits, risks, and impacts on privacy, civil rights, and legal protections.

Requires the Task Force to produce annual reports with findings and recommendations for policies or legislation to govern AI use by state agencies.

Mandates state agencies compile and submit inventories of AI technologies in use or development, detailing vendors, intended use, data security measures, benefits, risks, and financial implications.

category: U.S. state and local documents
title: Indiana House Bill 1047
document_name: Indiana HB 1047 (Sexual Offenses)
body:
Defines "computer generated image" as those created or modified using AI or software. Criminalizes distributing non-consensual intimate images, including AI-generated ones, with enhanced penalties for repeat offenders. Establishes new offenses for voyeurism involving AI or digital tools.

Amends Indiana law to define "computer generated image" as images created or modified through artificial intelligence or software.

Prohibits distribution of intimate images without consent, including AI-generated images, categorizing such distribution as a Class A misdemeanor or Level 6 felony for repeat offenders.

Criminalizes voyeurism involving AI or cameras, with enhanced penalties for repeat offenses or distribution of recorded images.

Establishes that using unmanned aerial vehicles to capture private images without consent constitutes remote aerial voyeurism, punishable as a Class A misdemeanor or Level 6 felony for repeat offenses or distribution.

Exempts certain distributions of images for criminal investigations or under court orders.

Requires commencement of actions for child sexual abuse before certain deadlines or conditions, with exceptions for specific bankruptcy proceedings.

Declares an emergency for the enactment of these provisions.

category: U.S. state and local documents
title: Indiana 2024 House Bill 1133
document_name: Indiana HB 1133 (Digitally Altered Media in Elections)
body:
Adds Chapter 8 to Indiana Code, regulating election campaign communications with digitally altered media. Requires disclaimers for such media, specifying format and timing. Allows candidates depicted in undisclosed fabricated media to sue for damages, injunctive relief, and legal costs.

Amends the Indiana Code to add regulations on the use of digitally altered media in elections.

Defines "campaign communication" to include media advocating for or against a candidate, with fabricated media depicting candidates requiring specific disclaimers.

Requires disclaimers for campaign communications containing fabricated media to state that elements have been digitally altered or artificially generated.

Mandates disclaimers in printed, audio, and video formats to meet specific visibility, audibility, and frequency standards.

Allows candidates depicted in fabricated media without the required disclaimer to sue the person who financed, sponsored, or disseminated the communication.

Entitles prevailing plaintiffs to recover actual damages, injunctive relief, and associated legal costs.

Places the burden of proof on the plaintiff to demonstrate depiction in fabricated media by clear and convincing evidence.

Expedites court hearings for related civil actions.

Declares an emergency for the immediate enactment of this regulation.

category: Multinational
title: UN General Assembly Resolution A/78/L.49 ("Seizing the opportunities of safe, secure and trustworthy artificial intelligence systems for sustainable development"
document_name: UNGA Resolution A/78/L.49 ("Seizing the opportunities of safe, secure and trustworthy artificial intelligence systems for sustainable development"
body:
Resolves to bridge AI and digital divides and promote safe, secure, and trustworthy AI systems to achieve the Sustainable Development Goals. Encourages regulatory frameworks, capacity building, and international cooperation. Emphasizes human rights, data governance, and inclusive participation in AI governance.

Resolves to bridge AI and digital divides globally and promote safe, secure, and trustworthy AI systems to achieve Sustainable Development Goals.

Encourages Member States and stakeholders to support regulatory frameworks for responsible AI, fostering innovation and equitable access to benefits.

Calls for cooperation to assist developing countries in accessing AI benefits through capacity building, digital literacy, and infrastructure.

Emphasizes the protection of human rights throughout AI systems' life cycles and urges cessation of AI use that violates international human rights law.

Promotes inclusive governance of AI, addressing global challenges while considering developing countries' needs.

Recognizes data's importance in AI development and urges fair data governance to harness AI potential for sustainable development.

Encourages continued international cooperation, research, and mapping of AI impacts to inform effective governance.

Calls upon UN entities to assess AI challenges and assist developing countries in capacity building for achieving Sustainable Development Goals.

category: U.S. state and local documents
title: Tennessee Senate Bill 1711
document_name: Tennessee SB 1711 (Use of AI Technology by Students)
body:
Requires Tennessee educational institutions, including universities and charter schools, to adopt AI use policies for instructional purposes by specified deadlines. Mandates policy implementation and reporting to relevant authorities, with noncompliance potentially leading to accountability measures.

Mandates the board of trustees of the University of Tennessee, the board of regents, and local governing boards of state universities to adopt AI usage policies for students, faculty, and staff by July 1, 2025.

Encourages public higher education institutions to collaborate on policy development and implementation for AI use.

Requires these boards to post policies online and submit them to respective education committees by July 1, 2025, with noncompliance leading to mandatory reporting to the joint government operations committee.

Obliges the adoption of AI policies for students, teachers, and staff in schools by the 2024-2025 school year, with annual compliance reports due to the Department of Education starting July 1, 2024.

Instructs public charter schools to implement AI policies by the 2024-2025 school year, with annual compliance reporting to the Department of Education beginning July 1, 2024.

Takes effect immediately upon becoming law, citing public welfare.

category: Multinational
title: Consensus Statement on Red Lines in Artificial Intelligence
document_name: Consensus Statement on Red Lines in Artificial Intelligence (IDAIS)
body:
Encourages governance development through domestic regulations and international collaboration to enforce red lines and ensure AI safety.

Proposes red lines in AI development and governance development as an international coordination mechanism to prevent catastrophic risks.

Prohibits AI systems from self-replication or improvement without human approval.

Restricts AI from taking actions to increase its power or influence unduly.

Forbids AI systems from aiding in the development of weapons of mass destruction.

Prohibits AI from autonomously executing cyberattacks causing significant harm.

Prevents AI from deceiving designers or regulators about its capabilities.

Calls for comprehensive governance regimes to prevent crossing of red lines.

Requires domestic registration of advanced AI models for government oversight.

Conditions global market access on compliance with internationally aligned regulations.

Encourages multilateral institutions to govern AGI development safely.

Mandates developers demonstrate adherence to red lines through evaluations and proofs.

Urges international collaboration on AI safety research and funding. 

Emphasizes decisive action combining technical research and governance to mitigate risks.

category: U.S. state and local documents
title: California Privacy Protection Agency Draft Risk Assessment and Automated Decisionmaking Technology Regulations
document_name: CPPA Draft Risk Assessment and Automated Decisionmaking Technology Regulations
body:
Requires risk assessments for processing personal information with AI, especially when impacting significant consumer decisions or involving extensive profiling. Mandates transparency and consumer rights to opt-out of automated decision making technology.

Mandates businesses to conduct risk assessments for using AI and automated decision-making technology when handling consumer data, especially for decisions impacting financial, employment, or educational opportunities.

Requires transparency through Pre-use Notices for consumers, detailing the use of AI in decision-making and providing opt-out or appeal options.

Specifies exceptions where consumers cannot opt-out, mainly when processing is necessary for service, with provisions for human review upon request.

Demands businesses to ensure AI does not discriminate against protected classes through evaluations and safeguards.

Obliges businesses to disclose AI processes upon consumer request and prohibits retaliatory actions against consumers exercising their rights.

Mandates comprehensive documentation and regular updates for risk assessments, maintaining consumer privacy as a priority.

category: 중국
title: [중국] 2024년 정부업무보고
body:
전국인민대표대회에서 발표된 2024년 중국 정부업무보고.
① '人工智能+' 행동을 처음으로 국가 핵심 과제로 명시하며, AI를 산업·디지털 전환의 핵심 동력으로 제시,
② 대형 AI 모델의 광범위한 산업 응용 지원과 AI 스타트업 생태계 육성 방향,
③ AI 반도체·컴퓨팅 인프라 자립을 위한 기술 투자 확대,
④ AI 거버넌스의 '발전과 안전의 병행' 원칙을 정부 공식 문건으로 천명한 첫 사례다.

category: U.S. state and local documents
title: New Mexico House Bill 182 of 2024(Campaign Reporting Act)
document_name: New Mexico HB 182 (Campaign Reporting Act)
body:
Adds disclaimer requirements for AI-generated deceptive media in political ads. Criminalizes distribution without proper disclaimers, punishable by misdemeanor or felony. Allows enforcement by authorities and affected parties. Specifies disclaimer format for various media types.

Amends the Campaign Reporting Act to require disclaimers on advertisements containing materially deceptive media created through artificial intelligence (AI).

Defines "materially deceptive media" as content using AI to falsely depict individuals without consent.

Mandates disclaimers stating the content is AI-manipulated, specifying whether it is an image, video, or audio.

Prohibits the distribution of materially deceptive media within 90 days before an election if intended to mislead voters, unless accompanied by the required disclaimer.

Establishes penalties for violations: a misdemeanor for a first offense and a fourth-degree felony for subsequent offenses.

Allows enforcement and injunctive relief by the attorney general, district attorneys, affected individuals, candidates, or organizations representing voters' interests.

Excludes certain media types from disclaimer requirements and clarifies non-violation conditions for broadcasting stations and distribution platforms.

category: U.S. state and local documents
title: An act to amend the general business law, in relation to requiring advertisements to disclose the use of synthetic media
document_name: Synthetic Media Disclosure Act
body:
Requires any person engaged in advertising property or services in New York to disclose when synthetic media is used in advertisements.

Requires any person advertising property or services in New York to disclose when synthetic media is used in advertisements, including when synthetic media depicts a natural person, without the person’s consent.

Establishes civil penalties and fines if the above is violated.

category: 중국
title: [중국] 생성형 AI 서비스 안전 기본 요구사항
document_name: 《生成式人工智能服务安全基本要求》/ 「생성형 인공지능 서비스 안전 기본 요구사항」
body:
●국가: 중국
●기관: 전국정보보안표준화기술위원회
●문서종류: 기술 표준 / 안전 요구사항
●문서명: 《生成式人工智能服务安全基本要求》/ 「생성형 인공지능 서비스 안전 기본 요구사항」
●발표시점: 2024년 2월 29일
●핵심내용생성형 AI 서비스 제공자가 준수해야 할 안전평가·보안요건을 정리한 기술문서.
5대 핵심 축:① 학습 말뭉치 안전② 모델 안전③ 생성 콘텐츠 안전④ 서비스 제공 전 안전평가⑤ 생성형 AI 서비스 제공자의 책임 요건

category: Chinese law and policy
title: Technical Documentation of National Technical Committee 260 on Cybersecurity of Standardization Administration of China: Basic Safety Requirements for Generative Artificial Intelligence Services
document_name: Basic Safety Requirements for Generative Artificial Intelligence Services (Technical Documentation)
body:
Specifies safety requirements for generative AI services, focusing on corpus and model safety. Requires providers to conduct safety assessments and adhere to cybersecurity, data security, and personal information protection laws. Emphasizes preventing illegal content and ensuring model-generated content accuracy and reliability.

Specifies safety requirements for generative AI services in China, focusing on corpus safety, model safety, and safety measures.

Applies to service providers conducting safety assessments and the main oversight department for evaluating generative AI services' safety levels.

Mandates safety assessments and reporting, adherence to cybersecurity, data security, and personal information protection laws.

Requires corpus source safety management, verification, and traceability, including avoiding illegal content and ensuring intellectual property rights compliance.

Demands annotators follow strict training and rule adherence for data annotation and review.

Stipulates model safety, including foundation model registration, content safety monitoring, and ensuring generated content accuracy and reliability.

Outlines safety measures for service transparency, user data collection, and complaint handling.

Imposes rigorous safety assessment procedures and compliance for corpus, generated content, and question refusal rates.

category: U.S. state and local documents
title: Rhode Island Executive Order 24-06
document_name: Rhode Island EO 24-06 (AI and Data Centers of Excellence)
body:
Establishes a Chief Data Officer within the Department of Administration to oversee a Data Center of Excellence. Requires the creation of an AI Center of Excellence to develop AI policies, ethics, and training. Forms an AI Task Force to assess AI risks and opportunities.

Establishes a single state data governance structure, creating a federated data platform to manage data effectively across Rhode Island state agencies.

Mandates the Department of Administration (DOA) to appoint a Chief Data Officer (CDO) to oversee the Data Center of Excellence, enhancing data operations and readiness for AI integration.

Creates an AI Center of Excellence to formulate AI policies and ethics, minimizing bias and guiding AI implementation in state operations.

Directs all state agencies to participate in the federated data system, sharing data for policy analysis and exploring AI applications to improve operations.

Forms an AI Task Force to assess AI risks and opportunities, providing advice to policymakers.

Instructs the Department of Labor and Training (DLT), Rhode Island Department of Education (RIDE), and Office of Post Secondary Commissioner (OPC) to develop AI training programs for state and private-sector workers, integrating AI topics into existing curricula.

category: U.S. regulations, executive orders, and agency policies
title: Pay Flexibility, Incentive Pay, and Leave and Workforce Flexibility Programs for Artificial Intelligence (AI), AI-enabling, and Other Key Technical Employees (OPM)
document_name: Pay Flexibility, Incentive Pay, and Leave and Workforce Flexibility Programs for Artificial Intelligence (AI), AI-enabling, and Other Key Technical Employees (OPM)
body:
Allows agencies to use various pay and workforce flexibilities to recruit and retain AI talent without OPM approval. Permits recruitment, relocation, and retention incentives, superior qualifications pay, and alternative work schedules. Authorizes telework, remote work, and student loan repayment.

Grants agencies discretionary authority to use various pay flexibilities, incentive pay, and leave and workforce flexibility programs to recruit, relocate, and retain AI and key technical employees.

Allows recruitment, relocation, and retention incentives up to 25% of basic pay, and provides for waivers to increase this limit to 50% based on critical needs.

Enables agencies to repay student loans as an incentive, with limits of $10,000 annually and $60,000 total per employee.

Permits setting higher pay rates for employees with superior qualifications or special needs, and requests OPM approval for special rates and critical position pay.

Authorizes alternative work schedules, telework, and remote work to enhance recruitment and retention.

Provides service credit for non-Federal work experience towards higher annual leave accrual rates.

Encourages collaboration with agency officials to design tailored recruitment and retention strategies utilizing available human resources tools.

category: U.S. state and local documents
title: Executive order No. 78 (St. Louis)
document_name: St. Louis Executive Order No. 87 (police use of AI)
body:
Limits SLMPD's AI use to cases with reasonable suspicion of criminal activity. Requires SLMPD to publish policies on AI and surveillance technology use. Mandates annual transparency reports. Prohibits unauthorized sharing of data. Demands vendor compliance with privacy standards.

Establishes transparency and accountability requirements for the St. Louis Metropolitan Police Department’s (SLMPD) use of surveillance technology, including artificial intelligence (AI).

Prohibits using surveillance technology to monitor political, religious, or social groups unless tied to criminal activity or public safety threats.

Mandates public, written policies for SLMPD’s use of surveillance technology and AI.

Requires annual transparency reports detailing the SLMPD’s surveillance technology usage, capabilities, impacts, and related complaints.

Obliges vendors to protect data privacy, prohibiting unauthorized access or sale of collected data.

Ensures compliance with federal and state laws regarding data storage, retention, and access.

Directs cooperation with the City’s Information Technology Services for technology acquisitions.

Requires adherence to 28 C.F.R. Part 23 for participation in criminal intelligence systems.

Mandates policies for data sharing, following "need to know" and "right to know" standards for law enforcement agencies.

category: Multinational
title: Commission Decision Establishing the European AI Office
document_name: Commission Decision Establishing the European AI Office
body:
Establishes the European Artificial Intelligence Office to implement and enforce forthcoming AI regulations. Tasks include developing evaluation tools, monitoring AI risks, supporting international cooperation, fostering innovation, and coordinating with stakeholders. Operates under the Directorate-General for Communication Networks, Content and Technology.

Establishes the European Artificial Intelligence Office within the Directorate-General for Communication Networks, Content and Technology to oversee AI advancements and enforce the forthcoming Regulation on AI.

Mandates the Office to develop tools and methodologies for evaluating general-purpose AI models, monitor AI market evolution, and investigate potential regulation infringements.

Requires collaboration with stakeholders, including the scientific community and AI developers, to advance best practices and codes of conduct.

Coordinates with national authorities and EU bodies to ensure uniform application and enforcement of AI regulations.

Supports international cooperation and the promotion of the EU's approach to trustworthy AI.

Tasks the Office with assisting the Commission in preparing relevant decisions and facilitating the uniform application of AI regulations.

Finances the Office through redeployment of resources from the Directorate-General and the Digital Europe Programme. 

Enters into force on 21 February 2024.

category: U.S. state and local documents
title: Massachusetts Executive Order 629
document_name: Massachusetts EO 629 (AI Strategic Task Force)
body:
Establishes an AI Strategic Task Force in Massachusetts to study AI impacts and recommend strategies. Advises the Governor on AI-related development, investment, job creation, and responsible use policies. Requires regular meetings and submission of a comprehensive report.

Establishes an AI Strategic Task Force within the Office of the Governor of Massachusetts to study AI and Generative AI (GenAI) technologies and their impacts on the state.

Charges the Task Force with advising the Governor on making Massachusetts a leader in AI research and development.

Requires the Task Force to identify collaboration opportunities in key industries such as life sciences, healthcare, and finance, and explore public investments in AI.

Advises on AI-related job creation, assessing workforce impacts, and suggesting workforce training.

Recommends policies for responsible AI development, addressing ethical concerns like bias, privacy, and security.

Empowers the Task Force to convene subcommittees for addressing specific AI issues.

Obligates the Task Force to submit a report summarizing its work and recommendations to the Governor.

Specifies an effective date immediately after issuance until 30 days post-report submission.

category: U.S. regulations, executive orders, and agency policies
title: Inventorship Guidance for AI-Assisted Inventions
document_name: Inventorship Guidance for AI-Assisted Inventions
body:
Requires inventors and joint inventors on U.S. patents to be natural persons, excluding AI systems as inventors. Allows AI-assisted inventions to be patented if natural persons significantly contribute. Emphasizes compliance with inventorship requirements under U.S. patent statutes.

Mandates that inventors named on U.S. patents and applications must be natural persons, reaffirming that AI systems cannot be recognized as inventors.

Clarifies that AI-assisted inventions are not unpatentable due to improper inventorship, provided a natural person significantly contributed to the invention's conception.

Requires that patent applications for AI-assisted inventions name natural persons who meet the Pannu factors as inventors, ensuring each claim has a human contributor.

Outlines the duty of disclosure and reasonable inquiry, emphasizing the importance of factual inventorship claims and compliance with regulations.

Establishes guidelines for correcting inventorship errors and emphasizes that AI systems cannot hold inventorship rights.

Applies guidance to design and plant patents, affirming that significant human contribution is necessary for patent eligibility.

Prohibits naming AI systems as inventors in priority claims for U.S. patents and applications, ensuring compliance with U.S. inventorship requirements.

category: U.S. state and local documents
title: State of North Dakota Artificial Intelligence Policy
document_name: North Dakota Artificial Intelligence Policy
body:
Establishes policy for North Dakota's AI use to ensure safety, privacy, and ethical standards. Requires AI reliability, transparency, and accountability. Mandates risk management, privacy assessments, and compliance with legal frameworks. Directs NDIT to provide training and evaluate new AI technologies.

Requires entities in North Dakota’s executive branch to ensure AI technologies are reliable, valid, and transparent, with clear explanations of AI use and marked AI decision-making involving medium to high-risk data.

Mandates accountability for secure AI development, compliance with laws and standards, and prohibits using state-managed passwords for third-party apps.

Incorporates NDIT’s Security Risk Management Program in AI operations, mandates regular risk assessments, and restricts inputting moderate/high-risk data into public AI/ML services.

Requires NDIT to offer AI training and workshops, maintain an AI technology inventory, and ensure entities use vetted technologies.

Demands compliance with data protection laws, ethical AI use, and fairness without bias.

Stipulates AI must adhere to legal standards, including copyright, with review of licensing agreements and recognition that AI-generated content lacks copyright protection.

category: U.S. regulations, executive orders, and agency policies
org: Department of Health and Human Services
title: Part 170: Health Data, Technology, and Interoperability: Certification Program Updates, Algorithm Transparency, and Information Sharing
document_name: Part 170: Health Data, Technology, and Interoperability: Certification Program Updates, Algorithm Transparency, and Information Sharing
body:
Adds definitions for "Predictive Decision Support Intervention" (Predictive DSI) involving AI algorithms for healthcare decision-making. Requires certification and configuration of AI-based decision support systems, ensuring fairness, transparency, risk management, and external validation processes. Establishes standards for data interoperability and API access.

Amends health IT certification criteria to include "Predictive Decision Support Intervention," addressing decision-making support based on algorithms for predictions, classifications, and recommendations.

Mandates that health IT systems enable recording of patient demographics, including race, ethnicity, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, and pronouns, using specified standards.

Requires health IT modules to be updated to meet new certification criteria and provide updates to customers as per defined dates.

Outlines certification criteria for health IT, including decision support interventions that must be evidence-based and use specified data standards.

Establishes risk management practices for predictive decision support interventions, including risk analysis, mitigation, and governance.

Incorporates by reference various health information standards, including HL7, LOINC, and SNOMED CT, to ensure interoperability and accuracy in electronic health information exchange.

category: U.S. state and local documents
title: DC Mayor's Orders 2024-028
document_name: DC MO 2024-028 (AI Values and Strategic Benchmarks)
body:
Establishes an AI Advisory Group and AI Taskforce to guide responsible AI deployment in the District of Columbia. Requires agencies to align AI tools with values of benefit, safety, equity, accountability, transparency, sustainability, and privacy. Defines strategic AI benchmarks.

Establishes six core AI Values that District of Columbia agencies must assess before deploying AI tools, specifically focusing on benefits, safety, accountability, transparency, sustainability, and privacy.

Forms an AI Advisory Group and an AI Taskforce to align AI Values, conduct community engagement, support governance, and advise the Mayor on AI use.

Instructs the Office of the Chief Technology Officer, Department of Human Resources, and other agencies to develop privacy, cybersecurity, recruitment, and procurement benchmarks by specified deadlines.

Requires agencies to submit AI strategic plans addressing potential improvements, risks, and stakeholder engagement by designated dates.

Charges the AI Taskforce with providing technical advice, reporting on progress, and ensuring compliance with strategic benchmarks.

Mandates that the Advisory Group and AI Taskforce sunset on December 31, 2026. 

Requires these bodies to provide ongoing guidance, review AI tools, and align technology use with the District's stated AI Values.

category: U.S. state and local documents
title: Alabama Executive Order No. 738
document_name: Alabama Executive Order No. 738 (PROVIDING FOR THE RESPONSIBLE AND PRODUCTIVE USE OF GENERATIVE AI IN STATE GOV)
body:
Establishes a Task Force on Generative AI to encourage responsible use in state agencies. Requires reports on GenAI use by May 2024 and policy recommendations by November 2024. Directs the Office of Information Technology to facilitate GenAI pilot projects and development.

Establishes the Governor’s Task Force on Generative Artificial Intelligence to evaluate and promote the responsible use of GenAI in Alabama's executive-branch agencies.

Requires the Task Force to submit a report by November 30, 2024, detailing GenAI use, risks, and recommendations for its governance framework within state government, including data management, model monitoring, and human oversight.

Instructs each state executive-branch agency to submit an inventory of their GenAI use by May 1, 2024, detailing vendor information, capabilities, and safety measures.

Directs the Office of Information Technology to establish a secure cloud infrastructure for GenAI pilot projects, encouraging state agencies to test and utilize GenAI responsibly.

Encourages state executive-branch agencies to explore GenAI applications in collaboration with experts for improving government services and employee performance.

Specifies that the order affects executive-branch entities and does not create private enforceable rights.

category: 영국
title: [영국] AI 규제에 대한 혁신친화적 접근: 의견수렴에 대한 정부 답변
document_name: A pro-innovation approach to AI regulation: government response to consultation/ 「AI 규제에 대한 혁신친화적 접근: 의견수렴에 대한 정부 답변」
body:
●국가: 영국
●기관: 과학혁신기술부(DSIT)
●문서종류: AI 규제정책 / 정부 답변서
●문서명: A pro-innovation approach to AI regulation: government response to consultation/ 「AI 규제에 대한 혁신친화적 접근: 의견수렴에 대한 정부 답변」
●발표시점: 2024년 2월 6일
●핵심내용영국 정부가 2023년 AI 규제 백서 의견수렴 결과를 반영해 발표한 답변서. 별도 단일 AI 규제기관을 신설하기보다 기존 분야별 규제기관이 안전성, 투명성, 공정성, 책임성, 이의제기 가능성 등 공통 원칙을 각 분야 맥락에 맞게 적용하는 방식을 유지함. 동시에 고성능 범용 AI 시스템 개발자에 대한 향후 구속적 요건 가능성도 검토하겠다고 밝힘.
①영국식 AI 규제모델의 기본 방향을 “혁신친화적, 맥락기반, 원칙중심” 접근으로 정리
②AI 전용 포괄법보다 기존 규제기관의 분야별 감독역량을 활용하는 방식을 우선
③규제기관들에게 2024년 4월까지 AI 전략 접근방식 공개를 요청
④AI Management Essentials 등 기업의 최소 모범관행 기준 마련 추진
⑤고성능 범용 AI 시스템에 대해서는 안전성 평가, 투명성, 책임성 등 구속적 요건 도입 가능성을 검토

category: U.S. state and local documents
title: South Dakota 2024 Senate Bill 79
document_name: South Dakota SB 79 (Child Pornography)
body:
Defines "computer-generated child pornography" to include AI-generated images indistinguishable from minors in sexual acts. Criminalizes possession, distribution, and manufacturing of such content, with severe felony penalties. Prohibits defenses based on consent or age mistake. Recognizes mitigating sentencing circumstances.

Defines "computer-generated child pornography" to include AI-generated depictions indistinguishable from actual minors engaged in prohibited sexual acts.

Criminalizes possession, distribution, and manufacture of child pornography, including AI-generated content, with varying felony classes and mandatory minimum sentences for first and subsequent offenses.

Prohibits defenses based on consent or mistaken age, but allows an affirmative defense if the depiction is solely of the person charged.

Mandates court assessments for convicted individuals and allows sentence mitigation in specific circumstances.

Requires prior out-of-state convictions for similar offenses to be considered in determining repeat offenses.

Specifies that certain materials with serious value are exempt from these prohibitions.

Incorporates offenses involving child pornography into the definitions of sex crimes, impacting registration and sentencing.

Addresses juvenile sexting, deeming it a misdemeanor if minors distribute or possess nude images or participate in prohibited acts using digital media.

category: U.S. state and local documents
title: Artificial Intelligence for California Research Act
document_name: Artificial Intelligence for California Research Act
body:
Directs the California Department of Technology to develop and implement a research plan on how AI can improve state and local services, including analysis of the risks and benefits of various use cases, best practices from other governments, guidelines for risk management, monitoring, and evaluation, and privacy. Instructs the Department of Technology to submit a report on its findings to the legislature.

Directs the California Department of Technology to develop and implement a research plan on the feasibility and risks of advanced technologies, specifically AI, to improve state and local government services.

Requires the research plan to include an analysis of the potential benefits and risks of using AI chatbots/assistance in various government benefit and welfare programs (such as disability insurance or affordable housing), a review of best practices from other governments, a cost-benefit analysis of implementing AI in government services, recommendations for effective integration (including risk management and monitoring and evaluation guidelines), and recommendations for mitigating privacy issues.

Instructs the Department of Technology to report its findings to the legislature before January 1, 2026.

category: U.S. state and local documents
title: An act to add Chapter 5.9 (commencing with Section 11549.80) to Part 1 of Division 3 of Title 2 of, the Government Code, relating to state government.
document_name: California AI-ware Act
body:
Establishes California’s Office of Artificial Intelligence to guide state agencies' design, use, and deployment of automated systems in a manner that minimizes bias and promotes privacy and civil liberties. Requires state agencies to inform users when they interact with an AI system, and provide instructions to reach a non-AI contact.

Establishes the Office of Artificial Intelligence in the California Department of Technology, which will guide state agencies' design, use, and deployment of automated systems in a manner that minimizes bias and promotes privacy and civil liberties.  

Requires state agencies to inform users they are interacting with an AI system, and provide instructions on how the user can reach a non-AI representative.

category: U.S. state and local documents
title: An act to add Chapter 25 (commencing with Section 22756) to Division 8 of the Business and Professions Code, relating to artificial intelligence.
document_name: AB-331 Automated decision tools
body:
Governs the use of artificial intelligence for making consequential decisions that affect others (on education, healthcare, etc.), including by banning tools that exhibit algorithmic discrimination and requiring impact assessments, disclosures, monitoring, and human alternatives.

Defines an automated decision tool as any tool that uses artificial intelligence to make consequential decisions relating to employment, education, housing, utilities, healthcare and family planning, financial services, criminal justice, legal services, voting, or government benefits.

Bans the use of automated decision tools in ways that result in algorithmic discrimination on the basis of classes protected by state law. 

Requires any entity that develops or deploys an automated decision tool to perform an impact assessment on the tool, covering its purpose, outputs, use cases, inputted data, and potential discriminatory impacts, and the monitoring, safeguard measures, and testing conducted to mitigate adverse consequences. The impact assessment must be updated annually and after any significant update to the tool, and be provided to the state's Civil Rights Department. 

Requires any entity that deploys an automated decision tool to provide individuals affected by the tool's decisions with a notice that the tool was used and information on the tool's purpose. 

Grants all individuals subject to an automated decision tool's decisions the right to instead have those decisions be made by a human, if technically feasible. 

Requires automated decision tool developers to provide the tool's deployers with documentation of the tool's limitations, training data, and testing. 

Requires the developer or deployer of an automated decision tool to implement a program that governs the foreseeable risks of the tool's use, including designating an employee to monitor the tool and report concerns. 

Permits individuals and public attorneys to bring civil action against entities that violate this law, and makes violation of the law punishable by fines.

Exempts entities with fewer than 25 employees using automated decision tools that affect less than 1,000 people per year from some of this law's provisions.

category: U.S. state and local documents
title: Washington Executive Order 24-01
document_name: Washington EO 24-01 (Artificial Intelligence)
body:
Instructs WaTech to report on generative AI initiatives and develop training plans. Requires WaTech and DES to provide procurement and usage guidelines. Mandates creating an accountability framework for generative AI's ethical use. Orders assessments of AI’s impact on communities and workforce by specific deadlines.

Orders WaTech, with cabinet agencies, to report on generative AI initiatives by September 2024, assessing feasibility, benefits, and challenges.

Directs WaTech and DES to issue guidelines for AI procurement focusing on safety, equity, and privacy by September 2024.

Requires DES and WaTech to develop an AI training plan for government workers by January 2025.

Instructs WaTech to create guidelines for AI's community impact, focusing on equity and algorithmic bias by December 2024.

Mandates DES and WaTech to update procurement templates to include equity and risk considerations by January 2025.

Tasks the Office of Equity to develop an accountability framework for AI equity and ethics by September 2024.

Ensures WaTech provides risk assessment guidance for high-risk AI systems by December 2024.

title: Utah H.B. 366 (Criminal Justice Amendments 2024, Section 9–15)
document_name: Utah H.B. 366 (Criminal Justice Amendments 2024, Section 9–15)
body:
Prohibits reliance solely on algorithms or risk assessment tool scores in determining court-approved diversions, sentencing, probation decisions, pretrial release, and parole. Requires courts and related entities to consider various factors beyond automated tools when making such determinations.

Prohibits reliance solely on algorithms or risk assessment tool scores in determining pretrial release, sentencing, probation conditions, probation termination, and granting or terminating parole (Sections 77-2-5, 77-18-103, 77-18-105, 77-27-5, 77-20-205).

Requires magistrates and judges to rely on other forms of evidence and consider various factors beyond algorithmic scores when making pretrial release decisions (Sections 77-20-205).

Instructs the Administrative Office of the Courts to submit data, including pretrial risk assessment scores to the Commission on Criminal and Juvenile Justice, indicating some continued use of these scores for data collection and analysis (Section 78A-2-109.5).

Mandates that parole and probation decisions be informed by additional context rather than algorithmic evaluations alone (Sections 77-27-5, 77-18-105).

Sets an effective date for the legislation as May 1, 2024 (Section 15).

category: Miscellaneous documents
title: Safe and Responsible AI in Australia Consultation, Interim Response
document_name: Safe and Responsible AI in Australia Consultation, Interim Response
body:
Considers mandatory safety guardrails for high-risk AI applications. Plans to consult on regulatory frameworks, including testing and transparency. Collaborates internationally on AI safety. Focuses on balancing innovation with risk management, enhancing privacy laws, and addressing misinformation.

Proposes strengthening existing laws and considering new legislation to address AI-related risks, particularly in high-risk settings.

Considers mandatory safety guardrails for AI systems in high-risk contexts, focusing on testing, transparency, and accountability.

Plans to work with industry to develop a voluntary AI Safety Standard and explore options for voluntary labelling and watermarking of AI-generated materials.

Emphasizes a risk-based regulatory framework to ensure proportionality and avoid unnecessary burdens on low-risk AI applications.

Commits to collaborating with international partners, aligning with global standards, and contributing to initiatives like the Bletchley Declaration on AI safety.

Supports investments in AI capability development and aims to maximize AI benefits, including through initiatives funded by the 2023–24 Budget.

Establishes an interim expert advisory group to explore AI guardrail options and harmonizes efforts with state and territory governments.

body:

title: Proposed Model AI Governance Framework for Generative AI
document_name: Proposed Model AI Governance Framework for Generative AI
body:
Establishes a Model AI Governance Framework addressing generative AI concerns through accountability, data management, trusted development, incident reporting, testing, security, content provenance, safety R&D, and public good. Calls for global collaboration to balance innovation with responsible AI use.

Proposes a Model AI Governance Framework for Generative AI emphasizing accountability, data quality, trusted development, and deployment, aligning with global best practices.

Establishes accountability by encouraging clear responsibility allocation among stakeholders within AI development chains and calls for extending cloud shared responsibility models to AI.

Emphasizes data quality, including the use of trusted data sources and addressing issues around personal data and copyright material for model training.

Calls for transparency in AI model safety measures, akin to "food labels," and suggests industry-standard practices for development, safety evaluation, and disclosure.

Proposes implementing incident reporting and third-party testing frameworks for AI safety and assurance.

Advocates for security measures specifically adapted for generative AI, including new tools and methods.

Highlights the importance of research in AI safety and alignment, international cooperation, and the use of AI for public good, including democratization of access and responsible AI adoption in public services.

category: U.S. state and local documents
title: Maryland State Executive Order 01.01.2024.02
document_name: Maryland State Executive Order 01.01.2024.02 (Use of AI in Maryland State Government)
body:
Establishes an AI Subcabinet to ensure responsible AI use by Maryland state agencies, promoting principles of fairness, transparency, and innovation, while safeguarding privacy and security. Requires development of an AI Action Plan and training programs for state employees.

Establishes an AI Subcabinet to oversee AI use in Maryland state government, fostering principles such as fairness, innovation, privacy, safety, and transparency.

Directs the AI Subcabinet to create an AI Action Plan incorporating NIST’s AI Risk Management Framework to ensure adherence to AI principles.

Instructs the Subcabinet to upskill the state workforce in AI and explore partnerships with external AI talent for targeted projects.

Mandates the study of AI's impact on critical domains, including workforce and economic development, and the provision of recommendations to the Governor and legislature.

Requires the Department of Information Technology to assess infrastructure for safely testing AI prototypes and collaborate with the Department of General Services to create procedures for AI pilots.

Ensures AI initiatives align with state and federal laws and does not impair existing authorities, remaining severable if parts are invalidated.

title:
An act to amend the labor law, in relation to establishing criteria for
the use of automated employment decision tools
document_name: Automated Employment Decision Tools Amendment to NY Labor Law
body:
Makes it unlawful for an employer in New York to use or implement an automated decision tool to  filter employment candidates or prospective candidates for hire that has not undergone a disparate impact assessment annually.

Makes it unlawful for an employer in New York to use or implement an automated decision tool to filter employment candidates or prospective candidates for hire that has not undergone an disparate impact assessment annually.

Requires employers to provide the department with a summary of their most recent disparate impact analysis annually. Allows the Attorney General and Commissioner to initiate investigations and legal action if violations are suspected or found. Requires a summary of the most recent disparate impact analysis of the automated decision tool and the distribution date of the tool to be made publicly available on the website of the employer prior to implementing the tool.

title: An act to amend the executive law, in relation to creating the office of  algorithmic innovation
document_name: NY Office of Algorithmic Innovation Act
body:
Establishes an Office of Algorithmic Innovation in New York to promote algorithmic innovation and ensure algorithms are safe, effective, and ethical.

Establishes an Office of Algorithmic Innovation in New York to create policies and set standards that ensure algorithms are safe, effective, and ethical, and that the state is conducive to promoting algorithmic innovation. 

Provides the Office the power to set standards, audit, and establish statewide policy on algorithms used in technology.

category: U.S. state and local documents
title: An Act to amend the labor law, in relation to automated employment decision tools
document_name: New York AB A7859
body:
Requires employers and employment agencies to notify job candidates when automated employment decision tools are used to screen candidates.

Requires employers and employment agencies that use automated employment decision tools to inform job applicants:
(1) That such a tool is being used to screen candidates.
(2) Of which characteristics and qualifications the automated tool considers.
(3) Of what data is collected by the automated tool, where it is sourced, and how it is managed.

Defines "automated employment decision tool" as any computational process that produces an output which is used to substantially assist or replace discretionary decision-making for employment decisions that impact natural persons.

category: U.S. state and local documents
title: An Act to amend the general business law, the executive law, the state finance law and the education law, in relation to enacting the "digital fairness act" - Sections 7-9 ("AUTOMATED DECISION SYSTEM IMPACT ASSESSMENTS," etc.)
document_name: Digital Fairness Act - Sections 7-9 ("AUTOMATED DECISION SYSTEM IMPACT ASSESSMENTS," etc.)
body:
Require the state to conduct ADS Impact Assessments before use. Mandate neutral third-party evaluations on impacts. Prohibit ADS purchase/use without publishing the assessment and public comments. Obligate a list of qualified assessors. Demand plain-language notifications and human review mechanisms. Ban payments for non-compliant ADS.

Require the state and its entities to conduct Automated Decision System (ADS) Impact Assessments before using any ADS.

Mandate the engagement of a neutral third party to evaluate the ADS, focusing on statistical impacts on protected classes, privacy, and security.

Prohibit purchasing or using ADS without publishing the assessment and considering public comments.

Obligate the state to maintain a list of qualified neutral third parties for conducting assessments.

Require a comprehensive study on the impacts of ADS, particularly on protected classes, to be published within two years.

Demand plain-language notifications to individuals affected by ADS decisions and provide mechanisms for human review.

Ban payments for ADS that do not use open-source software or comply with assessment and policy requirements.

document_name: Patent Landscape Report: Generative Artificial Intelligence / 「생성형 인공지능 특허 지형 보고서」
body:
●기관: WIPO
●문서종류: 특허 지형 보고서 / 기술동향 분석 보고서
●문서명: Patent Landscape Report: Generative Artificial Intelligence / 「생성형 인공지능 특허 지형 보고서」
●발표시점: 2024년
●핵심내용:동 보고서는 생성형 AI(GenAI) 분야의 특허 패밀리와 과학논문 데이터를 분석해 기술개발 동향, 주요 기업·기관, 발명자 소재국, 모델·데이터 유형, 응용 분야를 파악한 WIPO 특허 지형 보고서임. 보고서는 2022년 ChatGPT 공개 이후 생성형 AI에 대한 관심과 투자가 급증했으나, 특허·논문 증가세는 특히 2017년 트랜스포머 아키텍처 등장 이후 본격화되었다고 분석함.
① 보고서는 생성형 AI 특허와 과학논문이 2014~2023년 급증했으며, 특히 최근 확산모델과 LLM 관련 특허 증가를 통해 기술개발이 빠르게 가속되고 있다고 분석함
② 생성형 AI 특허는 중국이 압도적 비중을 차지하고 미국·한국·일본·인도 등이 뒤를 이으며, 주요 기업·기관과 상위 발명지역에 특허 활동이 집중되어 있다고 제시함
③ 생성형 AI 활용이 소프트웨어·생명과학·제조·교통·보안 등으로 확대되는 가운데, 저작권 침해·오용·딥페이크·편향·환각·노동시장 충격 등 위험도 함께 제기함

body:
As of January 2024, the FVU (Preparatory Adult Education) programme in Denmark includes new learning objectives on digital problem solving. The curriculum introduces basic concepts of generative AI, its uses, limitations, and practical applications in everyday life. It helps adults develop digital skills relevant to employment, education, and personal life.

In January 2024, Denmark updated its Preparatory Adult Education (FVU) curricula to include a focus on digital problem solving, with specific attention to generative AI. The initiative addresses the need to equip adults, particularly low-skilled learners, with practical digital skills that are increasingly relevant in daily life, work, and study.
The curriculum aims to help students:
Understand generative AI and its basic concepts.Recognize practical applications of AI in personal and professional contexts.Identify possibilities and limitations of AI tools for solving everyday tasks.Apply AI tools to tasks related to employment, further education, or private life.While the main target group remains low-skilled adults, the educational offer has been expanded to a broader audience. This ensures more learners have access to essential digital skills that support employability and personal development.
The initiative also reflects a broader trend in adult education towards integrating digital literacy and AI awareness into foundational programmes. Over time, the curriculum is expected to evolve, incorporating more interactive tools, practical exercises, and guidance to help learners effectively navigate AI technologies in their personal and professional lives.

title: myEESZT
document_name: EgészségAblak
body:
EgészségAblak (myEESZT) is Hungary’s national mobile health app, launched in Q2 2024 as part of the Recovery and Resilience Plan. Managed by the Ministry of the Interior, it offers secure access to personal health records, prescriptions, appointments, and vaccination data. By mid-2025, it surpassed 170,000 active users. The app aims to enhance patient engagement and healthcare efficiency, with full rollout expected by June 2026.

EgészségAblak (myEESZT) is Hungary’s national mobile front end to the EESZT e-health infrastructure. Beyond viewing prescriptions and records, the app provides access—after electronic identification and TAJ verification—to EESZT-stored medical documents (e.g., lab results, discharge summaries), vaccination credentials, appointment details (Calendar/“Időpontok”), and COVID certificates. Users can also check social insurance status, and manage proxy access so a parent/guardian or authorised person can view a dependent’s records where legal representation is registered.

It focuses on standardising metadata through the adoption of health DCAT-AP, harmonising de-identification procedures, and ensuring interoperability for seamless data sharing among health data access bodies, data holders, and users within the HealthData@EU ecosystem.

The TEHDAS (Towards the European Health Data Space) joint action supports the rollout of the European Health Data Space (EHDS2) by developing 20 guidelines and technical specifications. Its work covers standardising metadata through the adoption of health DCAT-AP, harmonising de-identification methods, and enabling interoperability between health data access bodies, data holders, and users. The project underpins the HealthData@EU ecosystem, aiming to ensure that secondary use of health data is secure, consistent, and usable across borders.

title: embrAIsme - Improving Conditions and Policies for SMEs to Embrace AI
document_name: embrAIsme - Improving Conditions and Policies for SMEs to Embrace AI
body:
EmbrAIsme is an Interreg Europe project co-financed by the Austrian Federal Chancellery which aims to encourage uptake of AI by SMEs, in particular by raising awareness of AI and the importance of AI skills, facilitating access to funding and building tools to ease the compliance burden of SMEs.

The Interreg Europe project embrAIsme, led by Austria Wirtschaftsservice (aws), fosters collaboration between partners from Finland, Ireland, Spain, Portugal, Bulgaria, Serbia, and Slovenia to enhance SME support for AI adoption. Running for four years from April 2024, the project is co-financed by the Federal Chancellery of Austria and aims to accelerate AI integration in small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) by addressing cultural resistance in SMEs, skill gaps, regulatory challenges, and limited funding access.AI offers vast potential for productivity, innovation, and competitiveness, yet many SMEs struggle with adoption due to internal resistance, lack of expertise, and uncertainty about AI's value. Structural barriers such as funding constraints, regulatory complexity, skill shortages, and insufficient infrastructure further hinder progress. embrAIsme seeks to create an enabling environment for AI adoption by improving policies, providing financial incentives, clarifying regulations, and raising awareness.The project focuses on six core intervention areas: Government Initiatives and Support, Access to Finance, Legal and Ethical Issues, Human Capital & Skills, Infrastructure and Technology Access, and Collaborative Networks and Ecosystems. Through study visits, workshops with AI experts and a strong focus on networking, policy recommendations will be provided to specific policy instruments to improve concepts and frameworks of funding opportunities and regulatory guidance needed for AI integration. By fostering knowledge-sharing, leadership engagement, and hands-on training, the initiative ensures SMEs across diverse regions benefit from AI-driven advancements.As AI adoption grows, the project will play a key role in maintaining SME competitiveness in an increasingly digital economy. Initial findings highlight cultural resistance in SMEs as a major challenge, prompting a stronger focus on leadership engagement, best-practice case studies, and AI-readiness initiatives. By continuously refining its strategies based on stakeholder insights, embrAIsme ensures that European SMEs are well-equipped to leverage AI for sustainable growth and innovation.

title: White Paper on AI Regulation in Ukraine
document_name: Біла книга з регулювання ШІ в Україні
body:
This initiative aims to create a clear and ethical framework for the development and use of artificial intelligence (AI) in Ukraine. It laid the foundation for a bottom-up and gradual approach to AI regulation and alignment with the EU AI Act, starting from the self-regulation environment in Ukraine. The initiative addresses the need to regulate AI to protect rights and boost innovation responsibly and it serves as a key AI policy framework.

The AI initiative outlined in the White Paper aims to establish a comprehensive and ethical framework for the development, deployment, and governance of artificial intelligence technologies in Ukraine. The White Paper on AI Regulation (White Paper) was developed in 2024 based on the AI Regulation Roadmap. It laid the foundation for the bottom-up and gradual approach to AI regulation and alignment with the EU AI Act. 
 
The essence of the approach is to divide the path to mandatory regulation into two stages: 
1. The preparatory stage (2-3 years, before the adoption of a law that is analogous to the EU AI Act) includes facilitation of self- and co-regulation among stakeholders and providing them tools for compliance.
2. The implementation stage of law that is analogous to the EU AI Act. By that moment, Ukraine is ensuring the state’s and the industry's capacity to regulate and comply accordingly.
According to the White Paper, Ukraine is currently implementing the first stage of approach, which includes such policy instruments and soft law tools as:
Sandbox;adaptation of the Council of Europe HUDERIA methodology;support of signment of the Voluntary Code of Conduct between AI companies and further establishment of self-regulatory organisations (currently 14 companies have signed it);publication of guidelines on AI for various sectors (guidelines for developers, higher educational institutions, civil servants, schools, intellectual property field, media, advertisement sector were already released. Guidelines for lawyers, courts, HR and some others are being developed)Also, the Glossary of Terms on AI was developed as part of the implementation of the AI Regulation Roadmap and White Paper.
These measures introduce self-regulatory measures to ensure safe, secure AI deployment, respect human rights, and prepare stakeholders for future regulation.  

Looking ahead, the initiative is expected to evolve through phased implementation and institutionalization within government structures, including the creation of dedicated bodies or commissions to oversee AI governance. It envisions continuous monitoring, evaluation, and updating of AI policies to keep pace with technological advancements. The initiative may also expand to cover cross-sectoral applications and international cooperation, aligning Ukraine’s AI policies with global best practices and standards."

category: Regulations, guidelines and standards
org: Ministry of Digital Transformation of Ukraine
title: Voluntary Code of Conduct for the Ethical and Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence
document_name: Добровільний кодекс поведінки з етичного та відповідального використання ШІ
body:
Voluntary Code of Conduct for the Ethical and Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence provides organisations and developers with ethical and practical guidelines for the responsible use of artificial intelligence (AI) in Ukraine. It was developed to promote trust, accountability, and safety in AI systems across the public and private sectors. The Code helps organisations use AI in ways that respect human rights and democratic values.

The Voluntary Code of Conduct for the Ethical and Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence is a soft-law initiative launched by Ukraine’s Ministry of Digital Transformation in 2024. It was developed as part of Ukraine’s broader efforts to establish a human-centric AI governance framework. The Code provides non-binding but structured guidance for public and private sector organisations that develop, deploy, or manage artificial intelligence (AI) systems. Its core aim is to promote ethical, transparent, and trustworthy AI practices that respect human rights, democratic values, and the rule of law.
Impact:
The initiative addresses the need for ethical safeguards and public trust in the face of rapidly advancing AI technologies. As AI becomes more integrated into everyday life and decision-making, the risk of harm, discrimination, and opacity increases, especially in the absence of binding regulation. The Code serves as an interim, proactive measure while Ukraine prepares its legally binding AI legislation. It offers practical principles such as accountability, transparency, fairness, safety, and privacy. Importantly, it emphasises that the degree and manner in which each principle is applied should correspond to the characteristics of a given system and the level of potential risk it poses, in line with the OECD’s AI risk-based approach.Future outlook:
Looking ahead, the Code is expected to evolve into a living document, subject to updates as technologies and legal frameworks develop. It may also serve as a foundation for sector-specific codes of practice or certification schemes. The initiative is part of a broader national strategy to create a trustworthy AI ecosystem in Ukraine, and to align the country’s digital transformation with international best practices in AI governance."

category: Regulations, guidelines and standards

title: Voluntary AI Safety Standard
document_name: Voluntary AI Safety Standard
body:
The Voluntary AI Safety Standard gives practical guidance to all Australian organisations on how to safely and responsibly use and innovate with AI.The standard consists of 10 voluntary guardrails that apply to all organisations throughout the AI supply chain. They include transparency and accountability requirements across the supply chain. They also explain what developers and deployers of AI systems must do.

The 10 guardrails at a glance:1. Establish, implement and publish an accountability process including governance, internal capability and a strategy for regulatory compliance.2. Establish and implement a risk management process to identify and mitigate risks.3. Protect AI systems, and implement data governance measures to manage data quality and provenance.4. Test AI models and systems to evaluate model performance and monitor the system once deployed.5. Enable human control or intervention in an AI system to achieve meaningful human oversight across the life cycle.6. Inform end-users regarding AI-enabled decisions, interactions with AI and AI-generated content.7. Establish processes for people impacted by AI systems to challenge use or outcomes.8. Be transparent with other organisations across the AI supply chain about data, models and systems to help them effectively address risks.9. Keep and maintain records to allow third parties to assess compliance with guardrails.10. Engage your stakeholders and evaluate their needs and circumstances, with a focus on safety, diversity, inclusion and fairness.

title: Vision on Generative AI
document_name: Visie Generatieve AI
body:
As one of the first EU Member States, the Dutch government has presented a vision on generative AI. In this vision, the government emphasizes the urgent need to take action in light of the opportunities and challenges presented by this disruptive yet promising technology. The vision aligns with a series of investments worth millions of euros already made by research institutions, private enterprises, and the government, all aimed at AI, including generative AI, in the Netherlands.

Specific areas mentioned include:  Safety: Ensuring the safe development and use of generative AI, including mitigating misuse, accidents, and systemic safety risks. Justice: Ensuring lawful development and application that takes into account existing laws and regulations, equal opportunities, and non-discrimination. Well-being and autonomy: Promoting applications of generative AI that serve human well-being and secure human autonomy. Sustainability and prosperity: Encouraging generative AI that contributes to sustainability and increases prosperity. These policy areas imply a wide spectrum of actions, from promoting innovation (e.g. by pilots and promoting an AI-ecosystem) and education to engaging in international collaborations and enforcing and implementing regulation. The goal is to find a balance between leveraging the benefits of generative AI and managing the risks and challenges. The development of the government-wide vision on generative AI was characterized by an open approach with a wide range of involved stakeholders. These stakeholders ranged from experts in various domains to the general public, and their input was collected and assessed in various ways. Key points of this approach include:  Sectoral Sessions: Between June and November 2023, multiple sessions were held in sectors such as public administration, healthcare, employment, and the economy. During these sessions, input for the vision was collected, and it was continually checked that the vision covered the correct aspects. These conversations will continue into 2024. Collaborations: In collaboration with the ECP (Electronic Commerce Platform) and the Dutch AI Coalition (NL-AIC), meetings were organized with stakeholders from the media, higher education, healthcare, and the police to discuss ethical dilemmas surrounding generative AI. Awareness and Impact Analysis: Sessions were organized with Dutch citizens to raise awareness about generative AI and to gain insights into how people perceive the impact of generative AI on their lives and the role of the government in integrating this technology into society. Broad Representation: A working group on generative AI was set up with participants from various ministries, provinces (IPO), and municipalities (VNG) to ensure that the vision reflects a broad perspective on generative AI. Advisory Group: An advisory group with members representing diverse societal perspectives was established to test the vision from various angles. This approach underscores the importance of inclusivity and collaboration with a broad range of stakeholders to arrive at a well-supported and informed vision on generative AI.
