category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
org: National Fund for Environmental Protection and Water Management
title: New Energy
document_name: Nowa Energia
body:
The New Energy (Nowa Energia) programme in Poland supports entrepreneurs and local governments in adopting innovative energy technologies. It promotes solutions such as Smart Cities for Growth and Self-Sufficient Energy Clusters. The programme strengthens sustainable development in the energy sector and public services.

Launched in 2022, the New Energy (Nowa Energia) programme is a national initiative to drive innovation and sustainability in Poland’s energy sector. It provides financial and strategic support to both entrepreneurs and local government bodies, helping them test and implement modern energy solutions.
The programme has two main thematic areas:
Smart Cities for Growth – developing technologies that enhance urban sustainability and efficiency through smart energy systems.Self-Sufficient Energy Clusters – supporting local communities and municipalities in building decentralised, renewable-based energy systems to increase resilience and reduce reliance on external supply.Key objectives include:
Encouraging entrepreneurship and innovation in the energy sectorSupporting local governments and public service providers in sustainable transformationStrengthening energy self-sufficiency and resilience across regionsPromoting the development of green technologies aligned with EU sustainability goals

category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
title: National Test Beds Network
body:
The National Test Beds Network in Portugal helps companies and researchers test and apply new AI and digital technologies. It provides access to real environments, equipment, and infrastructure for safe experimentation. The initiative supports collaboration across business, academia, and research to speed up digital transformation in key sectors.

The National Test Beds Network in Portugal complements the country’s Digital Innovation Hubs by creating spaces where new AI and digital solutions can be tested in real-world conditions. It was established to respond to the need for safe, practical environments that allow businesses, especially small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), to experiment with emerging technologies before deploying them more widely.
The initiative has three main objectives:
Accelerate AI and digital adoption through targeted testing and experimentation programmes.Provide infrastructure and technical support so that companies can trial new products, services, and processes in realistic settings.Promote collaboration among companies, universities, and research centres to modernise strategic sectors of the economy.Implementation focuses on bringing together public and private actors, ensuring that companies of different sizes and technological maturity levels have access to cutting-edge resources. By enabling practical experimentation, the network reduces the risks of innovation and increases the chances that AI solutions can be effectively integrated into business operations.
Looking ahead, the initiative is expected to expand in scope, building stronger institutional frameworks and extending access to more regions and industries. By scaling further, the National Test Beds Network could help Portugal establish itself as a leader in AI-driven transformation and enhance the competitiveness of its companies at both the national and European levels.

category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
org: Danish Ministry of Higher Education and Science
title: National Strategy for Quantum Technology
body:
In 2022, the Danish Agency for Higher Education and Science published a research mapping on the quantum field. This shows that Danish quantum research is considered to be world-class in a number of fields and enjoys great international recognition. Over the last ten years, the activities of the Danish research institutions within the quantum area have been on the rise. New research groups have been established, and we have succeeded in recruiting several international top researchers.

In 2022, the Danish Agency for Higher Education and Science published a research mapping focused on quantum science and technology. This study showed that Danish quantum research is considered world-class in several areas and enjoys strong international recognition. Quantum science holds great promise for advancing computing, communications, and other technologies, and Denmark’s strong position highlights its potential to contribute significantly to these fields.
The main goal of the mapping was to assess Denmark’s strengths and identify opportunities in quantum research. This helps guide national policies and funding decisions to support and grow the country’s expertise in this important area. By understanding where Denmark stands globally, the government can better target investments and collaborations.
Over the past ten years, Danish research institutions have increased their quantum activities significantly. New research groups have been formed, and several top international researchers have been recruited. Universities and research centers across Denmark have created a vibrant environment for quantum research, often collaborating internationally. The Danish Agency for Higher Education and Science supports this work by monitoring progress and providing strategic backing.

category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
title: National Strategy for Advanced Computing
body:
Portugal was one of the six pioneering countries to sign the EuroHPC Declaration in March 2017. Through its National Strategy for Advanced Computing, the country aims to establish itself as a European reference point in three areas: an advanced computing services economy, a cutting-edge laboratory environment, and the education and training of specialists in this field.

Portugal's National Strategy for Advanced Computing aims to create a robust HPC infrastructure, drive research and innovation, and foster international collaboration. The strategy highlights the importance of developing appropriate infrastructure, building a skilled workforce, and cultivating a culture that recognises advanced computing as essential to research and industry. Key areas of focus include: 
i) establishing a supercomputing network with data centres to support research and innovation, 
ii) developing and retaining talent with advanced computing skills, and 
iii) creating a policy "info-structure" to bridge infrastructure and users, enabling high-value services and software. The Strategy plays a critical role in promoting advanced scientific computing and data processing across various domains, including industry, academia, health, climate, energy, mobility, and social sciences.

category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
org: Department for Digital Transformation; Agency for National Cybersecurity; National Strategic Hub S.p.A
title: National Strategic Hub
document_name: Polo Strategico Nazionale
body:
The Polo Strategico Nazionale (PSN) is Italy’s high-reliability cloud infrastructure for public administrations. It hosts critical and strategic data and services, aiming to improve security, resilience, and efficiency in government IT. The project forms a central part of Italy’s cloud-first strategy to have 75% of public administrations using cloud services by 2026.

The PSN was officially activated on 21 December 2022 under Italy’s National Recovery and Resilience Plan (PNRR), as part of Mission 1, Component 1, Investment 1.1 (“Cloud PA / Polo Strategico Nazionale”). Its aim is to provide public administrations—including central administrations, Local Health Units (ASLs), and the main regional/local administrations—with cloud infrastructure meeting high standards of security, sovereignty, operational continuity, and environmental sustainability.
Key features include:
Ownership and governance via Polo Strategico Nazionale S.p.A., a special purpose company jointly owned by TIM, Leonardo, Cassa Depositi e Prestiti (CDP via CDP Equity), and SOGEI. Four data centres located in Acilia and Pomezia (Lazio), and Rozzano and Santo Stefano Ticino (Lombardy), designed with high availability, fault tolerance, and elevated environmental standards.Strong emphasis on digital sovereignty, meaning the infrastructure is intended to be independent of non-EU entities for critical services, with certified high security, resilience, and compliance with cloud-first principles.The initiative also encompasses migration support: administrations whose infrastructures are considered insecure or critical are prioritised for migration to the PSN. By 2026, the goal is for 75% of Italian public administrations to be using cloud services, including via PSN.
Recent developments include AgID (the Agency for Digital Italy) formally joining or migrating some of its services to the PSN cloud under an agreement signed in May 2024. This migration follows the “cloud-native” and “cloud-first” architectural model, ensuring equivalence in functionality and architecture

category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
org: Department of Trade, Industry and Competition (DTIC)

title: National Integrated Cyber Infrastructure System (NICIS)
body:
The National Integrated Cyber Infrastructure System (NICIS) provides integrated high‑performance computing, high‑speed networking and national research data infrastructure to support research, education and industrial development.

NICIS is South Africa’s national framework for delivering shared cyberinfrastructure to the research and education communities. It integrates high‑performance computing capability, high‑speed network capacity and a national research data infrastructure into a hierarchically organised system that connects local resources with globally connected infrastructures, enabling seamless access for users across disciplines.
Through this integrated approach, NICIS brings together national supercomputing facilities, research data services and advanced research and education networks as a coordinated platform. The initiative is designed to promote scientific and industrial development by supporting data‑intensive research, skills development and innovation, and by enabling South African researchers and institutions to participate effectively in national, regional and international research collaborations.

category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
title: National Health Strategy 2030
body:
Priority 4, "Electronic Healthcare," aims to create a digital transformation strategy for the healthcare sector, focusing on building a unified digital platform for improved diagnostics and treatment of key diseases. It will enhance communication among stakeholders while addressing concerns such as data privacy, cybersecurity, and workforce capacity.

Priority 4, called “Electronic Healthcare,” aims to improve how health care uses digital technology to better diagnose and treat major diseases. Right now, health systems often struggle to share important medical information quickly and safely, which can slow down care and create risks for patient privacy.
The initiative’s main goal is to create one digital platform that connects doctors, hospitals, labs, and patients, making communication smoother and health data easier to access and use. It also focuses on protecting sensitive data and ensuring health workers have the skills to use these new tools effectively.
This platform will allow different health care providers to share information securely, helping doctors make faster, more accurate decisions. It involves health authorities, medical professionals, IT experts, and patients working together. The plan is to start with key diseases and regions, then gradually expand the system and train more staff.
Over time, this digital health network will grow to cover more services and improve care quality, making the healthcare system stronger and more responsive to patient needs.

title: National Genomic Data Infrastructure (GDI) Node and 1+ Million Genome Project
body:
Romania is working towards a national genome data infrastructure to contribute to the 1+ MG project and share its available genome data.

Romania is joining the European effort to share genome and clinical data through its involvement in the European Genomic Data Infrastructure (GDI), part of the wider 1+ Million Genomes (1+MG) initiative. This effort addresses the challenge that many countries have useful genetic and health data, but lack the systems and connections needed to use them safely across borders. By building its own infrastructure, Romania aims to make its data usable for research, medical advances, and improved patient care, while respecting privacy and legal rules.
The main goals are to enable secure access to high-quality human genome data and matching clinical information; to align Romania’s systems with agreed European standards so data can talk to each other; and to support national research and health services in using genome information for better diagnosis, treatments, and prevention. It also seeks to strengthen Romania’s role in European genomics, helping Romanian institutions participate fully in transnational research and healthcare innovations.
Romania has institutions like the Genomics Research and Development Institute and the Authority for Digitization of Romania participating in GDI. There is coordination with the “Carol Davila” University of Medicine and Pharmacy and the National Genomic Research Network. The plan is to establish a “National Mirror Group” or equivalent body, build or upgrade national genome data hubs, and ensure these meet legal, technical, and ethical standards required by the European framework (like data protection, data quality, interoperability). Romania contributes its existing genome datasets and clinical data under these conditions.

The data and technical infrastructure5. body:
Greek Law 4961/2022 regulates emerging technologies like AI, IoT, and 3D printing to ensure their safe, lawful use. It aims to modernize public services, enhance digital governance, and promote Greece's digital transformation. Beneficiaries include public and private entities, as well as citizens who will experience improved services and data protection. The initiative addresses the need for a structured framework to manage the rapid adoption of advanced technologies.

Greek Law 4961/2022 addresses the need for a structured framework to manage the rapid adoption of advanced technologies like AI, IoT, and 3D printing. It aims to modernize public services, enhance digital governance, and promote Greece's digital transformationObjectives:Ensure lawful, safe, and secure use of emerging technologies.Enhance public service efficiency and data protection.Promote innovation and digital transformation.The law will be implemented through sector-specific regulations and horizontal guidelines, ensuring adaptability and scalability. It will be institutionalized by establishing control mechanisms and enforcement bodies. Since its enactment, the law has seen updates to align with the EU's AI Act and other international standards, ensuring continuous improvement and relevance. Specifically on AI, law 4961/2022 defines:Algorithmic Impact Assessment (Article 5) - Requires public bodies to provide technical information and assess the impact of AI systems on rights, freedoms and social groups before implementation.Transparency obligations (Articles 4, 6) - Requires public sector entities to provide information about the operation, characteristics and decisions of AI systems.AI contractor obligations (Article 7) - Contractors developing AI for public entities must disclose technical details and ensure that systems comply with human rights legal frameworks.Registry of AI systems for public entities (Article 8) - Requires public entities to maintain and update a registry of AI systems in use, detailing their purpose, date of commissioning and measures for safe operation.Disclosure of AI use in the workplace (Article 9) - Requires private entities to inform employees and job applicants about the use of AI in decision-making processes affecting employment.Ethical data use policy (Article 10) - Requires large and medium-sized private entities to maintain a policy on the ethical use of data in AI applications, including procedures and measures for ethical compliance.AI Coordination Committee (Article 11) - A committee responsible for the implementation and improvement of the national AI strategy. It ensures the alignment of national efforts with the strategic objectives.National AI Strategy Oversight Committee (Article 13) - Oversees the implementation of the national AI strategy and ensures the alignment of activities of all stakeholders. It focuses on implementation and compliance.AI Observatory (Article 14) - Collects data, monitors AI-related activities and provides key performance indicators for AI initiatives in the country. It identifies opportunities and assesses the impact of AI on fundamental rights.

category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
org: Federal Chancellery of Austria, Directorate General for Digitalisation and E-Government
title: Law as Code for Procedures of Public Administration
document_name: Law as Code fur Verwaltungsverfahren
body:
The Law as Code approach aims to represent rules or legal texts in the form of formalized and executable logic-based rules, using methods of symbolic AI. Such a representation ensures transparency, explainability and predictability of the execution of the underlying regulations, and hence is especially suited for procedures of public administration. The Law as Code-initiative aims to create a basis for such an approach in the context of Austrian public administration.

Following the žLaw as Code-approach (or rules as code approach), several international initiatives aim to introduce transparent and explainable methods for the creation and execution of regulations and legal texts in public administration. Examples include initiatives in Canada, social benefit calculators in Barcelona or New Zealand, or a recently established research centre for Computational Law in Singapore. Advantages of this approach are in particular increased transparency and explainability of the computations and evaluations based on these regulations in public administration, as well as the possibility of automatized procedures based on the underlying logic-based formal rules using methods of symbolic Artificial Intelligence.The successfully completed žLaw as Code for procedures of public administration-initiative aimed to provide a basis for such an approach in the context of Austrian public administration. This included both a theoretical analysis of current approaches and their suitability in this context, as well as a proof of concept implementation of an end-to-end workflow. The workflow started with a tool for extracting a logic-based formal rule representation close to the logic programming paradigm from legal texts given in natural language, followed by a tool for viewing these rules, comparing them to the original texts and modifying the extracted formal rules where needed. The resulting rule base could then be used for evaluating business cases using a rule execution engine.When employed on a broader basis, the formulation of legal texts and regulations in a logic-based language as envisioned in this initiative would enable a high degree of automation of processes in public administration with transparent, explainable and predictable results. In addition, it would enable also a more comprehensive analysis of laws and regulations with respect to their mutual relations as well as possible overlaps and conflicts. Ideally, such a formal representation would be developed already in the law-making process itself, to ensure that the intent of the texts is captured exactly.Wherever possible, the initiative employed standardised representations and methods. Standards are a prerequisite for optimal cross-border cooperation between European Member States, companies and developers. The Austrian government therefore endorses and participates in the development of international standards and reference systems for symbolic AI programming languages such as ISO/IEC 13211-1:1995 (Prolog) which are needed to implement AI services reliably, and to ensure digital sovereignty and vendor independence.

title: LANTA Supercomputer
body:
LANTA is Thailand's national supercomputer, operated by the NSTDA Supercomputer Centre (ThaiSC). Built on an HPE Cray EX system delivering 8.15 petaflops, it supports AI training, large-scale data analytics, and complex parallel processing for public and private legal entities. Applications include the development of ThaiLLM, a national Thai-language foundation model, healthcare AI platforms, and environmental forecasting tools.

LANTA's architecture comprises 346 compute nodes, 31,744 CPU cores, 704 NVIDIA A100 GPUs, a 200 Gbps HPE Slingshot network, and a 10-petabyte parallel storage system. The system employs liquid cooling technology that reduces energy consumption by 33% compared to conventional air-cooled systems, earning it the 24th position on the Green500 list in 2022 and the 91st in 2025, alongside rankings of 70th and 199th on the TOP500 list for the same years, holding the top position in ASEAN in its debut year.
LANTA underpins national projects across several sectors. In AI, it powered the development of Pathumma LLM, an open-source generative AI, and ThaiLLM, a national foundation model tailored to the Thai language and culture. In healthcare, the Medical AI Consortium uses it to build a centralised diagnostic AI platform, and the DMIND depression screening application is deployed via the national health application. The Pollution Control Department shifted from a three-day PM2.5 forecast requiring 22 hours of processing to a seven-day forecast generated in 45 minutes, while the Asian Institute of Technology uses the system for six-month weather forecasting to support precision agriculture.
Services are available to public and private legal entities through a Service Node-Hours pricing model starting at 5,000 THB, including computational software, expert guidance, Proof of Concept support, and periodic research voucher programmes. The centre also supports the Super AI Engineer initiative, training over 1,000 specialists annually.

category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
title: Khmer eKYC OCR API — AI-Powered Identity Document Recognition for Cambodian Citizens
document_name: ប្រព័ន្ធ Khmer eKYC OCR API
body:
Khmer eKYC OCR API uses AI to instantly extract data from Cambodian identity documents in Khmer and English, and already powers CamDigiKey, Cambodia's official government single sign-on application. Available completely free via CamDX to all 45+ registered public and private members, including banks, insurance companies, and government agencies, it requires no integration cost and is open to both public and private CamDX members. It has processed more than Khmer ID card images, as of now.

Background and problem
Reliable Optical Character Recognition (OCR) for Khmer-script documents has historically been unavailable, creating a significant bottleneck in Cambodia's digital transformation. Financial institutions, public agencies, and businesses were forced to rely on manual data entry for identity verification, a slow, error-prone, and costly process. TSC's response to this gap, the Khmer eKYC OCR API, earned the Best R&D Award 2023 from the Ministry of Post and Telecommunication (MPTC) of Cambodia, recognising it as the country's most impactful research and development achievement of the year. 
What the initiative does 
TSC's AI team built the eKYC OCR API from the ground up using deep learning models, extracting structured data from Cambodian National IDs (Khmer and English), Passports (MRZ and biographical), and Driving Licences. The API is available entirely free of charge via CamDX, Cambodia's national data exchange platform, to all 45+ registered members, including banks, insurance companies, microfinance institutions, and government bodies. Both public- and private-sector CamDX members can access it freely. Notably, it powers CamDigiKey, Cambodia's official government single sign-on (SSO) app, enabling citizens to authenticate and access public digital services such as online business registration using their national identity documents. 
Objectives
Eliminate manual identity data entry;accelerate eKYC compliance for NBC-regulated institutions;deliver inclusive digital services in Khmer;provide a sovereign, locally-hosted alternative to foreign OCR; and democratise access by offering the API free of charge through CamDX, removing cost as a barrier to digital transformation for all member organisations. Future evolution
Having surpassed 8 million processed requests (Khmer ID card images or passport images) with zero cost to integrators, TSC will continue expanding document coverage, growing the CamDX member base, and deepening integration with Cambodia's national digital identity infrastructure. title: Interpretative Circular on consumer protection against the use of artificial intelligence systems
body:
Adopted in 2022, this Circular provides interpretative guidance on the application of consumer protection laws in the context of AI systems. It aims to clarify how existing consumer rights (such as the right to truthful information, freedom of choice, non-discrimination, and data protection) apply when businesses deploy AI technologies. The document outlines five key axes: transparency of information, freedom of choice, safety in consumption, non-discrimination, and data protection.

This circular addresses the growing use of AI in consumer services, which brings both benefits and risks. While AI can improve personalization and efficiency, it also raises concerns about manipulation, discrimination, lack of transparency, and data privacy. These risks threaten consumer rights and deepen inequalities. The Circular interprets existing Chilean laws to ensure AI systems respect rights like transparency, freedom of choice, safety, and data protection. It supports responsible innovation and aligns with Chile’s National AI Policy and international best practices.

title: Information technology — Governance of IT — Governance implications of the use of artificial intelligence by organizations (ISO/IEC 38507:2022)
body:
ISO/IEC 38507:2022 provides guidance for members of the governing body of an organisation to enable and govern the use of artificial intelligence, ensuring its effective, efficient and acceptable use. It also guides executive managers, external specialists, public authorities and policymakers, and service providers. It applies to current and future uses of AI in any organisation, public or private, of any size, regardless of dependence on data or information technologies.

ISO/IEC 38507:2022 was prepared jointly by two subcommittees of Joint Technical Committee ISO/IEC JTC 1: SC 40, covering IT service management and IT governance, and SC 42, covering artificial intelligence. The initiative's objective is to guide the governing body of an organisation that is using or considering artificial intelligence, focusing on the human governance of an organisation's AI use rather than on the underlying technologies themselves.
It addresses the additional opportunities, risks and responsibilities that arise from AI use. The initiative examines both governance and organisational policies and how they apply to AI, noting that the operational aspects of these policies are carried out through management. It points to other standards for related matters such as social responsibility, trustworthiness (including risk management, bias management and quality) and compliance management.
Key terms are defined drawing on ISO/IEC 22989 and ISO/IEC 38500, including oversight, described as monitoring the implementation of organisational and governance policies and related tasks, services and products, and risk appetite, defined as the amount and type of risk an organisation is willing to pursue or retain. Development stakeholders include national bodies that are members of ISO or IEC, participating through technical committees, along with other international organisations, governmental and non-governmental, in liaison with ISO and IEC.

title: Grants4Companies
document_name: Grants4Companies – Förderungsvorschläge für mein Unternehmen
body:
Grants4Companies is an application in the Austrian Business Service Portal, the main point of contact between businesses and Austrian public administration. It uses methods of symbolic AI to display a list of grants, which match the logged-in business based on its data available in the registries of public administration. The internal representation of the grants also enables analysis of the landscape of Austrian business grants.

Business grants are an important tool for steering and supporting the economy. In addition, they can be used to quickly react to and counter crises. However, the search for suitable business grants can be a challenge for businesses in Austria, due to the large number of available business grants from a multitude of different providers. While there are dedicated search engines, businesses often are simply not aware of the existence of grants on a specific topic, and hence cannot use these engines in a targeted search. This is the starting point for the application Grants4Companies.Grants4Companies aims to provide a better visibility for business grants by suggesting grants in the context of the Unternehmensserviceportal (USP), supplementing existing dedicated search engines. This is achieved by listing relevant business grants for the company or business logged into the USP. Most importantly, whether a grant is relevant for the particular business is evaluated using methods of symbolic AI based on the data on that business available from the registers of the public administration. The grants for which the business satisfies the formal eligibility criteria, e.g., concerning the location or type of business, are shown more prominently. Of course the data used to evaluate the grants for a particular business is retrieved only after an explicit consent, and is visible only for this specific business. The employed methods of symbolic AI yield a higher transparency and explainability, since the ranking of the business grants is achieved by rule-based and hence explicitly explainable evaluations. These explanations as well as the relevant data are shown explicitly. For more information on the specific grants as well as the actual application process the user is referred to the websites of the funding agencies.The main benefit achieved by Grants4Companies for businesses is the better visibility of relevant and potentially interesting business grants and hence by easier discoverability of funding possibilities. But the employed methods and technologies also yield benefits for political institutions, public administration and funding agencies. In particular, the underlying machine-interpretable description of the business grants can be used in the future for formal and automated analyses of the considered grants, helping, e.g., to discover gaps in funding or multiple funding in the form of overlapping business grants. This was demonstrated in a proof of concept implementation using standardised AI programming languages.Standards are a prerequisite for optimal cross-border cooperation between European Member States, companies and developers. The Austrian government therefore endorses and participates in the development of international standards and reference systems for symbolic AI programming languages such as ISO/IEC 13211-1:1995 (Prolog) which are needed to implement AI services reliably, and to ensure digital sovereignty and vendor independence.

body:
A good practices guide that includes tools and public policy recommendations, to promote gender equity in the life cycle of artificial intelligence. The tools include: i) a decision tree designed to guide developers or purchasers of AI-based solutions in identifying and preventing gender bias;  ii) a catalog of tools available for identifying, preventing, and mitigating gender biases

The development of this guide of good practices aligns with the objectives outlined in CONPES 4080 of 2022, "Public Policy on Gender Equity for Women: Towards the Sustainable Development of the Country". This policy aims to "create the conditions necessary for the country to advance toward gender equity and ensure the economic, social, cultural, participation, and health rights of women, as well as the possibility of living a life free from gender-based violence, with a horizon extending to 2030." In accordance with this policy, the National Planning Department (DNP) is responsible for preparing and disseminating good practices guide to promote gender equity and mitigate biases in the application of artificial intelligence (Action 1.17).The development of the good practices guide incorporates multiple components, including:i) the conceptualization of gender equity within the ecosystem and life cycle of AI systems, as well as the mapping of initiatives (e.g., tools, ethical frameworks, recommendations) that promote gender equity in this context; andii) the creation of a comprehensive guide of good practices, complemented by a catalog of tools and a decision tree aimed at identifying, preventing, and mitigating gender biases in the development and adoption of AI systems. To develop practical tools, qualitative information was gathered from national and international stakeholders within the AI ecosystem. This approach ensured that the design and validation of the products incorporated a participatory process, fostering inclusivity and relevance across diverse contexts.

This body will manage access to health data, making sure it is shared responsibly between healthcare providers, researchers, and across borders. category: Regulations, guidelines and standards
title: Establishing a pro-innovation approach to regulating AI
body:
The UK initiative “Establishing a pro-innovation approach to regulating AI” outlines an emerging framework to regulate AI through a context-specific, risk-based and proportionate approach. It proposes cross-sector principles implemented by existing regulators to promote innovation, boost public trust and ensure safety.

The initiative sets out the UK Government’s emerging approach to regulating AI in a way that supports innovation while addressing risks and protecting public trust. It identifies the need to adapt existing regulatory systems to keep pace with the rapid development of AI technologies, which present both economic opportunities and challenges such as bias, safety risks and lack of clarity in current legal frameworks. The approach aims to improve clarity and coherence in regulation, thereby supporting business confidence and investment.
A key element of the initiative is the introduction of cross-sectoral principles covering areas such as safety, technical security, transparency, fairness and accountability. These principles are intended to guide how AI systems are developed and used, while allowing flexibility for regulators to tailor implementation to the context of different sectors. The approach also emphasises proportionate and risk-based regulation, encouraging lighter-touch measures such as guidance or voluntary actions before introducing stricter requirements.
The initiative involves engagement with a broad range of stakeholders, including regulators, industry, academia and civil society, and invites feedback to inform further development. It also highlights the importance of international cooperation, noting plans to work with global partners and standards bodies to promote interoperable and responsible AI governance.

title: Digital Decade Policy Programme 2030
body:
The Digital Decade Policy Programme 2030 establishes a governance framework and common targets for the Union’s digital transformation, including priorities directly relevant to artificial intelligence such as advanced digital skills, high‑performance computing, cloud and edge infrastructure, and the uptake of AI by businesses and public services.

The Digital Decade Policy Programme 2030 provides the European Union with a coordinated framework to steer and monitor progress towards shared digital objectives by 2030. It is built around four core areas: digital skills, digital infrastructures, the digitalisation of businesses, and the digitalisation of public services. Within this framework, artificial intelligence is explicitly recognised as a key digital technology alongside cloud computing, edge computing and advanced connectivity, and as a critical enabler of economic transformation, sustainability and innovation.
From an infrastructure perspective, the programme highlights the importance of strong capacity to process large volumes of data through sustainable digital infrastructures, including high‑performance computing, cloud and edge facilities. These elements are presented as foundational for AI development and deployment, particularly for data‑intensive applications and advanced AI systems. The programme also links AI and digital infrastructure to the European Green Deal, emphasising the need for energy‑ and resource‑efficient digital technologies and infrastructures.
The programme encourages coordinated action by Member States, including the development of multi‑country projects and joint investments in strategic digital capacities that support AI, such as computing infrastructure and advanced semiconductor technologies. It establishes monitoring and governance mechanisms to track progress towards digital targets, identify strategic dependencies and support the Union’s digital sovereignty in an open manner. Overall, the Digital Decade Policy Programme positions AI not as a standalone policy area, but as a cross‑cutting capability embedded in skills, infrastructure, business transformation and public‑sector digitalisation across the EU.

category: Regulations, guidelines and standards
title: Digital Compass/data policy
body:
Finland’s Digital Compass encompasses data policy, e.g. it outlines the country’s vision and goals regarding data management, sharing, and use.

Finland’s Digital Compass is a national plan that defines how the country manages its digital transformation, with a strong focus on data. It addresses the need for clear and coordinated rules around how data is collected, shared, and used. As digital services become a bigger part of everyday life, there is growing pressure to make sure that data is handled in ways that are safe, efficient, and fair for everyone—from individuals and businesses to public institutions.
One of the key objectives of the initiative is to make data more available and easier to use while protecting privacy and personal rights. The plan supports the use of open data, where possible, to help improve public services and support innovation. At the same time, it sets clear expectations around data security, transparency, and ethical use. The goal is to allow both public and private sector actors to use data in ways that create value without compromising trust.
The Digital Compass brings together a wide range of participants. It is led by the Finnish government, but involves collaboration with municipalities, companies, researchers, and civil society. The policy also aligns with wider European efforts to create a more unified and secure digital space. Through shared rules and coordinated action, the initiative helps ensure that data can flow between sectors and across borders, when appropriate, under common standards.
The approach is practical and structured. It includes steps like developing national data spaces—systems that allow different organisations to access and share data more effectively—and improving digital infrastructure to support this. It also promotes training and awareness so that organisations understand how to manage data responsibly. By setting out clear roles, goals, and tools, Finland’s Digital Compass helps make the country’s digital landscape more connected, secure, and useful.

These strategies, agreed upon through multi-year plans, aim to make government services more efficient and accessible by coordinating digital efforts across different levels of government.
The initiative addresses the need for better access to and sharing of data within the public sector. Standardizing data is essential for smooth communication and collaboration between various government bodies, which ultimately helps provide better services to citizens.
In 2022, the association of Danish municipalities (KL) introduced a data strategy asking local governments to make their data available in a standardized way. This encourages greater efficiency, transparency, and easier access to information for both the public and businesses.
Going forward, the initiative will continue to evolve by expanding cooperation and improving how data is shared and used across all levels of government. This ongoing effort ensures that Denmark’s public sector stays prepared to meet future challenges with better digital tools and services.

www.datavejviser.dk aims at enabling access to available data from the public sector and engaging in dialogue with users on their demand for further access to data so that future investments in quality and availability of public sector data is demand-driven.

Datavejviser.dk is a platform created to help people find and use data collected by public authorities in Denmark. The initiative recognizes that while a lot of data is available, it can be difficult for users to locate the right information or understand where to get it. By providing a clear, centralized directory of datasets, Datavejviser.dk makes it easier for businesses, researchers, government workers, and citizens to find the data they need and use it effectively.
The main goal of the platform is to improve transparency and support innovation by making public data more accessible. It does this by listing and describing data from many government agencies and linking users directly to the sources. This way, users don’t have to search through multiple websites or databases. Instead, they can use the platform as a one-stop resource to discover data on topics like the environment, economy, demographics, and more.
Datavejviser.dk works by collecting information about datasets available across the public sector and organizing them in a simple and consistent way. It uses standard formats to make sure the data is easy to find and compatible with different systems. The Danish Agency for Digital Government manages the platform, regularly updating it and responding to user feedback. This approach helps ensure that the platform stays relevant and continues to meet the needs of its users.
Looking to the future, the platform plans to expand its offerings and improve its features. It aims to include more datasets and improve user interaction by listening to what people want and need. By doing so, it hopes to encourage greater use of public data in areas such as research, business innovation, and public planning. Overall, Datavejviser.dk is a step toward making government data more open, useful, and aligned with the needs of society.

title: Central Government Guidelines on Cloud Policies
document_name: Valtiovarainministeriö päivitti valtionhallinnon pilvilinjaukset
body:
The Ministry of Finance updated the central government’s cloud guidelines on Cloud policies in 2023. The updated policies emphasise a “Cloud First” strategy, encouraging the use of cloud solutions as the primary option. They also address the handling of public and confidential data in cloud environments, ensuring that data protection and security measures are in place.

In 2023, Finland’s Ministry of Finance updated the central government’s guidelines on the use of cloud services. These changes respond to the growing need for more flexible, efficient, and secure digital systems across public administration. As government operations become increasingly digital, cloud services offer opportunities to improve service delivery, reduce costs, and support remote access. At the same time, these changes raise important questions about data protection, especially when handling confidential or sensitive information.
The main goal of the updated policy is to promote a “Cloud First” approach. This means that cloud-based solutions should be the default choice when public authorities plan new digital services or update existing systems. However, the policy also makes clear that security and legal requirements must always be met. Special attention is given to how public and confidential data is stored and managed in cloud environments, to ensure that information is handled responsibly and in line with national and EU data protection laws.
The updated guidelines provide practical support for government departments and agencies. They include rules on risk management, supplier responsibilities, and technical requirements for cloud use. The policy encourages organisations to evaluate the benefits and risks of cloud services early in the planning process. It also promotes cooperation between different public bodies to share knowledge and develop common practices.
These updates build on earlier cloud strategies and reflect Finland’s broader digital goals. As more government services move online, the new policy framework helps ensure that cloud adoption happens in a secure, consistent, and well-governed way across the public sector.

title: Cambodia Digital Government Policy 2022-2035
document_name: គោលនយោបាយរដ្ឋាភិបាលឌីជីថលកម្ពុជា ២០២២-២០៣៥
body:
In accordance with the Cambodia Digital Economy and Society Policy Framework 2021-2035, the Government sets out the Cambodian Digital Government Policy 2022-2035, focusing on the vision "Building a Digital Government to improve the quality of life and confidence of the people through better public service".

The process of building a digital government in Cambodia is still in an early stage, as the digitalization of ministries and institutions has not yet been fully harmonized. Most systems focus on developing applications to facilitate the work without having a strategy for long-term digital transformation and without considering the efficiency and effectiveness that data centralization provides.
The development of digital government in Cambodia faces many challenges, which are the weaknesses of the digital government system, including digital connectivity infrastructure that does not yet cover the entire country, problems with quality of services and access to financial resources, overlapped digital systems in ministries and institutions that were created according to individual needs, and the lack of a common national platform. Another weakness is the lack of a national data center for storing data and providing computing resources, while all ministries and institutions have almost no infrastructure and technical capacity for ensuring digital security.
The vision of this policy is to “establish a digital government to improve the citizens’ quality of life and build their trust through better public service provision.” To achieve this vision, the Cambodia Digital Government Policy 2022-2035 has set out 10 strategies: first, the establishment and improvement of digital connectivity infrastructure; second, the establishment and improvement of digital payment system infrastructure for public services; Page vii third, the establishment and strengthening of digital security infrastructure; fourth, the development of postal service infrastructure; fifth, the organization of digital government governance; sixth, the digital transformation of the government and public services; seventh, the development of digital human capital; eighth, the promotion of digital research and innovation; ninth, the organization of collaborations with digital technology companies; and tenth, the promotion of digital start-ups. Under the 10 strategies above, there are 83 priority actions comprising various projects.
Overall, selecting priority actions for the development of digital government demonstrates the interconnection, complementation, depth, and conformity with the clear strategies in line with concrete objectives and goals towards complete digital transformation as set out by the Royal Government for 2035. Furthermore, the implementation of those priority actions will be in line with the master plan that has a precise roadmap fueled by strong political will to achieve success, efficiency, and effectiveness. Each priority action is accompanied by concrete measurement indicators in the clear planning phases, with the ministries and institutions responsible for implementing those priority actions.

France’s agritech acceleration strategy uses AI and France 2030 funding to promote digital farming and data platforms. The AI Research Institute (ICIA) at Cluj-Napoca Technical University was inaugurated in 2024 as part of the Romanian AI Hub. Equipped with high-performance computing systems and advanced research facilities, it focuses on developing innovative AI-driven solutions across multiple sectors. Its work spans areas such as smart cities, robotics, e-health, e-agriculture, and cybersecurity.

The AI Research Institute (ICIA) at Cluj-Napoca Technical University (UTCN) represents a major investment in Romania’s artificial intelligence ecosystem. Officially inaugurated with its first symposium in October 2024, the institute is part of the Romanian AI Hub and was constructed between 2023 and 2024, with additional facilities still under development. Its mission is to provide state-of-the-art infrastructure and expertise to generate innovative AI-based solutions for both industry and society.
ICIA is equipped with cutting-edge research infrastructure, including:
High-performance computing (HPC) systems.Specialised servers for deep learning and Big Data storage.Advanced platforms for modelling, simulation, optimisation, and design.The institute’s research addresses a broad range of domains, such as:
Internet of Things (IoT) and cyber-physical systems.Autonomous and connected mobility and smart city applications.Sensors and integrated circuits for intelligent systems.Advanced multimedia data processing (text, voice, video).Social and service robotics, with AI applied to non-industrial robotics.Cybersecurity and civilian space applications.Smart agriculture (e-agriculture) through robotics and digital technologies.E-administration and e-governance.E-health, including early diagnosis, telemedicine, and software modelling.Human–machine communication technologies, supported by AI and natural language processing.The goal of ICIA is not only to advance scientific knowledge but also to create practical solutions that can be applied across strategic sectors. By combining advanced computing power with interdisciplinary expertise, it fosters innovation and strengthens Romania’s contribution to European and global AI research.
Looking forward, ICIA is expected to become a hub for collaboration between academia, industry, and government, serving as both a training ground for highly skilled AI specialists and a platform for developing technologies with real-world impact.

category: National – AI governance bodies or mechanisms
title: AI Governance Center
document_name: ศูนย์ธรรมาภิบาลปัญญาประดิษฐ์
body:
The AI Governance Center (AIGC) ensures responsible AI adoption in Thailand through policies, testing frameworks, and global collaborations.Founded under the National AI Strategy and action Plan (2022 - 2027), AIGC tackles AI risks, promotes ethical use, and aligns Thailand with global AI governance standards to ensure safe and sustainable AI development.Policymakers, businesses, and researchers benefit from its guidelines, AI testing tools, and advisory services.

The AI Governance Center (AIGC) was established to address the growing risks and ethical challenges associated with AI adoption in Thailand while positioning the country as a leader in AI governance. With AI becoming integral to various sectors, issues such as bias, privacy risks, and transparency gaps require robust governance. AIGC leverages this opportunity by developing comprehensive guidelines, risk assessment tools, and policy frameworks to ensure responsible and sustainable AI deployment. Additionally, it strengthens Thailand's alignment with global AI governance standards, facilitating international cooperation and investment.The initiative's key objectives include developing AI governance guidelines and toolkits, fostering AI ethics awareness, and enhancing testing frameworks to mitigate AI-related risks. By engaging policymakers, businesses, and researchers, AIGC ensures practical implementation of responsible AI principles. It has also introduced AI ethics education through training programs such as the AI Executive Program (AIX), AI Change Agent Program (AICA) and knowledge sharing, reaching over 20,000 participants in 2024. International collaboration is another priority, with Thailand serving as a key contributor to OECD AI governance initiatives and ASEAN AI ethics frameworks, reinforcing its regional and global leadership.Looking ahead, AIGC will continue to expand its impact by institutionalizing AI governance across sectors. It is set to co-host the UNESCO Global Forum on the Ethics of AI 2025, further elevating Thailand's presence in AI policy discussions. The AI Sandbox, which currently focuses on LLM testing, may evolve to encompass broader AI applications, enhancing regulatory preparedness. Scaling AI governance efforts across industries through partnerships with both public and private organizations will be crucial. Institutionalizing AI governance frameworks through regulatory integration and industry-specific adaptation will ensure long-term sustainability.Since its inception, AIGC has progressed from research and policy development to implementation and global advocacy. Early efforts focused on establishing AI governance principles, while recent initiatives emphasize practical application, such as the AI Readiness Scan (AIRS) and AI Risk Assessment tools. AIGC's expanding network of domestic and international stakeholders enables ongoing refinement of governance models, ensuring they remain relevant amid rapid AI advancements. As AI continues to evolve, AIGC's role in shaping responsible AI adoption will strengthen, ensuring Thailand remains at the forefront of ethical and sustainable AI governance.

document_name: FY2022 NDAA, Section 216 ("Improvements relating to steering committee on emerging technology and national security threats")
body:
Amends Section 236 of the FY 2021 National Defense Authorization Act by changing the structure of a steering committee on emerging technology and national security and featuring the intelligence community more prominently in the steering committee's responsibilities.

Amends Section 236 of the FY 2021 National Defense Authorization Act by adding the Director of National Intelligence as an official that can, with the Secretary of Defense, establish a steering committee on emerging technology and national security and receive recommendations from the committee. Amends members of the steering committee to consist of the Principal Deputy Director of National Intelligence, the Deputy Sector of Defense, the Vice Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staffs, and other appropriate officials. Adds that the Steering Committee shall be chaired by the Deputy Secretary of Defense, the Vice Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, and the Principal Deputy Director of National Intelligence jointly.

Amends the responsibilities of the steering committee by clarifying that the committee's strategy is to maintain the technological superiority of both the US military and intelligence community according to not only the National Defense Strategy, but also the National Intelligence Strategy and the National Security Strategy. Adds that the steering committee is responsible for making recommendations on any changes to the guidance for developing the National Intelligence Program budget and determining whether sufficient resources are available for the intelligence community, in addition to the Department of Defense, to defeat threats to the US.

Adds that the list of technologies classified as emerging technologies is to be determined jointly by the Secretary of Defense and the Director of National Intelligence. Adds the definition of intelligence community from the National Security Act of 1947.

title: Federal Senate Bill of Law No. 21, of 2020
document_name: Brazil Federal Senate Bill of Law No. 21, of 2020
body:
Establishes a framework of aims, foundation, and principles for AI governance in Brazil, defines guidelines for future regulations, including risk-proportionate regulation. Prioritising human rights, environmental protection, transparency, non-discrimination, competitiveness, and the balancing of innovation and self-regulation with safety requirements for high-risk systems.

Establishes foundations and principles for AI development and applications in Brazil and guidelines for the promotion and performance of public authorities. 

Defines AI systems as computational processes that, from goals defined by humans, can learn from data to perceive, interpret, and interact with the external environment, excluding automation solely guided by predefined parameters without learning capability.

Declares that AI implementation in Brazil is aimed at technological development, sustainable and inclusive economic development, societal well-being, competitiveness, increased participation in the value chain, improved public services, innovation, and environmental protection.

Declares that the foundations for AI development and implementation in Brazil are scientific and technological development, free enterprise and competition, human rights and democratic values, freedom of expression and communication, non-discrimination, recognition of the dynamic nature, the encouragement of self-regulation, protection of privacy, information security, national defence and sovereignty, freedom of business models, preservation of AI systems' security, stability, and functionality, free competition, and freedom from abusive market practices.

Declares that the principles for AI development and application in Brazil are beneficial purpose, human centrality, non-discrimination, neutrality, transparency, security and prevention, responsible innovation, and data availability.

Requires the Brazilian government to observe guidelines on necessity, sector context, specific risks, proportionality, evidence-based decision-making, public consultations, and regulatory impact analysis, as well as subjective liability rules when regulating the implementation of AI.

Establishing a tiering of the risk-based management guidelines, encouraging flexible regulatory techniques and responsible innovation in low-risk AI, and granting legal government power to inquire into high-risk AI's security and prevention, and mandating liability for AI-harm in consumer relations and for public service providing legal entities.

Established guidelines for the Brazilian government's performance regarding the usage and promotion of AI, including promotion of trust in AI, investment in research and development, promotion of interoperability, incentives for adoption, incentives for job market restructuring, educational innovation, stimulus for innovation-promoting regulation, stimulus for multi-stakeholder governance collaboration, promotion of international cooperation, as well as transparency and ethical usage. 

Mandates sectoral bodies and entities to apply the law and to monitor AI risk management, establish rights, duties, and responsibilities, and recognize self-regulatory institutions.

Grants exclusive authority to the federal Union for legislating on AI

title: 15 CFR part 7 ("Securing the Information and Communications Technology and Services Supply Chain")
document_name: 15 CFR part 7 ("Securing the Information and Communications Technology and Services Supply Chain")
body:
Establishes procedures by which the Secretary of Commerce may evaluate, direct, and/or prohibit information and communications technology or service (ICTS) transactions with foreign adversaries. Relevant ICTS include drones or any other unmanned aerial systems, autonomous systems, and artificial intelligence and machine learning software.

Establishes procedures by which the Secretary of Commerce may determine whether any information and communications technology or service (ICTS) transaction that has been produced or supplied by foreign adversaries poses certain undue or unacceptable cybersecurity risks. Relevant ICTS include drones or any other unmanned aerial systems, autonomous systems, and artificial intelligence and machine learning software.

Establishes procedures by which the Secretary may prohibit and/or direct the timing and manner of the cessation of an ICTS transaction.

Establishes procedures by which the Secretary may consider factors that may mitigate the risks posed by the ICTS transaction. 

Details penalties for entities that violate any issued final determination or direction.

document_name: Virginia HB 2154 ("Patient Access to Intelligent Personal Assistant")
body:
Requires hospitals and nursing facilities to establish policies for patient access to intelligent personal assistants. Ensures HIPAA compliance. Defines intelligent personal assistants as devices using AI and natural language processing. Mandates facility compliance with privacy and security standards.

Requires hospitals, nursing homes, and certified nursing facilities to establish and implement policies for patient access to intelligent personal assistants while receiving inpatient services.

Ensures policies protect health information in accordance with the federal Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA).

Defines "intelligent personal assistant" as a combination of an electronic device and specialized software application that assists users with tasks using natural language processing and artificial intelligence.

Mandates that these facilities allow the use of intelligent personal assistants for patients, ensuring compliance with privacy and security standards.

Includes intelligent personal assistants like "digital assistants" or "virtual assistants" in the definition provided.

title: Utah SB 34 (Governmental Use of Facial Recognition Technology)
document_name: Utah SB 34 (Governmental Use of Facial Recognition Technology)
body:
Regulates Utah government entities' use of facial recognition technology, limiting use to law enforcement investigations of serious crimes. Prohibits use for civil immigration violations, and requires public notice before usage, as well as annual reporting of statistical data.

Regulates government use of facial recognition technology by prohibiting its use on image databases, except under specific circumstances.

Limits use to law enforcement agencies for investigating felonies, violent crimes, or identifying incapacitated and at-risk individuals.

Prohibits the use of facial recognition systems for civil immigration violations.

Requires formal request procedures and restricts access to authorized personnel, with mandatory verification and review of algorithmic matches before results are shared.

Obligates public notice before a government entity begins using a facial recognition system and instructs government entities to notify individuals when capturing images for use with facial recognition technology.

Mandates that data relating to facial recognition comparisons remain confidential and restricts its use to the outlined purposes.

Requires annual reporting to the Government Operations Interim Committee on request types, numbers, and matches obtained through facial recognition use.

document_name: AI Video Interview Discrimination Act
body:

document_name: FY2021 NDAA, Division A, Title XV, Section 6505 ("GAO studies on trafficking")
body:
Instructs the Comptroller General of the United States to conduct a study on trafficking routes employed by transnational criminals. This emcompasses examining methods for laundering proceeds from trafficking, with a focus on the role of emerging technologies, including Artificial Intelligence, in facilitating the laundering of proceedings from trafficking.

Instructs the Comptroller General of the United States to carry out a study in consultation with law enforcement, relevant federal agencies, private sector stakeholders (such as financial institutions, data and technology companies), to investigate major trafficking routes used by transnational criminal organizations and to what extent the trafficking routes are related.

Directs the study to include commonly used methods to launder and move the proceeds of trafficking; the types of suspicious financial activity that are associated with illicit trafficking networks, and how financial institutions identify and report such activity.

Directs the study to include steps financial institutions are taking to detect and prevent bad actors who are laundering the proceeds of illicit trafficking, including data analysis, policies, training procedures, rules, and guidance,

Necessitates the study to include the role those emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence, digital identity technologies, distributed ledger technologies, virtual assets and online marketplaces can play in enabling the laundering of proceeds from trafficking. 

Requires the Comptroller General of the United States to submit a report to the congres, summarizing the results of the study and any recommendations for regulatory action.

category: U.S. federal laws;NDAA provisions;FY2021 NDAA
title: William M. (Mac) Thornberry National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2021, Division A, Title XCII, Section 9203 ("Spectrum information technology modernization efforts")
document_name: FY2021 NDAA, Division A, Title XCII, Section 9203 ("Spectrum information technology modernization efforts")
body:
A directive for covered agencies, including the Department of Defense, to employ updated algorithms, data, and AI tools in modernizing their infrastructure for managing Federal spectrum. This involves enhancing efficiency, validation, accuracy, modeling, and monitoring, with a specific emphasis on automated adjustments, collaborative spectrum sharing, and interoperability, while also mandating comprehensive plans, reviews, and oversight to ensure effective implementation and integration of these AI-driven advancements.

Use updated algorithms, data, AI tools, and algorithms to modernize infrastructure. Ways to improve infrastructure include efficiency, validation, accuracy, modeling, and monitoring. The directive aims to enhance covered agencies' capacity to meet mission requirements in congested Federal spectrum environments through the implementation of automated adjustments, the creation of a time-based mechanism for collaborative spectrum sharing among agencies, and fostering collaboration to ensure interoperability. 

Within 240 days of the enactment of this Act, the Assistant Secretary of Commerce for Communications and Information is required to submit to Congress a report outlining a plan for the National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA) to modernize and automate its infrastructure for managing the use of Federal spectrum by covered agencies, with the goal of improving efficiency in spectrum management in ways such as a timeline for implementation, plans for security enhancement, data model improvement, and workflow automation. 

Within one year of the enactment of this Act, the head of each covered agency is required to submit a report to the Assistant Secretary of Commerce for Communications and Information and the Policy and Plans Steering Group outlining a plan to modernize the agency's infrastructure. Each submitted report must include an assessment of their current capabilities, a timeline for completion, management capabilities, agency requirements or restrictions, existing infrastructure, and a plan for safe integration of government data.

The Comptroller General of the United States is mandated to conduct a review of covered agencies' infrastructure within 180 days of the Act's enactment and subsequently oversee the implementation of modernization plans submitted by the Assistant Secretary and covered agencies, providing regular reports and briefings to relevant congressional committees until December 31, 2030. The term "covered agency" includes any Federal entity, as determined by the Assistant Secretary, encompassing the Department of Defense, and "infrastructure" is defined as information technology systems and related tools and databases.

title: William M. (Mac) Thornberry National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2021, Division A, Title XC, Section 9004 ("Department of Homeland Security reports on digital content forgery technology")
document_name: FY2021 NDAA, Division A, Title XC, Section 9004 ("Department of Homeland Security reports on digital content forgery technology")
body:
Instructs the Secretary of the Department of Homeland Security to submit annually, for a period of 5 years, a report to Congress on the state of digital content forgery technology.

Instructs the Secretary of the Department of Homeland Security to submit annually, for a period of 5 years, a report to Congress on the state of digital content forgery technology. 

Requires the report to include an assessment of the underlying technologies used to create or propagate digital content forgeries, including the evolution of such technologies and patterns of dissemination of such technologies. 

Requires the report to include a description of the types of digital content forgeries, including those used to commit fraud, cause harm, harass, coerce, or silence vulnerable groups or individuals, or violate civil rights.

Requires the report to include an assessment of how foreign governments, proxies and networks thereof, and non-governmental entities use, or could use, digital content forgeries to harm national security. 

Requires the report to include an assessment of the uses, applications, dangers, benefits, and impact on individuals of deep learning or digital content forgery technologies used to generate realistic depictions of events that did not occur. 

Requires the report to include a description of the methods and technological countermeasures that are, or could be, used to identify forgeries and address concerns with digital content forgery technology.

title: William M. (Mac) Thornberry National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2021, Division A, Title VIII, Section 801 ("Report on acquisition risk assessment and mitigation as part of Adaptive Acquisition Framework implementation")
document_name: FY2021 NDAA, Division A, Title VIII, Section 801 ("Report on acquisition risk assessment and mitigation as part of Adaptive Acquisition Framework implementation")
body:
Requires each Department of Defense service acquisition executive to submit to Department leadership a report on how they are addressing a series of risks in acquisition programs, including potential complications posed by Department system changes created by artificial intelligence.

Requires each Department of Defense service acquisition executive to submit to the Secretary of Defense, the Under Secretary of Defense for Acquisition and Sustainment, the Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering, and the Chief Information Officer a report on how they are assessing, mitigating, and reporting risks in acquisition programs.

Requires the reports described above to cover, among other risk categories, technical risks in engineering, software, manufacturing and testing; integration and interoperability risks posed by changes to Department systems created by artificial intelligence; and supply chain risks, including those related to cybersecurity and the defense industrial base's potential inability to produce technology and systems as needed.

Requires the Under Secretary of Defense for Acquisition and Sustainment to submit to the congressional defense committees a report on their own views, and the views of the service acquisition executives, with regard to the risk mitigation measures covered herein.

The aim of the project is a training application to make complex AI-based projects "explainable" to employees at the interface between medicine and technology. A major disadvantage of AI-based technologies in the medical field is that these systems are not explained to users. Together with Women in AI and the DIO, "Xplain-AI" will explain innovative projects with AI-based content in a user-oriented way – for example, data-driven, automated technologies, integration of machine learning, recognition of biases in the application of algorithms. title: Taxonomy of Driving Automation for Vehicles
document_name: Taxonomy of Driving Automation for Vehicles
body:
China's six-level standards, called Taxonomy of Driving Automation for Vehicles, provides official definitions for self-driving cars from level zero (L0), which relies largely on human drivers, to L5 that achieves full driving automation.

China's Taxonomy of Driving Automation for Vehicles initiative addresses the growing need for a standardized and unified classification system to define and regulate the levels of vehicle driving automation. As autonomous driving technologies continue to evolve rapidly, the absence of a clearly defined framework posed challenges for technology development, legal enforcement, industry coordination, and consumer understanding. This initiative seeks to close that gap by establishing a comprehensive taxonomy aligned with international developments but tailored to China's regulatory, technological, and societal context.The primary objective of the initiative is to set clear definitions for the different levels of driving automation”from Level 0 (no automation) to Level 5 (full automation)”based on the functions performed by the automated system versus the human driver. This classification supports regulatory consistency, facilitates compliance with safety standards, and enables communication among automakers, suppliers, policymakers, and the public. It also promotes transparency in advertising and product labeling to prevent consumer misunderstanding or overestimation of system capabilities.Over time, the initiative is expected to evolve in line with advancements in AI, sensor technologies, and vehicle connectivity. As part of its institutionalization, the taxonomy has been incorporated into national standards such as GB/T 40429-2021, which came into effect in 2021. This standard outlines six levels of automation and provides terminology and technical definitions in alignment with both ISO and SAE international standards, while allowing for adaptations to China's infrastructure and governance systems. Future updates are anticipated as technology matures, especially to accommodate new forms of mobility and smart infrastructure integration.The initiative has been developed and updated through collaborative efforts involving national regulators, technical standardization committees, research institutions, and major Chinese automotive companies. It complements broader national goals under initiatives such as Made in China 2025 and the development of intelligent connected vehicles (ICVs). By establishing a robust foundation for automated vehicle classification, China aims to foster innovation, ensure road safety, and maintain its leadership position in the global autonomous driving ecosystem.

title: Sunet Data Center DC Orion in Kalix + EOSC data storage
document_name: Sunet Virtuellt Datacenter
body:
This project aims to establish a redundant data centre in Northern Sweden for Sunet's services.

Sunet, Sweden’s national research and education network, is responsible for providing secure and reliable digital infrastructure to universities, research institutions, and public bodies. To strengthen the resilience of its services, Sunet is establishing a new data centre in northern Sweden under the project known as DC Orion. This development responds to the need for greater redundancy in national digital infrastructure, reducing the risk of disruption from regional outages or other incidents in the Stockholm area where many of Sunet’s existing systems are currently located.
The main objective of the initiative is to ensure continuity of Sunet’s critical services—such as identity management (EduID), storage and archiving, virtual computing environments, media services, and DNS—by hosting them in a geographically distinct location with secure and scalable infrastructure. Locating the facility in the north offers additional benefits, including access to a stable power supply, robust fibre connectivity, and the natural advantages of a cooler climate for sustainable operations.
The project is led by Sunet and has been developed through a detailed planning process, building on earlier feasibility studies. The facility is designed to meet high standards of security and reliability, including redundant power and network connections. Services are being progressively migrated to the new site, with Sunet’s Virtual Datacenter (VDC) now available from DC Orion. This supports both Sunet’s own redundancy needs and the growing demands of Sweden’s research and education communities for high-performance, secure, and flexible digital services.

By integrating technology, public health, and social sciences, the project addresses challenges such as social isolation and the need for assistance and safety. It adopts an interdisciplinary approach, involving social sciences, software development, smart environments & security.

As the population ages, it's essential to support elderly people in receiving care at home rather than moving into nursing homes. Solutions at the crossroads of technology, healthcare, public services, and social sciences can address two major challenges in home care: (1) combating social isolation and (2) meeting assistance and safety needs. The ongoing COVID-19 crisis has dramatically demonstrated the need for better care solutions for older citizens. The aim of this project is to develop a home care solution to assist elderly individuals who wish to remain in their homes and to coordinate the efforts of all stakeholders around them (social workers, caregivers, family, neighbors, etc.).

Ireland’s Shared Government Data Centre was created to support the digitalisation of public services by providing a modern, secure, and energy-efficient facility for storing and managing government data. As more services move online, the government needed reliable infrastructure to replace outdated and scattered data centres across departments.
