body:
This initiative focuses on improving Croatia’s Central Health Information System (CEZIH) by implementing a TIER 3 data centre to guarantee continuous, dependable, and secure operations. The project aims to migrate the system to a state cloud environment, establish disaster recovery solutions, and enhance overall data management.

Croatia’s Central Health Information System (CEZIH) is essential for managing health data and services. However, its current setup lacks the reliability and security needed for a modern healthcare system. The system is vulnerable to outages and data loss, and it doesn’t meet high availability standards. To address this, the Croatian government launched a project to upgrade CEZIH’s infrastructure, ensuring stable, secure, and round-the-clock operations.
The main goal is to move CEZIH into a state-managed cloud environment and build two data centres—primary and backup—that meet TIER 3 standards. This ensures high system availability and protection against failures. The project also includes disaster recovery planning, improved monitoring, and data backup to prevent service disruptions and data breaches.
Led by the Central State Office for the Development of Digital Society and supported by Croatia’s National Recovery and Resilience Plan, the project runs from 2021 to 2025. Once completed, it will offer a stronger foundation for digital health services, with better reliability, data protection, and room to grow as technology and healthcare demands evolve.

This initiative consolidates several best practices to ensure that AI solutions are socially conscious and travel beyond the digital divide. The strategy builds upon previous approaches to bring under its ambit an accountable and utility-maximising approach to deploying AI solutions.

Drawn up across Parts 1 and 2, the strategy for Responsible AI consolidates several best practices to ensure that AI solutions are socially conscious and travel beyond the digital divide. The strategy builds upon the pervasive approach of AI for All, first discussed in the NSAI, to bring under its ambit, an accountable and utility-maximising approach to deploying AI solutions. The essence of AI for All includes within itself the maxims, Good AI for All, and AI for Good, which the strategy for Responsible AI sets to work on.In Part-1 of the Responsible AI paper released in February 2021, the various systems and societalconsiderations of AI systems have been studied and the principles for Responsible AI are outlined.Objectives:To identify broad areas for Government intervention and an institutional mechanism to support the implementation.To explore the institutional mechanisms for operationalizing the principles of responsible AI across private sector and research institutions.

body:
This initiative proposes principles for the responsible management of AI systems that may be leveraged by relevant stakeholders in India, derived from the Constitution of India, among others.

category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
title: Application Hub for a Circular Economy for Plastic Packaging through AI Methods
document_name: Anwendungszentrum für eine Kreislaufwirtschaft für Kunststoffverpackungen mittels KI-Methoden
body:
The Application Hub for a Circular Economy for Plastic Packaging uses AI methods to improve recycling and reduce plastic waste. It supports research and innovation to enhance circular economy practices in Germany. The initiative aims to make plastic packaging management more efficient and sustainable.

The Application Hub for a Circular Economy for Plastic Packaging through AI Methods is a German initiative financed by the Federal Ministry of Education and Research (BMBF). Its purpose is to develop and apply AI technologies that optimise the management and recycling of plastic packaging, supporting the country’s transition toward a circular economy.
Key objectives include:
Enhancing recycling efficiency using AI-based sorting, monitoring, and analysis toolsReducing plastic waste through smarter resource management and process optimisationSupporting research and innovation in materials, production, and recycling practicesThe hub fosters collaboration between academic institutions, industry partners, and technology providers, ensuring AI solutions are practical and scalable. By integrating AI into circular economy processes, the initiative contributes to both environmental sustainability and economic efficiency.

category: Regulations, guidelines and standards

title: Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard
document_name: Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard
body:
The world-leading ATRS establishes a standardised way for public sector organisations to proactively and openly publish information about how and why they are using algorithmic tools; specifically, those that either have a significant influence on a decision-making process with direct or indirect public effect, or directly interact with the public. The ATRS was jointly developed by the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT) and the Central Digital and Data Office (CDDO).

The initiative has the following objective(s):To facilitate trusted and trustworthy uses of algorithmic tools in the public sector.

category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
org: Ministry of European Investments and Projects of Romania
title: Aid scheme for the digitalisation of SME
body:
Under Romania’s National Recovery and Resilience Plan (NRRP), a dedicated investment supports the digitalisation of SMEs. It provides grants both for developing advanced digital technologies and for helping SMEs adopt them. Eligible areas include AI, cloud computing, blockchain, IoT, cybersecurity, and other key digital tools.

As part of the National Recovery and Resilience Plan (NRRP), Component 9 – Investment 3: Private Sector Aid Schemes was launched to accelerate the digital transformation of Romania’s small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). This initiative recognises that SMEs form the backbone of the economy, but often lack resources to access and implement cutting-edge technologies. By combining financial support with clear eligibility criteria, the programme seeks to foster both technological adoption and innovation-led growth.
The sub-investment is structured around two main instruments:
Grants for the development of advanced digital technologies – targeted at entrepreneurs who are building solutions in fields such as:Artificial intelligence (AI)Data and cloud computingBlockchainHigh-performance and quantum computingInternet of Things (IoT)Cybersecurity2. Grants of up to EUR 100,000 per enterprise for digital adoption – supporting SMEs in integrating new technologies into their operations. Eligible expenses include:
Purchases of ICT hardware and software licences.Robotic Process Automation (RPA) and software automation tools.Blockchain and artificial intelligence systems.Machine learning, augmented reality, and virtual reality applications.Cloud services and IoT solutions.Development of company websites.Staff training in the use of IT equipment.Advisory services and technical assessments for digital readiness.The overall objective is to strengthen the competitiveness of SMEs by enabling them to adopt and create digital solutions that increase efficiency, productivity, and innovation capacity.
Looking ahead, this investment is expected to deliver long-term benefits for the Romanian economy by:
Creating a more digitally skilled workforce.Enhancing SME participation in the digital single market.Supporting the growth of local digital technology providers.Facilitating the integration of Romanian SMEs into European and global value chains.By targeting both the supply side (entrepreneurs developing advanced technologies) and the demand side (SMEs adopting digital tools), the initiative ensures a balanced and sustainable approach to digitalisation.

category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
org: Ministry of Economic Affairs and Climate Policy
title: AiNed – “AI for energy and sustainability”
document_name: AiNed – ‘AI voor energie en duurzaamheid
body:
AiNed – “AI for Energy and Sustainability” is a public-private programme that explores how AI can accelerate the energy transition. It establishes AI Innovation Labs to develop practical solutions for sustainable energy. The initiative supports the Netherlands’ efforts to achieve climate goals by 2030 and beyond.

AiNed – “AI for Energy and Sustainability” is a multi-year public-private programme launched in 2021 to harness AI for the country’s energy and sustainability goals. The initiative focuses on creating AI Innovation Labs that explore applications of AI in renewable energy, energy efficiency, and other areas critical to the energy transition.
Key objectives of the programme include:
Accelerating the energy transition through AI-driven solutionsEstablishing AI Innovation Labs to test and deploy practical applicationsEnsuring alignment with the EU AI Act and broader sustainable energy frameworksContributing to a fair, reliable, and efficient energy systemThe programme encourages collaboration between industry, research institutions, and government to translate AI research into real-world solutions. By combining expertise from multiple sectors, AiNed seeks to create scalable, innovative approaches that can support the Netherlands’ climate targets and sustainable development ambitions.

category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
title: AiNed
body:
AiNed  is a multi-year public-private initiative that helps Dutch companies and public institutions capitalise on AI's economic and social opportunities. Funded by the National Growth Fund, AiNed focuses on AI investments in Ethical, Legal and Societal Aspects (ELSA) labs, learning communities, innovation labs, and SME innovations. It also supports research grants and the development of a robust AI ecosystem through start-ups and SMEs, aligning with EU AI legislation in a responsible manner.

The AiNed programme is a flagship Dutch initiative designed to strengthen the country’s position in artificial intelligence. Backed by the National Growth Fund, it pools resources from government, industry, and academia to accelerate AI development and adoption.
Its activities cover a wide range of areas: ELSA labs that address ethical, legal, and social aspects of AI; innovation and learning labs that connect researchers and practitioners; and targeted support for SMEs and start-ups to apply AI in practice. By fostering collaboration across sectors, AiNed seeks to build a cohesive AI ecosystem that balances innovation with responsibility, ensuring alignment with broader European AI regulatory frameworks.

category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
org: Ministry for Digital Transformation and Public Service
title: AgrarIA: AI applied to the value chain ​​of agricultural production 2050
document_name: AgrarIA: IA aplicada a la cadena de valor de la producción agrícola 2050
body:
This project explores the use of AI and other technologies to develop new agricultural production methods. It investigates solutions such as natural pest control, collaborative robotics, quantum computing, and digital twins. The goal is to make agricultural production more efficient, sustainable, and innovative.

The project is focused on assessing the applicability and viability of AI alongside other advanced technologies in agriculture. It seeks to create innovative solutions that improve productivity, sustainability, and efficiency across different stages of agricultural production.
Key potential initiatives include:
Development of new natural products for pest and disease control, offering alternatives to chemical synthesis while maintaining effectivenessUse of collaborative robotics to optimise product transformation and processing phasesApplication of quantum computing for managing and analysing satellite imagery to optimise agricultural productionImplementation of digital twins to enhance energy efficiency in refrigeration and storage facilitiesThe project encourages collaboration between research institutions, technology providers, and agricultural stakeholders to ensure practical, scalable solutions. By integrating cutting-edge technologies, it aims to modernise agriculture while promoting sustainability and competitiveness.
Future outlook:
Adoption of AI-driven and technology-enhanced production methods across farmsIncreased efficiency, sustainability, and resilience in agricultural operationsDevelopment of new methodologies that can be scaled and applied to various crops and production systems

category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
title: Advanced digitalisation – future solutions in Swedish industry
body:
This programme administered by Vinnova, Sweden’s innovation agency, supports approx. 100 innovation projects, including on secure data flows for applied AI edge technologies.

Sweden's Advanced Digitalisation Programme, administered by Vinnova, the Swedish innovation agency, is a strategic initiative aimed at fostering industrial innovation through digital transformation. The programme supports approximately 100 innovation projects, including those focused on secure data flows for applied AI edge technologies.

Objective: To strengthen Swedish industry's competitiveness and technological leadership by mobilising and facilitating collaboration across various sectors.Focus Areas: The programme targets system-changing innovations in electrification, data flows, AI, and digital infrastructure to accelerate the industry's digital transformation.Funding Structure: The programme operates in three stages, with funding available for pre-studies and subsequent project phases, potentially up to SEK 50 million per year for six years. Collaboration: Projects are expected to be carried out in collaboration between at least two actors, including companies, universities, research institutes, and other relevant organizations. .Strategic Goals:

category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
title: Advanced digital skills training program for civil servants
body:
The objective of this investment (under the RRP) is to increase the advanced digital skills of the civil servants, aiming to support the digitalisation of the public services by improving the availability of a qualified workforce for internal IT&C operations. The investment consists of training for advanced digital skills (database management, system management, business analysis, data analysis, programming) for 32,500 civil servants
(out of which 2,500 seniors).

As part of its Recovery and Resilience Plan (RRP), Romania is investing in advanced digital training for civil servants to accelerate public sector digitalisation. Many institutions lack in-house expertise for IT and data operations, slowing reform and leaving them dependent on external providers. The program aims to train 32,500 officials, including 2,500 senior staff, in areas such as database and system management, business and data analysis, and programming. By developing these skills internally, the government hopes to build a more resilient, capable workforce for ongoing digital transformation.
The initiative is coordinated by the National Agency for Civil Servants with training providers like the National Institute of Administration. It runs until June 2026 and is tied to specific milestones under the RRP.

category: Regulations, guidelines and standards
org: Ministry of Justice |Ministry of National Education|Ministry of Interior )|Information Technologies and Communications Authority |Turkish Justice Academy
title: Action Plan on Human Rights
document_name: Insan Haklari Eylem Plani
body:
The Action Plan on Human Rights sets certain aims, goals and activities in accordance with this background and framework. The Plan's point of origin is the state's obligation to protect, in all of its affairs and acts and with all of the state institutions and organisations, the physical and moral integrity and the honour and dignity of individuals.

The reformative spirit that has been maintained since 2002 without interruption has been tangibly set forth through the legislative amendments in the field of human rights. Throughout this process the presumption of innocence, one of the universal principles of law, has been established as an essential value to be borne in mind by judicial authorities at all stages. In this scope, certain amendments have been passed, especially recently, oriented at protecting personal data and guaranteeing the right of individuals not to have their honour and reputation tarnished as a criminal.Furthermore, in addition to amendments that expand the scope of rights and freedoms through a detailed screening over the legislation, another goal is to be able to offer public services in an accessible, accountable, equal, transparent and fair manner. Thus, the standards on human rights and freedoms will be raised higher, as a natural result of which a new momentum will be gained in the process of strengthening democracy with a focus on citizen satisfaction. Similarly, while the public sector's digital transformation will continue to be implemented with greater success via the e-government project on the one hand, the opportunities for political participation will be promoted in conjunction with this transformation, on the other. In this scope, digital negotiation methods will be developed with the use of new information and communication technologies.The initiative has the following objectives:Aim 8: Protecting vulnerable groups and strengthening social wealth - Goal 8.10: Protection of Human Rights in Digital Environment and Against Artificial Intelligence Applications (Around the 11 main principles which make up the backbone of the Plan, a total of 9 aims, 50 goals and 393 activities are set. The issues related to artificial intelligence are discussed under this aim.)

The Portuguese Action Plan for the Circular Bio-economy promotes the transition of the economy toward sustainable and circular practices. body:
The Autonomous Driving Act is one of several measures to create a legal framework to implement the German federal government's 2015 Strategy for Automated and Connected Driving. The Federal Ministry of Transport and Digital Infrastructure has authorized testing of connected vehicles under real-life conditions. In 2017, Germany amended its Road Traffic Act to allow drivers to transfer control of their vehicles to highly or fully automated driving systems and for them to be used on public roads.

document_name: ASEAN Digital Masterplan 2025
body:
The ADM 2025 will guide digital cooperation between ASEAN members over the next five years in order to position ASEAN as a leading digital community and economic bloc powered by secure and transformative digital services, technologies and ecosystems.

The ADM 2025 has set the following desired outcomes: ASEAN's recovery from the pandemic through digital services, improve the quality and coverage of fixed and mobile broadband infrastructure, enhance trusted digital services and the prevention of consumer harm, create a sustainable competitive market for the supply of digital services, increase in the quality and use of e-government services, digital services to connect business and to facilitate cross-border trade, increased capability for business and people to participate in the digital economy and a digitally inclusive society in ASEAN.

The establishment of an ASEAN Data Management Framework will promote sound data governance practices by helping organisations to discover the datasets they have, assign it with the appropriate categories, manage the data, protect it accordingly and all these while continuing to comply with relevant regulations.

This programme, piloted in 2019 under the auspices of the Ministry of Economic Development and Technology, aimed to teach secondary school students and help them develop competences related to the use of artificial intelligence.

category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
org: France, Slovenia, Italy, Ireland and Luxembourg
title: AI4T
body:
The Erasmus+ project 'AI4T (AI for and by Teachers)' was a three-year collaboration involving partners from five European countries: France, Ireland, Italy, Luxembourg, and Slovenia. With contributions from ministries of education, universities, research centers, and private companies, the project aimed to develop a professional learning path for secondary school teachers. Its goal was to help teachers better understand the opportunities and risks associated with AI in the classroom.

The project resulted in a handbook and a tailored training program to challenge biases, deepen knowledge, and promote the informed use of AI in education.

category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
title: AI-programmes in Business Finland’s Digital Native Finland mission
body:
The aim of the Digital Native Finland mission is to accelerate digital transformation and create a global competitive advantage for Finnish companies. By increasing digital capabilities, we can increase sustainable customer value and raise the productivity of companies to the next level.

The Digital Native Finland mission is an instrument of mission-based innovation policy aimed at accelerating the digital trans-formation of Finnish firms. The most AI-relevant programmes within this initiative include:

category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
org: Federal Ministry of Education and Research
title: AI-based assistance systems for in-process healthcare applications
document_name: KI-basierte Assistenzsysteme für prozessbegleitende Gesundheitsanwendungen
body:
In addition to the much-discussed potential in diagnostics, AI-based interactive systems can very effectively support processes in hospitals and comparable healthcare facilities and thus contribute to the improvement of medical, organizational and administrative processes. The aim of the projects in this funding measure is to research and develop AI-based assistance systems that lead to quantifiable and measurable improvements in clinical processes.

Beyond clinical outcomes, the initiative emphasises improving workflows, reducing administrative burdens, and enhancing resource management in healthcare facilities. title: AI-Triage for General Practitioners
body:
Huisartsencoöperatie West-Brabant (HCWB) began rolling out an general practitioner AI triage tool to reduce administrative workload and improve the job satisfaction of general practitioners.

The AI triage project by Huisartsencoöperatie West-Brabant (HCWB) aims to support general practitioners by automating parts of the patient intake and assessment process. The tool is designed to reduce administrative workload, improve workflow efficiency, and enhance job satisfaction among GPs. By using AI to assist in initial triage, the system helps prioritize cases, streamline communication, and ensure patients are directed to appropriate care pathways more quickly. The broader goal is to improve access to care while maintaining quality and reducing pressure on primary care services.

This Partnership is the European focal point for AI, Data and Robotics.

The AI, Data and Robotics Partnership is one of the 46 candidate Public Private Partnerships in the upcoming Framework Programme. The impetus for starting the preparatory work on this Partnership came by the European Commission, which adopted in 2018 the Coordinated Plan on Artificial Intelligence announcing the intention to establish a Public Private Partnership on AI, in order to increase available financing for AI in Europe. category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
title: AI virtual assistant/chatbot network
body:
This initiative aims to create a unified and centralised platform for managing government institutions' websites, improving public access to information and ensuring compliance with accessibility requirements under Directive 2016/2102. The platform enhances resource efficiency through a unified content management system and integrates 55 public authorities into a single system`.

The AI Virtual Assistant/Chatbot Network is a Latvian government initiative designed to centralise and streamline public access to information across multiple government websites. The platform addresses the challenge of fragmented digital services by providing a unified interface through which citizens and businesses can interact with public authorities, improving the efficiency and accessibility of online government services.
A core objective of the initiative is to ensure compliance with accessibility requirements under Directive 2016/2102, enabling equal access to information for all users, including those with disabilities. By integrating AI-powered virtual assistants and chatbots, the platform can respond to queries efficiently, provide consistent information, and support user navigation across government websites.
The initiative unites 55 public authorities into a single content management system, allowing for centralised administration and maintenance of web resources. This approach not only reduces operational costs and redundancies but also promotes standardisation of content and improves the overall quality and reliability of online public information.

category: AI policy initiatives, programmes and projects
title: AI for Thai – Thai AI Service Platform
body:
AI for Thai is a platform developed by the Artificial Intelligence Research Group at Thailand's National Center for Electronics and Computer Technology (NECTEC). It provides APIs across three modules, Language, Vision, and Conversation, covering natural language processing, image and video analysis, and speech and chatbot services, all tailored to the Thai language and context. It targets system developers, SME entrepreneurs, and start-ups, with a limited free testing tier available.

AI for Thai consolidates NECTEC's AI research outputs into an accessible API platform structured around three modules: Language (word segmentation, named entity recognition, machine translation, sentiment analysis), Vision (OCR, face recognition, object and activity recognition), and Conversation (speech-to-text, text-to-speech, chatbot). The platform's focus on "natural language processing of the Thai language, visual understanding in the context of Thainess, and Thai speech recognition and speech generation" addresses the specific challenge of adapting AI tools to a linguistic and cultural context underserved by international platforms.
Sectoral use cases described include retail chatbots, logistics driver fatigue detection, medical image analysis, and tourism translation tools. By offering APIs with a free testing tier and targeting SMEs and start-ups alongside larger developers, the platform aims to lower barriers to AI adoption and enable rapid application development across Thai industry and public services.

body:
As part of the German AI strategy, KIDA serves as a cross-institutional service centre for AI use cases in the agri-food sector. Led by the Federal Ministry of Food and Agriculture (Bundesministerium für Ernährung und Landwirtschaft, BMEL), it enables AI and big data applications in agriculture, supporting subordinate authorities in handling AI and data cases.

Germany’s KIDA centre was set up under the national AI strategy to strengthen the use of artificial intelligence and big data in the agri-food sector. Managed by the Federal Ministry of Food and Agriculture, it provides a shared service for authorities and agencies, helping them design and apply AI-based solutions to agricultural challenges.
The centre develops reference use cases, offers technical guidance, and ensures that data-driven tools are applied responsibly and effectively. By pooling expertise across institutions, KIDA lowers barriers to adoption and creates a foundation for scaling AI in areas such as crop monitoring, food safety, and resource efficiency.

document_name: AI Training for the Acquisition Workforce Act (Bill S-2551)
body:
This Bill requires the Director of the Office of Management and Budget to establish or otherwise provide an AI training program for the acquisition workforce and for other purposes.

The AI training program shall include information relating to: (A) the science underlying AI, including how AI works; (B) introductory concepts relating to the technological features of AI systems; (C) the ways in which AI can benefit the Federal government; (D) the risks posed by AI, including discrimination and risks to privacy; (E) ways to mitigate the risks described in subparagraph (D), including efforts to create and identify AI that is reliable, safe, and trustworthy; and (F) future trends in AI, including trends for homeland and national security and innovation.The initiative has the following objective(s):To ensure that the workforce has knowledge of the capabilities and risks associated with AI.

body:
Within France’s 2030 strategy, this programme accelerates innovation in key fields, including AI in healthcare. By supporting foundational AI research, it drives advancements in medical imaging, predictive analytics, and therapeutic development. The programme also fosters digital health innovation through AI-powered personalised medicine and diagnostics, while encouraging collaboration between research institutions, healthcare providers, and industry.

This program is a powerful tool supporting the national AI strategy, already encompassing nine ambitious projects. It aims to tackle key and fundamental challenges in machine learning across three complementary pillars:
 
Trustworthy and Distributed AI
Through a multifaceted approach to trust, this axis integrates:
The development of robustness foundations using statistical approaches.The incorporation of formal methods for the specification, learning, and safety validation of AI modelsThe development of decentralized learning mechanisms that ensure security.The integration of causal models with machine learning to provide explainable, evidence-based capabilities.Frugal and Embedded AI
This involves deepening the theoretical and algorithmic foundations of machine learning to ensure data and computation frugality by design. It includes:
Advanced model optimization and training guided by hardware constraints.The design of dedicated AI hardware architectures that are modular, flexible, and adaptive.The exploration of physics-informed computational models.
New Mathematical Foundations of AI, particularly in the field of mathematical analysis, this pillar includes:
The integration of tools and advances from partial differential equations, optimal control, and optimal transport.To develop novel architectures with stable optimization schemes, efficient solvers and approximations.The analytical treatment of generative and diffusion methods.

The AI Policy Forum was set up 2021 to support the inter-ministerial implementation of the national AI strategy. Its main tasks include the ongoing monitoring of AI strategy measures and the coordination of AI activities in the specialist ministries.

In order to support the cross-departmental implementation of the national AI strategy an inter-ministerial working group, the AI Policy Forum, was set up at the end of 2021, chaired by the Federal Chancellery (BKA) and the Federal Ministry for Climate Action, Environment, Energy, Mobility, Innovation and Technology (BMK). With members from all federal ministries, the AI Policy Forum contributes to a broad coordination of the federal government in the field of artificial intelligence. Its tasks include, among other things, coordinating AI implementation measures in the ministries, connecting experts in their specialist areas and the exchange of information on developments in the field of AI. The AI Policy Forum also contributes to shaping the content of the AI strategy and implementation plans and provides support with the implementation and ongoing and the ongoing monitoring of the AI measures contained therein. The AI Policy Forum Network Meeting is an annual series of events to which administration, academia, the business community and the interested public are invited to discuss developments in the field of AI and exchange information on current projects and topics.

body:
The AI Centre Lipik offers a six-month training programme in artificial intelligence and programming, combining theoretical and practical instruction. It supports emerging AI startups through an incubator that provides mentoring, business development, and infrastructure. It aims to strengthen skills, innovation, and AI-based entrepreneurship in the Lipik region and beyond.

The AI Centre Lipik, founded by the Lipik Development and Touristic Agency (LIRA d.o.o.) in 2020, consists of an Education Centre and a Startup Incubator. The Education Centre runs a six-month AI programmer training programme involving both theory and hands-on practice, offering over 1,000 hours of teaching, with stipends and living support for participants. After completion, successful graduates are offered employment or support in starting their own business.
The Startup Incubator is designed to help new and emerging companies working in AI and programming. It offers mentoring, business training, consulting, and access to infrastructure. As of the latest data, about 15 startups have been incubated in Lipik, employing several dozen people. The centre is also expanding its entrepreneurial modules, accelerator, and lab facilities.
AI Centre Lipik is part of the AI & Gaming EDIH network (European Digital Innovation Hub) focused on helping SMEs, the public sector, and startups adopt digital technologies like AI, gamification, blockchain, and IoT. It offers services like “test-before-invest,” training, consulting, networking, and business support.

title: White Paper on Artificial Intelligence
document_name: White Paper on Artificial Intelligence
body:
Within the framework of a wide range of digital initiatives taken by the European Commission, the White Paper on AI promotes a coordinated EU approach on the human and ethical implications of AI.

From 19 February to 14 June 2020, citizens and stakeholders shared their opinions on the forthcoming policy and regulatory measures regarding artificial intelligence (AI). The European Commission aimed to encourage the adoption of AI while simultaneously addressing the associated risks by proposing a White Paper outlining policy and regulatory options for creating an "ecosystem for excellence and trust." This document was released on 19 February 2020, alongside an online survey that focused on three key areas:- Specific initiatives to support, develop, and promote AI across the EU economy and public administration.- Potential regulatory frameworks for AI in the future.- Safety and liability considerations related to AI.This report presents a "future regulatory framework" for the EU to navigate the evolving landscape of AI technology. It adopts a comprehensive approach, suggesting methods to make AI accessible to small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and addressing appropriate regulations for high-risk applications and liability in cases of physical or material harm.- The proposed "Ecosystem of Excellence" highlights the necessity of collaboration with member states to invest in AI research and development. Education should enhance AI-related skills and incorporate ethical training. Facilitating access to AI technology for SMEs will accelerate its development and adoption. The private sector should play a role in the research and innovation agenda, particularly through significant public-private partnerships. The White Paper identifies healthcare and transportation as sectors poised to benefit from AI-driven products. Investments should focus on ensuring access to data and computing infrastructure. Additionally, there should be international collaboration among global AI stakeholders to promote EU standards and create a "level playing field."- The "ecosystem of trust" encompasses: (1) human agency and oversight, (2) technical robustness and safety, (3) privacy and data governance, (4) transparency, (5) diversity, non-discrimination, and fairness, (6) societal and environmental well-being, and (7) accountability.- Legislative Updates- Current legislation must be revised to account for AI. The integration of AI technologies into products and services may introduce new safety risks for users. Issues in AI design may arise from the quality and availability of data or other challenges related to machine learning. While some risks are not exclusive to AI-dependent products and services, the use of AI may exacerbate these risks. A lack of clear safety regulations addressing these concerns could lead to legal uncertainty for businesses in the EU that market AI-related products.

title: Ulysses - Legislative Demand Router
document_name: Ulysses - Roteador de demandas legislativas
body:
Ulysses - Legislative Demand Router is an AI solution designed to automatically distribute legislative demands from Members of Parliament (MPs) to appropriate expert groups within the Legislative Consultancy Department. It analyses the demand text and suggests up to three specialist groups based on thematic relevance. The system aims to increase distribution efficiency, reduce bias, and lower staff workload, with demands automatically routed when the AI's confidence exceeds 90%.

An AI system developed by the Brazilian Chamber of Deputies to automate the distribution of legislative demands from parliamentarians to specialized consultancy groups. When Members of Parliament (MPs) submit requests for bill drafting or research support, the system employs semantic analysis to interpret the content and thematic complexity of each demand, subsequently recommending up to three expert groups best suited to fulfill the request. A legislative consultancy staff member reviews these AI-generated suggestions before authorizing distribution, though demands with confidence scores exceeding 90% are routed automatically. 
The solution pursues three main objectives:
Enhance operational efficiency by accelerating the demand distribution process and reducing processing timeMinimize allocation bias by applying consistent, data-driven criteria rather than subjective human judgmentReduce administrative burden on legislative consultancy staff, allowing them to focus on higher-value supervisory tasks rather than manual classification work.The system leverages historical demand distribution data for model training and integrates with existing digital platforms used by MPs and legislative consultants. Success is measured primarily through Top-1 accuracy rates, assessing the percentage of demands correctly classified by the AI model. Key implementation challenges include maintaining model accuracy over time, adapting to evolving distribution rules, and monitoring organizational changes within lawmaking expert groups
Results, outcomes and impacts
Decrease the staff work for reading and interpretating the demand textsDecrease the likehood of biases for interpeting and choosing the group of experts to be in charge of the new bill draftingImproved the incorporation of new subjects in the bills, especially when there is a blend of many subjects that would encompass many groups of lawmaking expertsChallenges and lessons learned
To substantially enhance the performance of the AI model, it was necessary to join many legislative experts (from differrent groups of experts) to analyse historical data, which required a deep legislative knowledge, before the AI training.As demand distribution rules change over time, it was required to discard obsolete training data

body:
The Report takes a comprehensive look at a wide variety of stakeholder views on the impact of AI across the intellectual property (IP) landscape, including patent, trademark, copyright, and trade secret policy, as well as developing issues about database protection.

Building on the momentum of those discussions, on 27 August 2019, the USPTO issued a request for comments (RFC) on patenting AI inventions.The RFC sought feedback from stakeholders on a variety of patent policy issues, such as AI's impact on inventorship and ownership, eligibility, disclosure, and the level of ordinary skill in the art. The comment period closed in November 2019. The USPTO received 99 comments from a wide range of stakeholders, including individuals, associations, corporations, and foreign IP offices. In October 2019, the USPTO issued a second RFC related to the impact of AI on other IP policy areas, including copyrights, trademarks, database protections, and trade secret law. The comment period for the second RFC closed in January 2020. The USPTO received 98 comments from a wide range of stakeholders. Following the conclusion of the comment periods, a team of experts assembled from across the USPTO examined the responses and generated the Report on Public Views on AI and Intellectual Property Policy.The initiative has the following objective(s):To promote the understanding and reliability of IP rights in relation to AI technology.To ensure that appropriate IP incentives are in place to encourage further innovation in and around this critical area.

title: The Robustness and Explainability of Artificial Intelligence
document_name: The Robustness and Explainability of Artificial Intelligence
body:
The EU has identified the concepts of robustness and explainability of AI systems as key elements for a future regulation of this technology.

This report puts forward several policy-related considerations for the attention of policy makers to establish a set of standardisation and certification tools for AI. First, the development of methodologies to evaluate the impacts of AI on society, built on the model of the Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIA) introduced in the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), is discussed. Secondly, a focus is made on the establishment of methodologies to assess the robustness of systems that would be adapted to the context of use. This would come along with the identification of known vulnerabilities of AI systems, and the technical solutions that have been proposed in the scientific community to address them. Finally, the promotion of transparency systems in sensitive systems is discussed, through the implementation of explainability-by-design approaches in AI components that would provide guarantee of the respect of the fundamental rights.The initiative has the following objectives:To contribute to this movement for the establishment of a sound regulatory framework for AI, by making the connection between the principles embodied in current regulations regarding to the cybersecurity of digital systems and the protection of data, the policy activities concerning AI, and the technical discussions within the scientific community of AI, in particular in the field of machine learning, that is largely at the origin of the recent advancements of this technology.

body:

TRAIL is a Belgian initiative dedicated to advancing ethical artificial intelligence (AI) development through a combination of collaborative research, industry partnerships, and targeted projects, including the ARIAC project. The initiative addresses the growing need to ensure that AI technologies are developed and deployed in ways that are transparent, accountable, and socially responsible.
The primary objective of TRAIL is to foster innovation while maintaining a strong focus on ethics and societal impact. By promoting collaboration between academic researchers, industry actors, and public institutions, the initiative encourages the development of AI solutions that are both technologically advanced and aligned with human-centred principles.
Projects within TRAIL span multiple sectors, including healthcare, energy, and environmental technology, exploring applications such as predictive analytics, decision support systems, and sustainable solutions. The initiative integrates rigorous ethical standards, data governance practices, and transparency measures to ensure that AI outputs are trustworthy and beneficial for society.

title: Sunet Drive – collaborative data space for research data
body:
Sunet Drive is a storage and file sharing service, making it possible for researchers to be able to work and collaborate with large amounts of data.

Sunet Drive is a national storage and file-sharing service provided by Sunet, Sweden’s research and education network. The service addresses the growing need for secure, reliable, and high-capacity data storage for researchers, enabling them to work with large datasets and collaborate efficiently across institutions and geographic locations. 
The primary objective of Sunet Drive is to provide a user-friendly platform that supports both individual and collaborative research workflows. Researchers can upload, store, and share large datasets, ensuring data integrity and compliance with relevant security and privacy requirements. The service is designed to handle high volumes of data, which is critical for fields such as bioinformatics, environmental research, AI model training, and other data-intensive scientific activities.
Sunet Drive is integrated into Sunet’s broader digital infrastructure, which includes high-speed networking, identity management (EduID), and other cloud-based services. The service is accessible to universities, research institutes, and other partner organizations, providing a seamless environment for secure collaboration and data exchange. Users benefit from features such as access control, versioning, and synchronization across devices, facilitating both local and cross-institutional projects.

category: National – Strategy
org: The Government of the Republic of Serbia
title: Strategy for the Development of AI in the Republic of Serbia for the Period 2020-2025
document_name: Стратегија развоја вештачке интелигенције у Републици Србији за период 2020–2025. године
body:
The Strategy for the Development of AI in the Republic of Serbia defines objectives and measures for the development of AI whose implementation should result in economic growth, improvement of public services, advancement of scientific staff, and development of skills for the jobs of the future.

Strategy is in line with the European AI Initiative, which sets out the European Commission's AI policy. In this context, the Republic of Serbia, as a candidate for EU membership but also as a participant in the European Union Framework Program for Research and Innovation, seeks to provide the necessary extent of compliance with the European Union, which will enable full integration into the European Research Area and closer co-operation. This Strategy is also tightly connected to several other national strategies, including:- Smart Specialization Strategy of the Republic of Serbia- Industrial Development Strategy of the Republic of Serbia- Strategy for Development of New Generation Networks by 2023- Proposal of the eGovernment Development Program in the Republic of Serbia for the period from 2019 to 2022 and Action plan for its implementation- Scientific and Technological Development Strategy of the Republic of Serbia for the period 2016“2020 “ Research for Innovation. In accordance with the decision of the Government of the Republic of Serbia on the formation of a workgroup for the preparation of the Strategy for the Development of AI in the Republic of Serbia (Official Gazette of the RS, No 73/19), a workgroup for the preparation of the Strategy (hereinafter: Workgroup) was formed at the initiative of the Prime Minister's Office. The workgroup is composed of representatives of the Prime Minister's Office, ministries (Ministry of Education, Science, and Technological Development, Ministry of Economy, Ministry of Trade, Tourism, and Telecommunications, Ministry of Finance, Office of the Minister without portfolio in charge of innovation and technological development), institutions (Office for Information Technologies and Electronic Governance, the Science Fund of the Republic of Serbia, Science and Technology Park Belgrade), representatives of the University of Belgrade (Faculty of Electrical Engineering, Faculty of Mathematics, Faculty of Mechanical Engineering, Faculty of Organizational Sciences, Teacher Education Faculty, Mihajlo Pupin Institute), the University of Novi Sad (Faculty of Technical Sciences), the University of Kragujevac (Faculty of Natural Sciences and Mathematics), and the University of Ni(Faculty of Electronic Engineering), representatives of the business sector engaged in the development and implementation of AI, as well as representatives of the Vojvodina ICT Cluster, the Petlja Foundation, the Serbian Chamber of Commerce, and the World Bank. With the support of the World Bank, an international expert in this field was hired to hold consultations and a workshop with members of the Workgroup with the aim of defining the vision and objectives of the Strategy. The document is the result of a comprehensive consultation process with the representatives of all stakeholders.

title: Skills Bootcamps (AI & Digital)
body:
Free, flexible training courses of up to 16 weeks co-designed with employers, enabling adults to rapidly gain in-demand digital and AI skills, with a guaranteed job interview on completion.

Launched from Autumn 2020 as part of the UK Government's Lifetime Skills Guarantee and National Skills Fund, Skills Bootcamps are delivered across England by training providers, further education colleges, and employers in partnership with local areas. They are funded by the Department for Education (DfE) and, from 2025–26, directly through Mayoral Strategic Authorities and other local areas. The programme covers a wide range of sectors including digital (coding, cybersecurity, data analytics, AI, software development), green, construction, engineering, health and care, and HGV driving. Bootcamps offer training at Levels 3–5 (and Level 2 in some sectors), delivered online, face-to-face, or blended, and typically last up to 16 weeks. Learners must be 19 or over; the programme targets employed adults, self-employed, unemployed, and those returning to work or transitioning careers. Co-funding is required from employers for employed learners (typically 10% for SMEs, 30% for large employers). On completion, participants are guaranteed a job interview with a participating employer. In 2022–23, the DfE committed GBP 150M for Wave 3 alone. By 2024, the programme had supported hundreds of thousands of learners across England with AI and digital skills among the highest-demand areas. The programme is being progressively devolved to mayoral combined authorities and local areas from 2025–26.

title: Safe Schooling and Distance Education Project
document_name: Güvenli Okullaşma ve Uzaktan Eğitim Projesi
body:
The project aims to enhance the capacity of the education system to provide e-learning equitably to school-age children during and following the COVID-19 pandemic and future shocks. In cooperation with the World Bank Group, within the education policies of the country, it is aligned to Turkey's Education Vision 2023, MoNE's Strategy Paper 20119-2023, and the 11th Development Plan.

The COVID-19 emergency has proven that online schooling is no longer an alternative but a necessity. The project will be implemented by the Ministry of National Education (MoNE) and consists of three components: 1. Emergency Connectivity and IT Infrastructure for Education in Emergencies. This component finances the expansion of the country's e-learning platform - Digital Education Platform (EBA) - as part of MoNE's response to COVID-19. The component also supports the development and roll out of a New Digital Education System (NDES) for the future. 2. Digital Content for Safety and Quality. This component will finance goods, services, consultants, training and small refurbishments to support the distance education content, during the period of school closures due to COVID-19, for a gradual return to classroom-based teaching, and to strengthen blended teaching and learning (classroom-based and on-line). 3. Institutional Capacity for Education Technology Resilience. This component will strengthen MoNE's capacity for the coordination, management, monitoring and evaluation of the Project and for the continued delivery of safe and equitable digital education services. The project includes equity interventions for students most vulnerable to learning loss due to COVID-19 school closures. Activities to address gender-based distance education needs and risk mitigation are included, and its monitoring indicators are disaggregated by gender. In addition, it will increase the weekly use of the online distance education platform to almost 12 million K-12 students and provide certified on-line training to more than 900,000 teachers. By the end of the project, 5,000,000 students will be able to concurrently use the IT education platform, including through 100,000 on-line classrooms. he EdTech Innovation Hub, to be established, will support the development, testing and roll out of more than 30,000 new digital educational materials and pedagogical tools for K-12, special education and blended learning. Within this context, working groups for artificial intelligence education will be established, capacity building activities and R&D studies will be carried out for the application of artificial intelligence in education.The initiative has the following objectives:To enhance the capacity of the education system to provide e-learning equitably to school-age children during and following the COVID-19 pandemic and future shocks.

title: Review Into Bias in Algorithmic Decision-making
document_name: Review Into Bias in Algorithmic Decision-making
body:
The Centre for Data Ethics and Innovation (CDEI) has published its review into bias in algorithmic decision-making.

The review draws on a detailed analysis of the use of algorithms in four sectors (financial services, local government, policing and recruitment), and proposes significant measures for government, regulators and industry to take to tackle the risks of algorithmic bias. Key recommendations within the report include: Organisations should be actively using data to identify and mitigate bias. They should make sure that they understand the capabilities and limitations of algorithmic tools that they are using, and carefully consider how they will ensure that individuals are fairly treated. Government should place a mandatory transparency obligation on all public sector organisations using algorithms that have an impact on significant decisions affecting individuals. Government should issue guidance that clarifies the application of the Equality Act to algorithmic decision-making. This should include guidance on the collection of protected characteristics data to measure bias and the lawfulness of bias mitigation techniques.The initiative has the following objective(s):To issue cross-cutting recommendations that aim to help build the right systems so that algorithms improve decision-making.

title: Resolution on Automated Decision-making Processes
document_name: Resolution on Automated Decision-making Processes
body:
On 12 February 2020 the European Parliament adopted a resolution on automated decision-making processes: ensuring consumer protection and free movement of goods and services.

This resolution was adopted in 2020 and focuses on automated decision making in the context of consumer protection. It calls for a review of existing laws such as consumer law, product safety legislation and market surveillance. The document advocates for a risk-based approach to regulation that reflects different contexts and types of technology and expresses the need for additional legal safeguards. The resolution highlights the need for proper information about systems for consumers, who should be properly informed about how it functions, about how to reach a human with decision-making powers and about how the system's decisions can be checked and corrected'. The resolution also calls for additional human oversight: humans must always be ultimately responsible for, and able to overrule, decisions that are taken in the context of professional services' and the use of high-quality of data and explainable and unbiased algorithms.' The Resolution will be put before the EU Council and the Commission for consideration.The initiative has the following objectives:- To reinforce information rights of consumers when interacting with virtual assistants and chatbots, for a risk-based approach to regulation in these areas, and for internal review structures in businesses to remedy mistakes in automated decisions.

category: AI Policy Frameworks and Initiatives (intergovernmental or supranational)
title: Resolution on AI: Questions of Interpretation and Application of International Law
document_name: Resolution on AI: Questions of Interpretation and Application of International Law
body:
The European Parliament drafted a report entitled Artificial intelligence: questions of interpretation and application of international law in so far as the EU is affected in the areas of civil and military uses and of state authority outside the scope of criminal justice.

A significant portion of the report is devoted to the military uses of AI, the development of which for their armed forces is regarded as a priority by all the main global powers.  The report approaches the issue from three different angles.First of all, it reiterates the principles which should govern all military uses of AI, whatever form they may take: processing of information for military purposes, military logistics, collaborative combat' and real-time support for decision-making, defensive systems, all weapons using AI including lethal autonomous weapons systems (LAWS). Secondly, specific principles are set out for LAWS, given the threat level they pose as highlighted by the European Parliament in its resolution of 12 September 2018. Finally, the report addresses the role of the European Defence Fund, which already finances military research projects implementing AI, evidence that the EU is already directly involved in the military use of AI. Date of adoption of the resolution at the European Parliament plenary: 19 January 2021.The initiative has the following objectives:To address military uses of AI, the implications of AI for the authority of states in non-military matters and the impact of the use of AI on international private law.

title: R&D Tax Allowance
document_name: Forschungszulage
body:
A German federal R&D tax credit introduced in 2020, providing a 25% tax allowance on qualifying R&D costs for all taxable German companies (raised to 35% for SMEs from 2024), applicable to AI development and research activities.

The Forschungszulage (Research Allowance Act, FZulG) was introduced effective 1 January 2020 to align Germany with the R&D tax incentive structures of other major economies. It applies to all taxable companies in Germany, regardless of size or sector, that conduct basic research, applied research, or experimental development. Eligible costs include R&D personnel costs, external contract research costs (eligible at 70% since 2024), — from 2024 — depreciation on R&D capital assets acquired after 27 March 2024 and from 2026 overhead and other operating costs, in the form of a 20 percent flat rate of the other eligible costs incurred during the fiscal year. The standard credit rate is 25%; SMEs (fewer than 250 employees) can receive an enhanced rate of 35% (effective from 2024 under the Wachstumschancengesetz/Growth Opportunities Act). The maximum annual eligible expenses were raised from EUR 4M to EUR 10M in 2024 (yielding a maximum annual benefit of up to EUR 3.5M for SMEs); from January 2026, this cap rises further to EUR 12M (EUR 4.2M maximum for SMEs). The credit is offset against income or corporate tax; any surplus is paid as an (corporate) income tax refund, making it particularly valuable for loss-making startups. The application is a two-step process: first, obtain a project certificate from the BSFZ (Certification Office); second, claim the credit via the research allowance application at the responsible tax office. The application can be submitted up to 4 years after the entitlement to the research allowance arises. From 2025, companies can offset the credit against quarterly income or corporate tax prepayments for faster liquidity. By 2026, over EUR 2.5B had been paid out under the scheme.

The scheme grants a 10% volume‑based tax credit for eligible R&D activities, as confirmed by the OECD INNOTAX Portal, which recognises this rate as part of Italy’s current national R&D incentive framework. Alongside R&D support, Italy also offers a 5% tax credit for technological innovation, design, and creative activities for fiscal years 2024–2025, as documented by professional tax analysts examining the 2025 incentive measures. These credits apply broadly to all companies operating in Italy, including permanent establishments of non‑resident entities, without restrictions related to company size, sector, or legal form. Together, these incentives form a core component of Italy’s industrial modernization agenda, encouraging companies to integrate advanced digital technologies—such as artificial intelligence, automation, and cloud computing—into their production and innovation processes as part of their transition to Industry 4.0 and beyond.

body:
A Japanese income-deduction / deductible-expense incentive that supports corporate–startup open innovation by allowing eligible corporations to deduct up to 25% of the acquisition cost of qualifying startup shares, subject to conditions and limits.

Introduced as part of the FY2020 Tax Reform (effective 1 April 2020) and administered by METI and the National Tax Agency, the Open Innovation Promotion Tax System allows eligible blue-return corporations to deduct 25% of the acquisition cost of qualifying startup shares from taxable income in the year of acquisition, subject to statutory conditions. The deducted amount is booked to a special account and reversed into taxable income if defined trigger events occur (such as disposal of shares). Investment thresholds: a minimum of ¥100M for acquisitions in domestic Japanese startups; ¥500M for foreign-based startups; ¥10M for SMEs investing in domestic startups. The target startup must be unlisted, incorporated, and have commenced operations within the past 10 years. An M&A-type variant was added for transactions from 1 April 2023, covering majority voting-right control acquisitions. Under the FY2026 Tax Reform Outline (agreed 19 December 2025, enacted March 2026), the application period was extended by a further two years, moving the end date from 31 March 2026 to 31 March 2028.

title: OECD programme on AI in Work, Innovation, Productivity and Skills
document_name: OECD programme on AI in Work, Innovation, Productivity and Skills
body:
The OECD programme on AI in Work, Innovation, Productivity and Skills (AI-WIPS) - with the support of Germany “ analyses the impact of AI on the labour market, skills and social policy.

The OECD is working with governments around the world to try to measure and analyse the impact of AI on training needs and labour markets. This site aims to help governments to shape AI-related policies that are responsible and human-centred, and that improve individual and societal well-being.Last year's AI WIPS Conference “ the OECD International Conference on AI in Work, Innovation, Productivity, and Skills “ took place the 12 and 13 December 2024.The 2023 and 2024 International Conference on AI in Work, Innovation, Productivity, and Skills brought together leading voices from the policy, academic, business, technical and civil society communities to discuss how AI affects employment, skills, productivity, and innovation and how policymaking can respond. Alongside the implications of ChatGPT-like tools, participants discussed new OECD evidence on the impact of AI in the workplace and education, whether AI is the solution to skills shortages, risk-based approaches for AI governance and much more.AI is widely expected to complement humans in some tasks, replace them in others, generate new types of work and transform the way people organise and carry out today's work. Governments around the world are faced with managing the AI transition, and ensuring that AI is developed and deployed across economies and societies in a way that is responsible and human-centred, and that improves individual and societal well-being.The OECD AI Principles call policy makers' attention to a critical policy area: building human capacity and preparing for a fair labour market transformation. The OECD is now working to inform policy makers in implementing the AI Principles; through the OECD AI Policy Observatory, OECD.AI.Germany's support enables OECD.AI to house a dedicated Programme on AI in Work, Innovation, Productivity and Skills (AI-WIPS). This collaboration aims at producing in depth analyses, measurement, opportunities for international dialogue and concrete policy assessments on how AI impacts labour markets and societies. Through collaboration with international policy, research and business communities, as well as labour representatives and civil society, the OECD will identify necessary employment, skills and social policy reforms. The AI-WIPS benefits from synergies with the wider programme of work and policy communities that make up the OECD AI Policy Observatory.With the German AI Observatory launched by the Policy Lab Digital, Work and Society (Federal Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs), Germany is promoting public understanding, trust and acceptance of AI and developing people-centred AI policies for a changing world of work.

By connecting companies with research institutions, technology providers, and industry experts, the hubs create an environment that fosters innovation and practical experimentation.

Comprising 16 partner institutions in Vienna and Upper Austria, it offers manufacturing companies comprehensive support in digitalisation, including the development of AI-driven production processes, predictive maintenance, and optimization of operational workflows. title: National Plan for the Development of AI
document_name: Nacionalni plan za razvoj umjetne inteligencije
body:
The Croatian government is currently working on a National Plan for the Development of AI. This section will be updated with more information as soon as it is published.

The National Plan for the Development of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Croatia aims to address the growing need for a comprehensive framework that promotes the responsible development, adoption, and regulation of AI technologies across the country. As AI continues to reshape industries, economies, and societies worldwide, Croatia seeks to leverage this transformative technology to enhance its digital economy, improve public services, and ensure sustainable and inclusive growth. The initiative recognizes challenges such as skill shortages, ethical considerations, data governance, and innovation capacity, and strives to create an ecosystem conducive to AI advancement while safeguarding societal values.The primary objectives of the National AI Plan include fostering innovation through research and development, strengthening digital infrastructure, promoting AI adoption in public and private sectors, and enhancing human capital through education and skills development. The strategy also emphasizes ethical AI use, data privacy, transparency, and trustworthiness, aligning with European Union standards and global best practices. Collaboration among government agencies, academia, industry, and civil society is a central pillar, ensuring that diverse perspectives inform AI policies and practices.Looking ahead, the initiative is designed to evolve through iterative implementation phases supported by the Central State Office for the Development of the Digital Society, which coordinates multi-stakeholder engagement and monitors progress. Institutionalization involves integrating AI strategy goals into broader digital transformation efforts, with a focus on scalability and adaptability to emerging technological trends. The plan includes mechanisms for ongoing stakeholder consultations, periodic reviews, and alignment with EU AI frameworks, ensuring that Croatia remains agile in responding to new challenges and opportunities in the AI landscape.Since its adoption in late 2022, the National AI Plan has progressed from strategic formulation to active engagement with over 40 organizations spanning public authorities, business associations, academia, and civil society. This collaborative approach has facilitated a shared understanding of priorities and challenges, driving targeted initiatives in research funding, skills development, and ethical governance. The initiative continues to evolve with updates informed by technological advancements, stakeholder feedback, and international developments, positioning Croatia as a proactive player in the global AI ecosystem.

body:
The National Data Strategy will help ensure that people, businesses and organisations trust the data ecosystem, are sufficiently skilled to operate effectively within it, and can get access to data when they need it.

The Strategy sets out how best to unlock the power of data for the UK. It builds upon initiatives such as the Industrial Strategy, the AI Review, the AI Sector Deal and the Research and Development Roadmap. The government believes that unlocking the value of data is key to driving growth both within the digital sector and across the economy.A number of interconnected issues currently prevent the best use of data in the UK. These are reflected in the core pillars of this strategy:* Data foundations: The true value of data can only be fully realised when it is fit for purpose, recorded in standardised formats on modern, future-proof systems and held in a condition that means it is findable, accessible, interoperable and reusable. By improving the quality of the data, we can use it more effectively, and drive better insights and outcomes from its use.* Data skills: To make the best use of data, we must have a wealth of data skills to draw on. That means delivering the right skills through our education system, but also ensuring that people can continue to develop the data skills they need throughout their lives.* Data availability: For data to have the most effective impact, it needs to be appropriately accessible, mobile and re-usable. That means encouraging better coordination, access to and sharing of data of appropriate quality between organisations in the public, private and third sectors, and ensuring appropriate protections for the flow of data internationally.* Responsible data: As we drive increased use of data, we must ensure that it is used responsibly, in a way that is lawful, secure, fair, ethical, sustainable and accountable, while also supporting innovation and research.The initiative has the following objective(s):To drive the collective vision that will support the UK to build a world-leading data economy.

title: National AI Advisory Committee
document_name: National AI Advisory Committee
body:
The NAIAC is tasked with providing an independent assessment of the Initiative and making recommendations to the President and the NAIIO on topics related to AI R&D, ethics, standards, education, technology transfer, commercial application, security, and economic competitiveness.

The National Artificial Intelligence Advisory Committee (NAIAC) was established under the National AI Initiative Act of 2020 as part of the United States' broader strategy to promote the responsible and effective development and deployment of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies. The initiative addresses the growing need for expert, multi-stakeholder guidance on how the federal government should advance AI in alignment with democratic values, national competitiveness, innovation, and public trust. As AI becomes increasingly integral to economic development, public services, national security, and societal well-being, NAIAC's role is to ensure that U.S. AI policy is forward-looking, inclusive, and strategically coordinated.The committee advises the President and the National AI Initiative Office on a wide range of AI-related issues, including research and development priorities, ethical and trustworthy AI principles, workforce impacts, international collaboration, and regulatory frameworks. It brings together experts from academia, industry, civil society, and government to provide balanced and evidence-based recommendations. Its key objectives are to ensure U.S. global leadership in AI innovation while upholding civil liberties, enhancing public-private partnerships, and guiding national investments in AI education and infrastructure.NAIAC is expected to evolve into a permanent fixture of the federal AI governance landscape. It operates through regular meetings, public consultations, and the publication of formal reports and recommendations. Over time, the initiative aims to institutionalize ethical and policy guardrails for AI use across sectors, support the adoption of technical standards, and promote coordinated federal AI actions through transparent and inclusive policymaking. As AI technologies scale, the committee's work is crucial in guiding responsible implementation across critical domains such as healthcare, education, transportation, defense, and justice.Since its formation, NAIAC has already begun shaping national dialogue on trustworthy AI. It has issued public recommendations on AI risk management, equity, algorithmic accountability, and public sector AI adoption. Future efforts may include expanding subcommittees on specialized topics like generative AI, privacy-preserving machine learning, and AI for social good. The committee's adaptive structure and ongoing engagement with stakeholders position it to respond to fast-evolving challenges and opportunities presented by AI innovation.

body:
The Méi Weed initiative adapts a grass growth prediction model to Luxembourg’s soil and climate conditions. Delivered through a digital tool, it helps farmers manage pastures more effectively, respond to climate change, and improve both economic efficiency and sustainability.

The Méi Weed initiative, part of the EIP-AGRI (European Innovation Partnership for Agricultural Productivity and Sustainability) programme, aims to optimise grazing management in Luxembourg. By adapting an existing grass growth prediction model to the country’s pedoclimatic conditions, the project offers farmers more accurate data for planning pasture use.
Key objectives include:
Providing forecasts that help farmers adjust grazing areas and supplement livestock feedEnabling better pasture management to cope with climate change impactsImproving economic efficiency and sustainability in livestock farmingThe model is delivered through a digital tool, making it easy for farmers to access and use the forecasts in day-to-day decision-making. This innovation helps farmers not only improve productivity but also reduce environmental pressures from overgrazing and inefficient feed use.
Looking forward, the project could be expanded to integrate additional environmental indicators, link to broader EU agricultural data platforms, and support wider adoption of climate-smart farming practices across Luxembourg and potentially other regions.

title: Juri Reports on "Making AI European"
document_name: Juri Reports on "Making AI European"
body:
The European Parliament Committee on Legal Affairs (JURI) adopted reports on AI.

In early October 2020, the Legal Affairs Committee of the European Parliament (JURI) approved three reports related to artificial intelligence (AI). These reports address (i) an ethical framework for AI, (ii) civil liability for AI-related damages, and (iii) the safeguarding of intellectual property rights concerning AI.1. The first report proposes an ethical framework for AI, aimed at establishing foundational ethical principles for the development, use, and deployment of AI within the EU. The guiding principles closely align with those outlined in the Ethics Guidelines for Trustworthy AI, emphasizing safety, transparency, accountability, protection against bias and discrimination, the right to redress, social and environmental responsibility, and respect for fundamental rights. The report advocates for the European Commission to create a comprehensive and adaptable legal framework of ethical principles governing AI, robotics, and related technologies including software, algorithms, and data across the Union. It also suggests that the Commission incorporate various guiding principles for high-risk AI and related technologies into upcoming legislation, such as human oversight, transparency, accountability, non-bias, social responsibility, gender equality, environmental sustainability, and privacy considerations. Furthermore, EU law should impose specific requirements on high-risk technologies that could significantly harm individuals or violate EU fundamental rights and safety regulations. The Commission is encouraged to develop common guidance and compile a list of high-risk sectors (e.g., employment, healthcare) and high-risk applications (e.g., recruitment, automated driving, electoral processes) to identify AI technologies that require compliance assessments. The Parliament proposes that national authorities issue a European certificate of ethical compliance for technologies that meet these guiding principles, particularly regarding safety and the right to redress.2. The second report addresses liability for AI-induced damage, focusing on civil liability claims related to AI systems (led by MEP Axel Voss). This report recommends the establishment of a uniform and harmonized legal framework for civil liability claims, which would include a new regulation identifying high-risk AI systems and the critical sectors in which they operate. The Commission, with assistance from the standing Technical Committee for high-risk AI systems, should review and update this list every six months, potentially through a delegated act. The report suggests that operators of high-risk AI systems should be held strictly liable for any harm or damage resulting from activities, devices, or processes driven by those AI systems and should be required to maintain mandatory insurance coverage.
